#6227. Aer Lingus to Introduce First Premium Economy Cabin

Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

The carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

“[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”

The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

The carrier will also roll out new Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

New interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Plans call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

All seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

#6225. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#6222. Boeing Vs. Airbus Cockpits: How Yokes & Sidesticks Change The Way Pilots Fly

Michael Derrer Fuchs | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Airbus and Boeing had the same technology available and reached opposite conclusions about what to do with it. The A320 introduced a digital fly-by-wire system to a commercial airliner for the first time, and with the mechanical linkage removed, a control column was no longer technically necessary. Airbus took that option and fitted a sidestick. Boeing arrived at fly-by-wire later with the 777 and 787, had no mechanical requirement for a yoke either, but kept one.

The difference most people notice is the shape of the control. The differences that matter to the pilots flying them sit elsewhere. Boeing yokes are linked, so each pilot can see and feel the other’s inputs. No fly-by-wire Airbus has linked sidesticks. Boeing’s yokes and thrust levers move with the autopilot engaged, while an Airbus leaves both stationary and puts the information on the displays instead. The same split runs through general aviation and business jets, where Cirrus built a control that looks like a stick and works like a yoke, and Dassault put the first sidestick in a business jet in 2001.

Airbus did not start with sidesticks. Up until the A320, Airbus aircraft were designed with conventional control columns, the same arrangement found in Boeing cockpits. What changed was the A320, which introduced a digital fly-by-wire system, a first on a commercial airliner. With that system in place, a control column was no longer technically necessary.

Airbus removed it. Boeing reached fly-by-wire later and made the opposite decision, keeping the yoke on the 777 and the 787 despite neither aircraft requiring one for mechanical reasons any more than the A320 did.

What separates them is intent rather than capability. Simple Flying puts it directly: Boeing’s fly-by-wire software aims to replicate the feel of flying an aircraft with mechanical flight controls, which is not the case for Airbus aircraft. The Boeing cockpit delivers a more traditional flying experience that many pilots find engaging, at the cost of a yoke that is large and sits directly in front of the pilot. Airbus treated fly-by-wire as a reason to redesign the interface rather than to reproduce the previous one in software, and the sidestick followed from that decision rather than driving it.

The visible difference is the shape of the control. The consequential one is whether the two controls are connected to each other. The yokes in a Boeing cockpit are linked, and no fly-by-wire Airbus aircraft features linked sidesticks.

On a linked system, when the captain moves their yoke, the first officer’s yoke moves with it. Each pilot can see what the other is doing and feel it through their own control without looking across the cockpit. The arrangement is not unique to airliners. AOPA notes that in typical light aircraft with dual yokes, the controls are directly connected, with a sprocket behind each tube and a chain driving both simultaneously. A student pilot learning in a Cessna is flying a control linked to the instructor’s in essentially the same way a 787 captain’s is linked to the first officer’s, which is part of why the arrangement feels conventional to most pilots arriving at a Boeing flight deck.

On an Airbus, each sidestick is an independent input to the flight control computers, and moving one does nothing to the other. A pilot watching the other side of the flight deck sees a control that is small, mounted outboard, and largely out of view. That difference has shaped the debate around Airbus flight deck design for decades, and it is the reason active sidesticks were later developed. Whether unlinked controls represent a meaningful safety distinction or simply a different convention remains contested among pilots, and the two manufacturers have not converged on an answer.

Airbus and Boeing aircraft are built from the ground up with different design philosophies that completely change what it's like to fly them.

The second difference appears the moment the autopilot engages. On a Boeing, the yoke continues to move as the autopilot flies and the thrust levers advance and retard with the autothrottle. In a modern Airbus cockpit, neither the sidestick nor the thrust levers move when the autopilot and autothrust systems are engaged.

This is a design philosophy rather than a technical limitation. Backdriving a control is achievable engineering, and Boeing does it on aircraft that have no mechanical connection to the control surfaces either. Airbus concluded the information belongs on the displays. If a pilot wants to know what thrust the engines are producing, the answer is on the screen in numerical form rather than inferred from a lever position.

Which approach suits a given pilot depends on what they want from monitoring. Boeing’s design provides a continuous peripheral sense of the aircraft’s state without requiring anything to be read. Airbus’ design requires an active instrument scan but removes moving hardware from the flight deck and presents the data in the form the aircraft is using. This is among the first things pilots notice when switching between the two, ahead of the shape of the control itself, because a cockpit where nothing moves under automation feels substantially different from one where the hardware tracks the aircraft. The thrust levers are the clearer example of the two. On an Airbus, they sit in a detent through the entire cruise, giving no indication of what the engines are doing, while a Boeing’s advance and retard continuously as the autothrottle works.

The explanation for unlinked sidesticks is more mundane than the debate around them suggests. Such a system was not economically feasible in the 1980s when the A320 was being designed. Airbus built what the technology and the budget of the period allowed, and the arrangement has carried forward through every fly-by-wire aircraft the manufacturer has produced since.

Active sidesticks addressed the problem later. Rather than a mechanical connection, they use electric servos to link the two sticks electronically so that both move together, and the same servos can supply tactile feedback during manual flight. The Gulfstream G500 and G600 were among the first aircraft to fly them. The capability has implications beyond linking the two controls, since a stick that can push back against the pilot can also signal the edge of the flight envelope through the control itself rather than only through the displays, which is closer to what a yoke does naturally.

The most interesting case sits inside Airbus itself. Many newer aircraft, including the Airbus A220 and many business jets, include linked sidesticks. The A220 was designed by Bombardier as the CSeries and acquired by Airbus in 2018, which means its flight control system was built by a different company with a different philosophy. The result is an Airbus aircraft doing something no Airbus-designed fly-by-wire aircraft does. The technology to link sidesticks has existed for years, and Airbus has elected not to adopt it on its own designs rather than been unable to.

Explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

The same divide runs through general aviation and business jets, with some arrangements that fit neither category cleanly. AOPA traces the yoke back to at least the Curtiss 1 in 1909, and it remains the standard control in light aircraft, where most installations are mechanically interconnected between the two seats. Early aircraft used something approximating a car steering wheel, while most of today’s designs use half a wheel, and the yoke can be panel-mounted or floor-mounted in either a U shape or the less common M arrangement.

Cirrus built the notable exception. AOPA describes the side yoke as a control that looks like a stick but functions like a yoke, with distinct pushing, pulling, and turning motions, and credits Cirrus with popularizing it in general aviation. The arrangement is not an Airbus-style sidestick. It commands conventional control surfaces through mechanical linkages rather than a computer. Cirrus itself moved away from the design when it built a jet. AOPA reported that the Vision Jet replaced the SR series’ unusual side yoke with a more conventional sidestick, while the handling characteristics remained close enough that transitioning pilots found the two aircraft eerily similar.

Business jets split along manufacturer lines much as airliners do. Dassault announced the Falcon 7X at the 2001 Paris Air Show, and Aviation Week describes it as the world’s first fly-by-wire business jet, drawing on four decades of Dassault military fly-by-wire development, and the first business jet with sidestick controls. Gulfstream followed with sidesticks on the G500 and G600. Embraer went the other way, fitting conventional yokes to the E-Jet series despite the aircraft’s electronic systems.

#6220. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”

#6219. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

What do you make of this new Delta and Hyatt partnership, and American being dumped?

#6218. TAP Air Portugal Adds Major New 9-Hour US Nonstop Route: See Map Now

TAP Air Portugal has big long-haul plans for next summer, with the Portuguese flag carrier and Star Alliance member set to launch a new transatlantic route from Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport (OPO) in Porto. This route will serve Dulles International Airport (IAD) in Washington DC, with three flights a week planned using the Airbus A321LR. All of its transatlantic flights from Porto use these narrowbody twinjets.

Their long-range capabilities and lower capacity than TAP's Airbus A330 family widebodies make them a good fit for secondary transatlantic routes like these, which have enough demand but not enough to consistently fill a twin-aisle jet. There are some comfort concerns, but at least in business class, TAP puts passengers at ease with spacious flatbeds, some of which are 'thrones.'

According to AeroRoutes, TAP will begin flying from Porto to Washington on March 30, 2027. This follows the switch to the IATA Summer Schedule on March 30, with these flights operating three times a week on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. Flying westbound from Porto to Dulles, the maximum block time is eight hours 35 minutes, with flights departing relatively late in the evening for this route.

On Saturdays, TP263 departs Porto at 5:10 PM and reaches Dulles at 10:45 PM local time. Meanwhile, the Tuesday and Thursday flights depart later, at 7:20 PM, arriving in Dulles at 10:55 PM. In both cases, TAP's Airbus A321LR has just a 90-minute turnaround, with the 7.5-hour return leg, TP264, departing at 10:15 PM on Saturdays and 12:25 AM on Wednesdays and Fridays.

The A321LRs that TAP is set to use on its new flights from Porto to Dulles are relatively premium-heavy for a narrowbody twinjet, with 16 business class flatbeds located at the front of the aircraft. This reflects their use on long-haul routes, with the seats laid out in an alternating 2-2/1-1 setup, with the latter featuring single 'throne' seats. There are also 155 economy seats in the classic 3-3 configuration.

The Airbus A321LR is also the jet of choice for TAP's two existing transatlantic routes from Porto, which also serve destinations on the East Coast of the United States of America. According to current scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the airline currently links Portugal's second-largest city with Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

The Boston route operates just twice a week during the winter, but in late March, the switch to the summer schedule will double its frequency to four flights a week. The Newark route is served more or less daily all year, albeit with a slight drop in frequency to six flights a week in February. With Newark being a hub for fellow Star Alliance member United Airlines, this route has particular strategic importance.

Lufthansa officially signs its TAP acquisition agreement, positioning Lisbon as its seventh hub and targeting Latin American growth.

TAP's main hub is Humberto Delgado Airport (LIS) in Lisbon, the capital city of the western European country. Its transatlantic network is much more extensive, with nonstop flights to nine destinations in the US and another two in Canada. However, the airport's slot restrictions can limit growth opportunities, hence the importance of growing in Porto.

In terms of TAP's two Canadian routes this November, it serves Montreal three times a week and Toronto eight times a week. In the US, its top destination is currently Newark, with an average of 13 weekly departures, followed by Boston with 12 and Miami with 11. Less-than-daily flights serve Chicago, Washington Dulles, Los Angeles, New York-JFK, Orlando, and San Francisco.

#6216. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

#6215. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

#6214. 710 Pounds Of Linemen: Frontier Airlines Signs 2 College Football Stars To Launch First Class

Frontier Airlines has signed a name, image, and likeness partnership with Juan Gaston and Jahzare Jackson, who are University of Georgia offensive linemen. These college football giants are promoting the airline's new 2-2 configuration first class product.

The full first class product will be available in the first two rows of Frontier, offering legroom up to 37 inches (94 cm). Extra legroom seating will also be an option in rows three to eight, with 34 inches (86 cm) of pitch. The seats are also wider and more comfortable, resembling premium economy on a long-haul airline.

The reason for choosing the college football stars to promote the first class product is obvious. It shows that even the United States' biggest athletes can be comfortable while flying with the low-cost airline. The pair weigh in at a combined 710 pounds (322 kg) and have 13 feet and five inches (409 cm) of height between them.

Frontier launched a promotional video named 'It Comes Her,' as embedded above. It shows the pair sitting on their contracts. Jackson said “more room, no middle seat, and a contract you sign sitting down? I’m in." Gaston gave his endorsement for the seat, telling Frontier:

“When Frontier called, I didn’t expect my seat to be part of the deal. But at 6-foot-7 and 360 pounds, I take having enough room pretty seriously. This is a partnership I can get comfortable with.”

Gaston and Jackson's promotion is for Frontier's new two rows of first class that will be at the front of the aircraft. The seats have more legroom and width, and have a more comfortable construction. The 2-2 layout means there's no middle seat. Passengers can access this product with the first class bundle, starting at $129 per passenger one-way.

It also includes two checked bags, a carry-on bag, and priority boarding, and is available for flights from March 5, 2027. Alongside the first class product, the airline is also introducing extra legroom in rows three to eight. The UpFront Plus product guarantees that the middle seat is empty.

This product is also available from March 5, 2027, and can be purchased with the Premium bundle from $90 one-way.

You'll get a carry-on bag and priority boarding. Another cabin upgrade planned is at-seat power for the first eight rows, with installation beginning in 2027, with progression scheduled throughout the year. Starlink Wi-Fi installation will also be conducted throughout 2027.

The new class will include eight seats with improved legroom, more comfortable seats and priority boarding.

#6213. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6211. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

#6210. Delta Air Lines Cancels 10 International Routes: See Full List Now

Delta Air Lines has discontinued ten international routes during 2026, removing services to destinations across Europe, Canada, Mexico and the Caribbean. Five of the cancellations involve New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), while Atlanta, Minneapolis and Detroit have also lost routes. The changes primarily affect shorter-haul international services operated by narrowbody aircraft.

However, an analysis of US Department of Transportation (DOT) T-100 International Segment Data reveals a broader strategy behind the changes. Most of the canceled routes recorded load factors well below Delta's international network average, while several established routes have received substantial capacity increases. The figures suggest Delta is increasingly concentrating aircraft capacity in markets with stronger passenger demand, particularly those served from its Atlanta megahub.

The cancellations span January through October of this year, with JFK accounting for half of the affected routes. Six destinations are in the Caribbean, while Brussels, Reykjavík, Mazatlán and Vancouver complete the list. Most notably, nine of the international services were operated using narrowbody aircraft, with the route from JFK to Brussels Airport (BRU) the sole widebody exception.

The concentration of Caribbean cancellations is particularly striking. Delta has withdrawn services from several smaller leisure markets, including Antigua, Bridgetown and Kingstown. The changes illustrate how macro factors such as higher fuel costs are forcing the airline to be increasingly selective about where it deploys capacity, particularly where demand may not support year-round operations.

Not every cancellation represents a complete market withdrawal. Delta transferred its New York–Bermuda service from JFK to LaGuardia Airport (LGA), while WestJet continues operating Atlanta–Vancouver under its partnership with Delta. These distinctions matter when assessing the changes, as the removal of a Delta-operated flight does not necessarily mean passengers have lost access to nonstop service.

Passenger data helps to explain the decisions. Analysis of DOT T-100 International Segment data shows that eight of the ten discontinued routes recorded load factors below Delta's 85% international average. The weakest was Atlanta–Kingstown, at just 50.4%, followed by New York JFK–Kingston at 54.3%. These results point to significant differences in demand across Delta's international network.

The Caribbean results are particularly revealing. Bridgetown and Antigua achieved load factors of only 67.1% and 69.3%, respectively, substantially below Delta's network average. Minneapolis–Sint Maarten and Mazatlán performed somewhat better, but were only flying three-quarters full.

These figures do not establish profitability, since ticket yields and operating costs also matter, but a route operating well under the network average is far more likely to be in the red. Two routes require additional context. Detroit–Reykjavík achieved a respectable 83.1% load factor.

However, it has been withdrawn as Delta looks to re-establish the seasonal route to Iceland from its hub at Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) instead. Atlanta–Vancouver, meanwhile, recorded an exceptional 95.0%, but this was just a once-weekly Delta operation, and the route will continue to be served by daily nonstop flights by WestJet.

Delta filed seven domestic route cuts in September 2026. Each one has a specific reason, and none of them is a retreat from the airport.

The more revealing question is where Delta has been adding capacity. Comparing this year with last year reveals eight established regional international routes that have received additional seats, six of them originating from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL).

As such, rather than introducing entirely new services, Delta has been reassigning capacity to markets where passenger demand was already strong, particularly across the Caribbean and Central America. The figures show that all eight expanded routes maintained load factors above 85%, despite the addition of more capacity.

Atlanta–Providenciales recorded the largest increase, with seats rising by nearly half, while still maintaining an 86.2% load factor. In the case of the route from Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) to Vancouver International Airport (YVR), it performed even better: its load factor increased from 87.3% to 88.8%, even as its capacity increased by nearly 17%.

The net result is that, against a backdrop of volatile fuel prices and heightened economic uncertainty, Delta is prioritizing network density over network breadth. It is concentrating capacity on proven routes, rather than experimenting or spreading aircraft across newer markets. Much of that capacity is flowing through Atlanta, where Delta's enormous connecting network helps sustain consistently high load factors across its international operations.

The strategy underlines the extraordinary commercial strength of Delta's Atlanta megahub: a formidable competitive advantage that has helped make Delta the most profitable airline in the Americas. Rather than chasing marginal opportunities elsewhere, Delta is increasingly placing its bets on the money-making machine that it knows best.

#6209. JetBlue Adds New Destination in Latin America, Caribbean Expansion

JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

On Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

JetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline said.

“We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, said in a news release. “With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”

American has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently launched service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

#6208. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

#6207. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6206. Southwest Signs Interline Deal With French Bee

Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.
