It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

#6204. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6203. United Airlines Cancels All Flights To 7 Destinations: See Full List Now

United Airlines, a founding member of Star Alliance, has been continuously reviewing its route network. Just recently, Simple Flying reported that the airline had removed several routes from its third-busiest hub.

Looking at its broader network, however, it has also removed all flights to seven destinations from its summer 2027 schedule compared to this summer. Five of these are domestic destinations, including two airports in Michigan, while the remaining two are international.

According to scheduling data from aviation analytics company Cirium, United has removed all flights to five domestic destinations. These are Nantucket Memorial Airport (ACK) in Massachusetts, Yellowstone Airport (WYS) in Montana, Rhinelander–Oneida County Airport (RHI) in Wisconsin, Pellston Regional Airport (PLN), and Chippewa County International Airport (CIU) in Michigan.

Internationally, the airline has also pulled out of Tulum International Airport (TQO) in Mexico and Blaise Diagne International Airport (DSS) in Dakar, Senegal. All of these services, except Tulum, ended in recent months, as shown in the table below. The Star Alliance member’s last scheduled flight to Tulum is due to operate in January 2027.

None of these destinations currently has United flights scheduled for summer 2027. With that being said, the airline could still bring back some of these flights (such as its seasonal service to Rhinelander) for next summer. However, with the rest of its summer 2027 schedule already on sale, there is very little time for it to add these flights back.

United will operate its final flight to Tulum from Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in January 2027. This will mark its complete withdrawal from the Mexican Riviera Maya destination. The airline began serving Tulum in April 2024, just a few months after the airport opened for commercial flights in December 2023.

Following its opening, several airlines were quick to introduce flights, including United, which initially served this Mexican gateway from four hubs: Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), and Houston. However, the Star Alliance member only operated its Los Angeles service for one season and dropped Chicago last year.

It is now scheduled to end its Newark flights on January 2, followed by Houston two days later. This comes because demand for flights to Tulum has been lower than initially expected. According to US Department of Transportation (DOT) T-100 data, United's flights to the Mexican resort city recorded average load factors ranging from 60 to around 70%.

Other airlines have also reduced their services. JetBlue, for instance, which launched daily nonstop flights from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in 2024, has since discontinued the route. American Airlines and Delta Air Lines continue to serve Tulum, although the overall number of seats available on flights from the US has fallen considerably, as noted above in the table.

All these places have stopped seeing the carrier, and nearly all in September and October.

Furthermore, United's Dakar service also seems to have suffered from weak demand. The airline only began serving Senegal in May 2025, which marked its entry into the West African country. It initially offered three weekly year-round flights from Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), using its Boeing 767-300ER aircraft.

However, the Chicago-based airline decided to discontinue the service less than a year after its launch. According to US DOT data, the route recorded an average monthly load factor of just 58% across the nine months. In fact, during two of those months, the airline filled fewer than 40% of its seats.

With United's departure, Delta will be the only airline offering nonstop flights between the US and Dakar. The SkyTeam founding member operates five weekly flights from New York JFK using its 767-300ER, although this drops to three weekly during the summer season.

JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a new daily route between New York City and Dallas, the company announced this week.

The new service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb. 17, with one daily flight in each direction.

JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Those restrictions limit JSX to only selling those New York flights to members of its free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. When logged into that platform, the new route is currently bookable from TEB.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on the route, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Introductory fares start at $799 one-way.

"New York City and Dallas are two of America's most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” Alex Wilcox, CEO of JSX, said in a statement. "With this new daily service, we're bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country's most important travel corridors."

The new flight to Dallas is JSX second New York City expansion in as many weeks; the carrier announced new flights between New York and Boston earlier this month. The Dallas route is the company's fifth route from New York — aside from Boston, JSX flies from New York to Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE); Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF); Naples Airport (APF); and President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT), formerly known as Palm Beach International, all in Florida.

JSX operates out of 30 airports across the U.S. and Mexico and functions as a public charter service, rather than a formal "airline." This lets the carrier's flights work more like private ones — although anyone can buy a ticket, the flights use posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals. That allows passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. The carrier has a fleet of 56 ERJ-family jets and 4 ATR 42-600 turboprop aircraft. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

JSX passengers used to bypass security screening, like passengers on most private flights. In 2025, the carrier implemented its own in-house screening process to address security concerns.

#6201. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6200. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6199. Why The Boeing 737 MAX Is Often Heavier Than Its MTOW At The Gate

MC MEDIASTUDIO | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

On a commercial airliner, every pound weighs profit against physics. Financial margins are thin in today's aviation industry, and narrowbody aircraft like the Boeing 737 MAX frequently fly close to their maximum carrying capacity. Airlines employ a clever regulatory provision to fit every passenger, bag, and drop of fuel onto an aircraft without violating safety regulations. Extra fuel is dispensed at the gate as temporary fuel that will burn off prior to takeoff.

Because rolling on the ground and flying place different pressures on the frame, an airplane has two distinct weight restrictions from an engineering perspective. When a jet sits at the gate or taxis slowly on flat concrete, only the tires, wheels, and landing gear support the load. Because the plane moves at a walking pace, engineers certify a higher ground limit called Maximum Taxi Weight (MTW), allowing a 737 MAX 8 to weigh 182,700 pounds (82,871 kilograms) at pushback.

Takeoff demands a lower limit called Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW), which drops the allowance to 182,200 pounds (82,644 kilograms). When pilots advance the throttles to accelerate down the runway, the wings, engines, and brakes take over the workload. The aircraft must be light enough to lift off safely or climb away if one engine fails. That 500-pound (227-kilogram) difference lets dispatchers load extra taxi fuel on top of a full cabin, burning off the surplus before takeoff.

Aviation safety laws clearly distinguish between rolling slowly on pavement and accelerating down a runway. When taxiing at around 15 knots, a jet experiences slight vertical pressures that rarely exceed 1.2 times normal gravity. The primary frame and large landing gear may readily handle extra mass during this slow roll. Because the wings are not yet lifting the aircraft, engineers allow a higher ground-weight restriction without jeopardizing the aircraft's structural integrity.

For basic safety of flight, a substantially lower weight limit is mandated while taking off at high speed. If an issue arises before liftoff, the tires and brakes must be able to safely stop the aircraft once it is positioned on the runway. Additionally, the aircraft must be light enough to maneuver over surrounding hills or buildings with just one engine in the event that the other fails. The lower takeoff limit is set by these stringent safety regulations.

The amount of weight a plane can safely lift off the ground is further restricted by local weather and runway conditions. Hot summer air and high-altitude airports make the air thinner, which reduces wing lift and engine power. Wet or icy pavement also makes it much harder for the brakes to stop a heavy jet during a canceled takeoff. Because conditions change every day, pilots cannot exceed the strict takeoff limit by even a single pound.

Airlines make good use of this weight differential on crowded flights. A Boeing 737 MAX 8, which weighs about 99,360 pounds empty, hits its zero-fuel limit of 145,400 pounds when 172 passengers, luggage, and freight are added. In order to carry the required flight fuel and weather reserves without bumping paying customers, dispatchers load the aircraft to its legal takeoff limit before adding 500 pounds of specialty taxi gasoline on top.

To handle this extra weight, the flight crew employs precise ground procedures and fuel monitoring. The cabin air conditioning and electronics are powered by a small tail generator that burns about 100-200 lbs (45-90 kg) of gasoline per hour prior to pushback. The engines gradually use up the remaining buffer when the crew starts both main engines and starts taxiing. Pilots closely monitor the onboard computer weights and fuel gauges during the taxi to the runway.

Crew expertise becomes critical whether airport traffic moves faster or more slowly than expected. Pilots must hold short of the runway and burn off excess fuel before advancing the throttles if air traffic control permits the aircraft to take off right away, before the 500-pound buffer is gone. On the other hand, lengthy ground delays force the crew to closely monitor fuel levels to ensure they never run out of what is required for the actual flight.

Pilots must make a difficult choice if a traffic bottleneck on the taxiway consumes all of the buffer and begins depleting flying reserves. Before trying to fly, they had to leave the departure line and return to the gate for more fuel. Passengers experience annoying delays when returning to the terminal, but it guarantees the aircraft never takes off without the legally mandated reserves needed to reach its destination without incident.

The Airbus A321XLR and Boeing 737 MAX 10 represent the pinnacle of evolution in the aviation industry, pushing narrowbodies to their absolute limits.

Only when airport traffic moves at a typical speed does the overloaded ground fuel approach succeed. A jet consumes about 250 pounds of fuel during a normal 12-minute taxi at a busy hub, easily lowering its weight below the permitted takeoff limit. A sudden air traffic control shortcut that shortens the drive to under four minutes leaves the aircraft hundreds of pounds too heavy because both engines consume roughly 20 pounds of fuel per minute when idle.

Strict federal safety regulations prohibit pilots from starting their takeoff roll even one pound over the certified takeoff weight. When an unexpectedly fast taxi leaves the jet overweight, the flight crew faces an awkward choice. They must either turn down an immediate takeoff clearance or pull aside onto an open concrete pad to burn off the extra gas while holding the wheel brakes.

To shed that surplus weight as fast as possible, pilots advance the throttles slightly and turn the cabin air conditioning systems up to full power. The irony is clear to anyone watching from the terminal. Modern airliners operate so close to their strict structural limits that crews sometimes have to waste valuable time, runway slots, and expensive jet fuel sitting still simply because they reached the runway too early.

A closer look at how one key design choice from the 1960s still impacts the Boeing 737's performance today.

When compared to its primary European competitor, the 737 MAX's narrow weight gap is much more pronounced. Pilots have an 882-pound taxi fuel cushion, while a typical Airbus A320neo is rated for a 174,165-pound takeoff and a 175,047-pound ground limit. Boeing's 500-pound limit is almost doubled on larger aircraft like the A321neo, allowing pilots to manage congested taxiways or lengthy gate waits without depleting crucial flight reserves.

When revising the 737 design, Boeing engineers had far less flexibility. The MAX ended up roughly 7,000 pounds heavier than the older 737 model because of stronger wing supports, added fire barriers, and massive new engines mounted higher and farther forward on the wing. That extra base weight squeezed every remaining pound of structural margin out of the classic airframe.

Because Boeing could not heavily reinforce the landing gear mounts without altering the jet's low ground stance, engineers locked the ground-to-takeoff-weight gap at just 500 pounds. Keeping that buffer slim preserved valuable passenger seats and cargo space on paper. However, it leaves flight crews managing razor-thin fuel margins whenever they fly the jet at its maximum range.

A closer look at how one new jet was so controversial that it forced a fleetwide redesign.

Stretching a 1960s body design to fly long cross-country routes creates hidden trade-offs in passenger comfort. When cruising at 41,000 feet, the cabin pressure inside a 737 MAX feels like standing on an 8,000-foot mountain because its classic aluminum skin can't handle as much internal pressure. Newer rivals maintain a lower cabin altitude, around 6,500 feet, leaving MAX travelers with slightly less oxygen and noticeably more fatigue after landing.

Cabin moisture is another victim of that traditional metal construction. Because aluminum frames can corrode if moisture collects inside the wall insulation, engineers cannot pump extra humidity into the air system. During long five-hour flights at maximum takeoff weight, cabin humidity drops to roughly 10%, making the air drier than most deserts and leaving passengers feeling dehydrated.

Pushing the 737 MAX to its absolute ramp weight limit allows airlines to carry nearly 180 passengers and cross-country fuel on a single-aisle jet. Those impressive economics keep ticket prices competitive and routes profitable for carriers. However, that efficiency comes at a physical cost, asking travelers to endure a drier, higher-altitude cabin than newer jets flying the same routes.

#6198. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

#6197. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6195. American Airlines Launches 9 New International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Fort Worth-based American Airlines is set to add nine new international routes in 2027, as the carrier expands its reach to Europe, Asia, and South America. The airline's first new service will be between Miami and Venezuela, while Chicago to Tokyo will be the first long-haul route added in March.

Using data from Cirium, an online aviation analytics company, the oneworld carrier will gradually add services in 2027 between January and late May, with a mix of the Embraer E175, Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, 777-200ER, Airbus A321XLR and A321neo.

Nonstop flights from Miami to Barcelona, Venezuela will launch on January 15. The services to General Jose Antonio Anzoategui International Airport will begin three times weekly on the E175. This is the shortest flight in this analysis, and the only service with American Eagle-operated aircraft.

Tokyo Narita will be connected nonstop from Chicago this March. The airline will begin the daily 787-9 service on March 19; American will become the fourth airline on the route after All Nippon Airways (ANA), Japan Airlines (ending in late March), and United Airlines. American already serves Tokyo Narita from Dallas/Fort Worth.

Charlotte to Barcelona is up next, with March 27 scheduled for the airline's first flight between the North Carolina city and the Catalan capital. These flights will run daily on the airline's 777-200ER. These flights will join year-round services to Barcelona from Miami and Philadelphia, with seasonal additions from Chicago, Dallas/Fort Worth, and New York-JFK.

In 2027, American will leverage the long-range capabilities of the Airbus A321XLR to add European destinations to its network. This begins in March, with the airline adding nonstop flights from New York-JFK to Amsterdam. These flights are scheduled to run daily.

Porto is the airline's latest Portuguese connection, with the narrowbody aircraft able to fly nonstop from Philadelphia to Porto, a city famed for its downtown core UNESCO World Heritage Site. These routes are scheduled to operate once daily in each direction.

From New York-JFK, nonstop flights are set to begin to Nice, connecting the French Riviera to the Big Apple. These services will begin on May 6 and operate daily. The final A321XLR route to be added will fly between Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Vienna, Austria (VIE). This service will also begin on May 6 and operate daily.

American Airlines launched six new nonstop transatlantic routes in 2026, connecting US hubs with Edinburgh, Budapest, Prague, Athens, Zurich and Milan

American is set to return to the Levant, with the oneworld carrier scheduling nonstop flights from New York to Tel Aviv from March 27. These services are set to operate daily on the 777-200ER and will be the first time the airline has operated to the region since tensions saw major US carriers withdraw service. United and Delta have already resumed operations to Tel Aviv, with American the last of the US legacy carriers to return.

Nonstop flights to Iceland are the last of the nine international routes American plans to add in the first half of next year. Direct flights from Philadelphia to Keflavik, Iceland's primary international gateway, will take off on March 27 and operate daily on the A321neo.

If you’re eligible for the card, there’s no reason not to apply.

This is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and it’s arguably Chase’s most rewarding and best value business credit card. In this post I’d like to go over the Ink Business Preferred bonus details, including eligibility requirements.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card with 100K bonus points

The Chase Ink Preferred Card currently has a welcome offer of 100,000 Ultimate Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

#6193. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6192. Allegiant Air Drops 34 Airports In 10 Years: See Full List Now

Allegiant Air carried more than 157 million scheduled passengers in the past decade, all of whom were domestic. Some context is needed. In this period, all US airlines had eight billion domestic passengers. As such, Allegiant only transported around 2% of the market.

Despite carrying one in 50 passengers, Allegiant continues to play a major role in leisure markets, particularly involving small and medium-sized cities, just like Volotea in Europe. Allegiant's dominance will increase slightly following the acquisition of Sun Country by the Allegiant Travel Company.

All airlines have route and airport churn, and this ultra-low-cost carrier is no exception. ULCCs are particularly renowned for greater churn. Some say this is because of their dartboard approach to network planning, while others believe it is because they are more entrepreneurial in what they try. They may also have less tolerance for what does not work.

Between January 2016 and October 2026, Cirium Diio data shows that Allegiant stopped flying to all the following places. The list does not include Minneapolis, as Allegiant is returning there in 2027. Chicago Midway, which the airline is ditching in 2027, is also not featured. Allegiant itself will no longer serve Chicago (Rockford is far away), but Sun Country will, just at O'Hare.

Eliminated Market Served By Allegiant (Excluding Sun Country)

Casper, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, Youngstown

Albuquerque, Amarillo, Cleveland, Ogden, Raleigh-Durham, Redmond, State College

Baltimore, Gulfport/Biloxi, Reno, San Antonio

El Paso, Grand Junction, Norfolk, San Diego

Columbia (SC), Los Angeles International, Oakland, Palm Springs

The cuts mean that Allegiant has pulled out of some states entirely. They include Alaska, Hawaii (for which the short-lived Boeing 757 was used), New Mexico, Vermont, and Wyoming, along with the US territory of Puerto Rico. Naturally, the airline no longer serves most areas at all. For example, it pulled out of the San Francisco Bay after ditching Oakland. Stockton, which remains part of Allegiant's network, is not part of the Bay Area.

The ULCC's debut in Alaska took place in May 2019, exactly seven years before the arrival of Southwest Airlines in the Last Frontier. Allegiant operated from Bellingham, located between Seattle and Vancouver, to Anchorage for just one season. Departures existed between May 22 and September 2, 2019, with just 31 takeoffs, all on the Airbus A319. It was the first and only time that Bellingham had scheduled flights to Alaska.

US Department of Transportation data shows that Allegiant carried 6,272 round-trip passengers on what was a brand-new route. As usual, this is just a number, and says little in itself. When related to seats for sale, the load factor was just 67.2%. Given the poor result, even for a new market, it's no wonder it was cut so quickly. While fare information is unavailable, whatever was achieved was clearly insufficient.

They include three airports brand-new to the carrier's map. Find out more here!

Between January 2016 and October 2026 only, Allegiant had a total of 49,955 from the 34 airports that are no longer part of its network. Of course, the number would be even higher if the time frame were expanded beyond a decade. With 13,391 of them, Los Angeles International was utterly critical. The airport accounted for more than a quarter of the total departures.

Los Angeles International joined Allegiant's network in 2009. But focusing on 2016-2026, 40 routes were served, with more flights to Bellingham than anywhere else. The carrier pulled out in January 2026. In the first ten months of 2027, analysis shows that 23 of the 40 destinations will have nonstop flights by at least one carrier. Moreover, some of them are now served by Allegiant from the other LA Basin airports that it serves, whether Burbank, Orange County, or both.

#6190. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

#6189. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.
