#6188. Why United Airlines Is Betting On Premium To Bring Revive Popularity Of 50-Seater Jets

Habanero Pixel | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

United Airlines is attempting something that might have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: making the widely disliked, aging 50-seat regional jet attractive to passengers again. Instead of abandoning the 20-year-old Bombardier CRJ200, the Chicago-based carrier is transforming it into a substantially more luxurious aircraft, complete with a first class cabin, extra-legroom seating, and high-speed satellite internet.

The resulting CRJ450 represents an unusual strategy in an industry focused on larger regional aircraft and premium-heavy cabins. But why is United investing in an aircraft with just 41 seats when other airlines have been moving away from 50-seater jets? The answer involves pilot union agreements, regional connectivity, the CRJ550's success, and United's ambitions to attract higher-paying passengers even on its smallest routes.

United's decision to introduce the CRJ450 is primarily about making its regional network more profitable without sacrificing connections to smaller communities. The aircraft is a heavily reconfigured Bombardier CRJ200 operated by SkyWest Airlines under the United Express brand. Rather than purchasing an entirely new aircraft, United is giving an existing regional jet a different commercial purpose by replacing its traditional 50-seat economy configuration with a 41-seat, three-cabin interior. The move also demonstrates that the airline believes there is still a place for smaller regional aircraft when the onboard experience is sufficiently attractive.

Timing is notable because 50-seat regional jets have struggled with passenger perceptions for years. Frequent flyers have often nicknamed the CRJ200 the Devil's Chariot, reflecting its cramped cabin, limited overhead storage, and relatively uncomfortable experience. Its narrow fuselage and 2-2 seating arrangement leave little room for the amenities passengers expect, particularly those traveling in premium cabins. According to The Points Guy's coverage of the CRJ-450 and Runway Girl Network, United intends to address these shortcomings through a comprehensive interior redesign.

However, the CRJ450 is not an attempt to make an old aircraft a private jet with flamboyant luxury. Its introduction reflects a structural limitation affecting United's regional operations: agreements with its pilots limit how many larger regional jets it can deploy. This raises the question of why United cannot simply replace its smallest aircraft with larger jets.

The explanation lies in pilot scope clauses: contractual provisions negotiated between major US airlines and their pilot unions. These agreements regulate the number and characteristics of aircraft that regional partners can operate on behalf of mainline carriers. United faces particularly restrictive limitations on larger regional aircraft, while its contractual framework provides considerably more flexibility for 50-seat jets. Consequently, retiring every smaller regional aircraft would not necessarily be practical, even if larger jets offered better passenger economics.

United previously demonstrated how it could work around this limitation with the CRJ550, introduced in 2019. Based on the larger Bombardier CRJ700, the aircraft was reconfigured from its conventional 70-seat arrangement into a 50-seat aircraft with three cabins. It offered eight First class seats, 16 Economy Plus seats, and 26 standard economy seats, along with additional luggage storage. The strategy lets United offer a more premium experience while keeping the aircraft in the 50-seat category. The Points Guy explains the contractual advantage in its analysis of United's CRJ-450 business case.

The CRJ-450 takes the same principle further, this time using the smaller CRJ200 airframe.

United may not be choosing the CRJ450 over a larger aircraft solely because of passenger capacity. Instead, it is opting for the aircraft category that offers the greatest contractual flexibility. Still, keeping 50-seaters in the fleet only makes commercial sense if passengers are willing to fly on them. The CRJ450's redesigned cabin could help make that possible.

The modified CRJ200 will feature many premium uprades.

One of the biggest changes to the CRJ200 is in the cabin, not the engines or airframe, which remain the same. United is removing nine seats from the original 50-seat layout to create three cabins: seven United First seats, 16 Economy Plus seats, and 18 standard economy seats. The new layout changes how the aircraft is marketed, giving passengers the option to buy a first class seat on one of United's smallest regional aircraft.

The redesign follows the philosophy behind the CRJ550, although United is making more substantial changes to the passenger experience on the smaller aircraft. According to Upgraded Points' CRJ450 cabin tour and Live And Let's Fly, the objective is to make the aircraft feel considerably more spacious despite retaining the narrow CRJ200 fuselage. However, removing nine seats raises another question: can the additional premium revenue offset the reduction in passenger capacity?

United's decision becomes easier to understand when viewed against the airline's extensive history of regional aircraft operations. United Express has relied on numerous aircraft families over the decades, ranging from small turboprops to larger regional jets. These aircraft have allowed the airline to serve communities that could not consistently support mainline Boeing or Airbus services while feeding passengers into major hubs.

Historical United Express fleets have included aircraft such as the ATR 42 and ATR 72, British Aerospace BAe 146 and Avro RJ, BAe ATP, Jetstream 31 and 32, Jetstream 41, Dornier 328, de Havilland Canada Dash 8, Embraer EMB-120 Brasilia, and Saab 340. United Express also operated several generations of regional jets, including the Bombardier CRJ100, CRJ200, and CRJ700, as well as the Embraer ERJ-135, ERJ-145, E170, and E175. Each type served a different operational need, based on route demand, aircraft availability, and the economics of connecting smaller markets.

Planespotters.com's United Express fleet overview illustrates the range of aircraft operated over time. It lists 901 historic aircraft across the regional fleet categories and 480 currently in service. Of those, 78 are Bombardier CRJ200s. These figures show that the aircraft family remains part of the regional aviation network.

With 50 seats, the CRJ200 enabled regional operators to connect smaller cities with major hubs without relying on the passenger demand required to fill larger aircraft. United later expanded its regional operations with the ERJ145 and CRJ700, while the E170 and E175 offered more capacity and a newer passenger experience. The CRJ550 showed how an existing airframe could be adapted for a premium product. Now, the CRJ450 applies that approach to the smaller CRJ200, potentially giving the aging aircraft family another role in United's network.

But the aircraft's historical importance is only part of the story. Its real value will depend on where United deploys it and whether smaller communities can generate enough premium demand.

United plans to use the CRJ450 to connect smaller communities with its major hubs, particularly Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and Denver International Airport (DEN). These airports are key connection points for passengers traveling beyond the airline's regional network, including those connecting to domestic transcontinental and international services. The CRJ450 will do more than move passengers between two smaller cities: it will help United sell premium itineraries that begin or end in markets with limited air service.

Connecting big cities with smaller communities remains critical to the airline's network. The first CRJ450 is expected to enter passenger service through Chicago O'Hare in December 2026, with smaller destinations such as Akron-Canton and Fort Wayne among the potential markets The Points Guy discussed. SkyWest will operate the aircraft under the United Express brand, with a multi-year agreement covering the first 40 aircraft.

The commercial argument is compelling for passengers connecting to international flights. A business traveler departing from a smaller Midwestern community could purchase a single itinerary featuring United First on the regional segment and United Polaris on a subsequent long-haul flight. Previously, the regional portion of that journey might have involved a cramped, economy-only CRJ200. United is effectively extending its premium positioning to the first and last stages of the journey rather than concentrating its investment exclusively on larger aircraft.

The CRJ450 also fits into United's wider premium expansion strategy. In March 2026, the airline announced plans to add more than 250 aircraft over the following two years, alongside new premium configurations for its Airbus A321neo and A321XLR fleets and its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. United reported that premium seats per North American departure had increased by 40% since 2021. Nevertheless, converting older regional jets introduces another challenge: the aircraft must remain economically viable despite its reduced seating capacity and substantial interior modifications.

The CRJ450's biggest advantage is that United does not need to develop an entirely new aircraft to introduce the product. It can use existing CRJ200 airframes, after the necessary interior modifications. This provides an alternative to purchasing new regional aircraft, although conversion costs, maintenance requirements, and the age of the underlying airframes will remain important considerations.

SkyWest is targeting approximately 50 CRJ200 conversions by 2028, while its agreement with United covers 40 aircraft. The first two conversions were still underway in November 2026, and SkyWest expected subsequent modifications to take about two to three weeks per aircraft. According to Aviation Week, the regional operator sees the program as a longer-term investment in a premium product. SkyWest executives have also suggested that demand for converted aircraft could eventually extend beyond the initial United program.

The financial test will be whether the additional revenue from seven First class seats and 16 Economy Plus seats offsets the nine fewer passengers the aircraft can accommodate. Lower passenger capacity also means less weight, which SkyWest's management identified as a potential fuel-related advantage. United will additionally have to demonstrate that passengers are willing to pay premium fares on relatively short regional journeys, rather than simply appreciating the improved cabin without generating additional revenue.

The CRJ450 is an unusual attempt to extend the commercial life of an aircraft that many passengers would rather avoid. Its success could encourage further regional aircraft conversions, particularly as airlines search for ways to offer differentiated products without waiting for entirely new aircraft programs. Whether United can turn the Devil's Chariot into a genuinely desirable premium product will become clearer once the aircraft begins operating regularly across its regional network.

#6187. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#6186. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

In January 2026, Lufthansa formally announced plans to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks…

Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and currently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its new Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”

With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

In recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

Lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the new Allegris seats up there.

For once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the new Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a new business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

Rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

Lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

The  is getting a significant overhaul, pairing a higher annual fee with new Atmos Rewards earning rates and a collection of perks for businesses that regularly fly on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

Starting Nov. 18, new applicants can earn 10 points per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos™ for Business, receive four Alaska Lounge passes annually and work toward flight discounts and bonus status points through spending.

The biggest winners may be companies with multiple employee cardholders that regularly book Alaska or Hawaiian flights. They'll pay a flat $195 annual fee regardless of how many employee cards they issue, while benefiting from new travel perks.

However, the refresh also eliminates some valuable benefits, including the annual $99 Companion Fare and the $100 discount on an Alaska Lounge+ membership. Existing cardholders won't automatically transition to the new version and can keep their current benefits.

New applicants can earn a limited-time offer of 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening, worth about $1,440 based on TPG's November 2026 valuations. By point total, that's the largest offer in TPG's recorded history for the card, but it's not the richest because the new offer doesn't include Alaska's famous $99 Companion Fare.

Starting Nov. 18, the Atmos Rewards Business card will feature a new flat annual fee regardless of the number of cards, stronger rewards on flights booked through Atmos for Business and several new travel-day perks.

Annual fee: $195 for the company, with no additional fee for employee cards (was previously $70 + $25 per card, including for the primary cardholder)

The refresh also takes a few things away.

New cardholders will no longer earn 2 points per dollar spent on gas, electric vehicle charging, shipping and local transit/ride-hailing. New cardholders will also lose the ability to earn the annual Companion Fare through card spending and the $100 discount on an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership.

Overall, the theme is clear: The refreshed card concentrates its value around Alaska and Hawaiian travel, especially for companies willing to book through Atmos for Business and issue cards to multiple employees.

If you opened your before Nov. 18, 2026, you won't automatically receive the refreshed benefits or move to the new annual-fee structure.

Instead, Bank of America says existing cardholders will keep their current benefits, including the opportunity to earn the annual $99 Companion Fare under the previous card's terms.

If you're interested in switching to the refreshed card, you can call Bank of America at 1-800-892-3219 to explore your options.

Applications submitted before Nov. 18 will also remain under the previous card offering, even if they're still pending.

One of the biggest changes is the new annual-fee structure.

The previously charged $70 per company plus $25 per card, including the owner’s card. Now, it’s a flat $195 regardless of how many cards you have. A solo business owner will now pay more than double what they paid before, a company with five cards pays the same as before, and one with six or more pays less. This is arguably the most significant part of the refresh.

Each cardholder will continue to receive a free checked bag for themselves and up to six guests on the same reservation when the flight is paid for with the card. They also receive preferred boarding on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

That could make the card particularly appealing to small businesses with several West Coast or Hawaii-based road warriors. The more employees who consistently use the travel benefits, the easier it becomes to justify the companywide fee.

Solo owners who do not need employee cards may find one of the personal Atmos cards better suited to their needs.

In that case, you won't earn points from business spending, but you can enjoy similar perks with the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card for a lower annual fee or take advantage of more generous benefits (albeit with a higher fee) on the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card.

However, neither is a direct replacement for a business card, particularly for owners who want to separate business expenses or issue employee cards.

Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: The Summit is better—but not for everyone

In addition to checked-bag and preferred-boarding perks, the refreshed card will include one Alaska Lounge pass per calendar quarter, for a total of four per account anniversary year. That cadence is best suited to a consultant or salesperson who flies throughout the year, rather than a company whose only major trip is an annual conference.

Meanwhile, the waived fee for same-day confirmed changes ($50 on most Alaska flights) could be particularly useful for employees whose meetings finish early, run late or move unexpectedly. That practical flexibility may save some employees frustration — and save the business itself money on fees.

The card also adds a $50 Instant Travel Delay Credit voucher, which can be used toward a meal or drink at the airport when an eligible flight is canceled or delayed by at least two hours on the day of travel.

Despite the new higher fee, even a solo business owner could potentially offset much of the $195 annual fee through these travel benefits. Someone who checks a bag on two round-trips would save $180; visit a lounge on each of those trips and you'll save another $130 compared to buying day passes.

Related: Alaska Airlines airport lounges: How to get access to this VIP space

Earning 10 points per dollar sounds exceptional, but it only applies to flights booked through the Atmos for Business website, the airlines’ self-managed booking platform. That means companies that don't qualify for Atmos for Business — it requires a minimum of $5,000 in annual travel spend — or businesses that book through a corporate travel agency or another platform won't earn this higher return.

Other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases earn 3 points per dollar spent, dining earns 2 points per dollar spent and everything else earns 1 point per dollar. Companies with an eligible Bank of America business account also receive a 10% bonus on points earned from card purchases, effectively turning the 10-point rate into 11 points per dollar.

Lastly, travelers who select the Price Paid earning option and hold Atmos Platinum or Titanium status can earn 20 points or more per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos for Business.

The card's weak general spending rate makes it better suited as a secondary card specifically for Alaska and Hawaiian spending than as a business’s only credit card.

The refreshed no longer includes its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23), which cardholders prior to Nov. 18 earned after spending $6,000 during an account anniversary year.

That is a significant loss for owners who could redeem it for two travelers flying together. Four lounge passes and same-day change flexibility may be more useful for employees traveling alone, but they aren't an automatic replacement for a Companion Fare.

While the new discounts could be valuable for businesses with substantial spending, the $100,000 threshold is significantly higher than the previous $6,000 requirement for earning a Companion Fare.

The welcome offer drops the Companion Fare too, but it includes more points than past offers. Its 90,000 points are enough for three round-trip economy tickets between the West Coast and Hawaii on Alaska or Hawaiian, a one-way ticket on American Airlines in transatlantic business class or a round-trip premium economy ticket from Seattle to Tokyo on an Atmos partner airline.

The refreshed Atmos Rewards Business Card has a higher starting price, but it also has a clearer identity: It's built for companies with multiple cardholders and for recurring Alaska or Hawaiian travel.

Businesses that need employee cards, book substantial airfare through Atmos for Business and have employees who can use the lounge passes and same-day change waiver may come out well ahead.

However, the loss of the Companion Fare and several business spending bonus categories makes the card less appealing for some existing cardholders.

Sole proprietors or companies that don't book through Atmos for Business may still have a case for the card, but they'll need to run the numbers more carefully. And companies that rarely fly either airline or primarily need rewards on everyday operating expenses will likely find the card too specialized.

#6183. JetBlue Cancels All Flights To 6 Destinations: See Full List Now

JetBlue continues to undergo many changes. Despite this, OAG data shows that the carrier has 892 daily movements (takeoffs and landings combined) in November, up 4% compared to the same month last year.

Benefiting from the end of the now-defunct Spirit, JetBlue's domestic activity has risen by 8% in 12 months, especially at Fort Lauderdale (+57%). In contrast, international service has fallen by 9%. Like with most airlines, various airports have been dropped recently.

The carrier's network between January and October 2026 was compared to what's available from November 2026. This process identified that the following US airports have been removed. They were not served for long. None were significant, at least not to JetBlue. But the airline was important for them.

Initially between January 2016 and January 2019. Returned in December 2025 but pulled out in September 2026

Boston and New York JFK. Boston only had flights in 2025 and 2026

Fort Lauderdale, Fort Myers, New York JFK, Orlando

In the first nine months of 2026, JetBlue had 17% of the flights at Daytona Beach (18% of the seats due to higher-capacity equipment). It also provided the only service from Boston and JFK to the Florida destination. Delta still flies from LaGuardia, but that is it for the Big Apple.

JetBlue had a smaller role at Manchester-Boston Regional Airport, which is by far New Hampshire's busiest facility. Between January and July 2026, JetBlue had 6% of the services but 10% of the seats for sale. However, Manchester no longer has nonstop service to Fort Lauderdale or New York JFK. The short link to JFK was surely partly for slot-sitting purposes, although also for those transiting elsewhere.

All of these places saw the airline at some point between January and October this year but no longer do so. With JetBlue's exit, only one of the four destinations remains served from New York JFK. That's Antigua, which remains served by American Airlines. Delta Air Lines ended flights in May 2026. However, United Airlines flies from Newark to Antigua, Bonaire, Belize City, and Tulum, although all flights to Tulum will end in January 2027.

The US Department of Transportation shows that JetBlue transported a total of 91,226 round-trip passengers between New York and Tulum. The load factor was a paltry 70.4%, against 83.2% for the airline's overall network from JFK to Mexico. More than half of the months that had Tulum flights saw fewer than seven in ten seats filled. Fare data is unavailable.

Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula and has been a growing tourist destination for years. This is despite what seem to be clear problems, such as sewage and very high-priced taxis. Historically, people traveled there via Cancun. But despite the opening of Tulum's airport, ground transport from Cancun appears to be easier than ever.

The carrier wants to fly to this European airport, but slots are a major problem. Find out more here!

Let's narrow the focus to November 2026. As mentioned earlier, JetBlue's activity at Fort Lauderdale has jumped by a considerable 57% year-on-year. This development played a critical role in the airline's domestic growth. Other major airports grew much more shallowly or declined, such as Boston (+4%) and JFK (-14%).

JetBlue really benefited from the exit of Spirit at the South Florida airport. Last November, Fort Lauderdale was JetBlue's third most-served airport. Now it is first, also influenced, of course, by the decline at JFK. The growth at Fort Lauderdale was driven by the number of routes jumping from 37 last November to 61 now. On November 19, the airline will begin flying to San Diego.

#6182. Amex Gold Card Credits: How To Maximize $424 In Uber, Dining, Resy, & Dunkin’ Value

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the best cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it also has an excellent welcome offer. The card is ideal for anyone who spends a lot on dining, whether at restaurants or supermarkets, and in my experience, getting approved for the card is quite easy.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), though the card also offers up to $424 in annual credits, which could more than offset the annual fee, not even accounting for all the other perks.

Now, a vast majority of cardmembers aren’t going to maximize all the Amex Gold Card credits, since it is a bit of a “coupon book” vibe, in terms of how the credits are issued. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Amex Gold Card credits, including the restrictions, and how they can be redeemed.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

With the Amex Gold Card credits, cardmembers can potentially receive statement credits with Uber, select dining establishments, Resy, and Dunkin’. The terms associated with using each of these Amex Gold credits varies, so it’s worth covering all the details. Below is a chart with the basics, and then I’ll cover all the credits in more detail.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit? As someone who uses both Uber and Uber Eats more than once per month, the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit benefit is basically as good as cash to me. Obviously if you don’t use Uber or Uber Eats that often, try to remember to use it earlier in the month, so you don’t forget to use it later on. That’s especially true if you have international travel plans, given that the credit only works in the United States.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in dining credits annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold dining credit? Everyone has different spending patterns. Personally, I don’t frequently dine at any of the establishments included with the Amex Gold dining credit, though I do use Grubhub once in a while. So when I can remember to use the perk, that saves me $10 per month on those purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

Let me emphasize that you don’t have to jump through hoops at a restaurant to take advantage of the Amex Gold Resy statement credit. You don’t even have to make your reservation through Resy, as long as it’s a Resy partner restaurant.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Resy credit? If you dine out frequently and live in a decently sized city, visiting a Resy restaurant should be super easy. Personally I’m able maximize this without even trying, since I go to restaurants associated with Resy all the time.

Admittedly, this is of limited use to those in small towns, where not many restaurants may use the Resy platform. In those situations, remember to consider Resy restaurants when you’re traveling to a larger city, as that’s your best bet for maximizing that perk.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

You can maximize the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit by spending at least $7 per month at a Dunkin’ location with your eligible card.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit? Admittedly, this is niche, and seems like an odd fit for a premium card. Dunkin’ isn’t exactly a high-end brand, and the $7 credit seems quite random. However, I think this is easy enough to manage. It’s also worth emphasizing that as of now, simply loading your Dunkin’ account through the Dunkin’ app with $7 per month seems to trigger the credit.

Based on how I read the terms, that’s not even a fluke. The terms say the credit can’t be used for gift cards, though loading a Dunkin’ account isn’t a gift card. So as things currently stand, basically view this as an $84 annual Dunkin’ credit (which you must load monthly, but the credit as such won’t expire).

Just about any credit card with perks that are distributed throughout the year and where enrollment is required will have a significant amount of breakage. That’s only natural, and as I see it, it’s a double-edged sword. On the plus side, I view it as an opportunity for savvy consumers to get outsized value from a card. At the same time, “credit card fatigue” is a very really concept.

With that in mind, how much do I value the up to $424 in credits offered on the Amex Gold Card? Here’s my general thought process:

When all is said and done, I’d say that I value the credits on the Amex Gold Card as maybe being within $100 of the card’s annual fee, give or take. To me, that essentially puts this Membership Rewards points-earning powerhouse in line with other mid-range cards, in terms of the cost of holding onto it. Everyone’s math will differ, so crunch the numbers to decide how much value the card offers to you.

The Amex Gold Card is a product you primarily get for the excellent return it offers on everyday spending. The card has a steep annual fee, though the good news is that this can largely be offset thanks to the up to $424 in annual credits it offers. Hopefully, the above is a useful rundown of how each of the Amex Gold Card credits can be used.

The Amex Gold credits won’t be equally valuable for everyone, but if you dine at Resy restaurants and use Uber (for rides or food delivery) with any frequency, you should be able to recoup much of the annual fee thanks to the credits.

What do you make of the Amex Gold Card credits, and how much value are you able to get out of them?

#6181. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

#6179. Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story…

Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only showed as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

But anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

As I said above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

#6178. Independents decide the election, again!

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6177. Park Hyatt Brisbane Opening 2031, As Brand’s Fourth Australia Hotel

Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

Hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

There are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:

“The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”

There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

World of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:

The area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any…

The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

It’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.

Flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying. More than 18,000 flights were canceled between Friday and Sunday, affecting millions of travelers. It appears there will be no spillover from that meltdown into the big Thanksgiving travel week that’s on the horizon, though.

It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.

But there are plenty of worries about the possibility of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.

And that’s a stressful and costly reality whether you’re a passenger, a crew member, an airline executive or a front-line aviation worker.

In recent years, travelers have gotten one reminder after another about how strained our aviation infrastructure is.

For years, the Federal Aviation Administration has been plagued by both severely outdated technology and short staffing in air traffic control.

Those concerns have grown even louder in the wake of several recent incidents.

After 9/11, the U.S. went more than 20 years without a nationwide ground stop like the one we saw on Friday.

We’ve now seen two happen since 2023. Both instances involved outages to critical FAA systems.

Meanwhile, the vital air traffic control workforce that directs the flow of planes in our airspace has been chronically understaffed. Controllers routinely work six-day weeks and mandatory overtime.

Together, these problems have fueled several of the most high-profile air travel disruptions in recent memory.

Last fall, ATC staffing was a major factor in the mass flight cancellations and delays we saw at the height of the government shutdown.

In 2025, equipment outages plus undermanned air traffic control centers contributed to the weeks of chaos travelers endured at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

In the wake of the latest technology failure on Friday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford was asked bluntly whether he could say for certain that there wouldn’t be a repeat of this past weekend’s chaos.

“I can say with certainty that the system is really, really old,” he told CBS News Tuesday.

“Let’s not kid ourselves,” Bedford added. “This system has been fragile, and it does go down.”

There has been momentum to fix both problems, which have festered for decades under the leadership of both political parties.

In recent years, the FAA has upped its air traffic control hiring efforts, in a push to reduce long-standing vacancies.

Meanwhile, Congress last year earmarked $12.5 billion for infrastructure upgrades.

The Department of Transportation has started that work, but says it needs a lot more money to make truly sweeping upgrades.

The travel sector has broadly supported that request: “They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wrote in a social media post Sunday.

But securing that funding will hinge on political dealmaking in Washington, D.C., which in January will be led by a divided government.

And however that fight ends, these problems won’t be solved overnight.

It takes years to fully train air traffic controllers.

And to add to the complexity, overhauling aviation infrastructure while tens of thousands of flights operate each day is painstaking work with significant consequences — even if the money is there in the first place.

Look no further than last week’s FAA outage, where crews replacing a router apparently triggered a chain-reaction outage that upended air travel in the U.S. for days — a disruption American Airlines now counts among the most significant in its 100-year history.

“The transition itself needs to be carefully analyzed and tested,” said Capt. Shem Malmquist, a longtime Boeing 777 captain and visiting professor at the Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics. “Otherwise, an upgrade intended to solve one problem can introduce another."

Despite all the concerning headlines, industry experts largely agree:

“Both things can be true,” Malmquist said, pointing to the many safety layers that allow planes to safely operate even when problems arise.

Keep in mind: Every plane that was in the sky during last week’s FAA disruption landed safely.

And the move to halt thousands of flights? That was ultimately meant to protect travelers, leaders have emphasized.

"Passengers experience delays and cancellations, but those restrictions help keep the system safe," Malmquist said. “That doesn’t mean the underlying vulnerabilities are acceptable.”

Remembering God’s gift to New York City girls and beyond.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. It also captures the quiet steadiness of Sister Martha Kunesh, O.P. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. She took the religious name Sister Teresa Avila (“the ‘of’ was silent,” it was said). She eventually returned to her birth name, but she never lost the contemplative spirit of her first patron.

#6173. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

#6172. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)…

When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”

Meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a company identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”

In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:

While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order…

Aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”

For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

Starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the company’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

South African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

The callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

#6171. Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie said. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor."
