#6170. LATAM Unveils New Airbus A321XLR Business Class Suites, Coming March 2027

LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the new long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

The airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”

Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

We can expect LATAM to offer an all-new passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:

Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

While American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”

While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

In early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is currently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two new wide body business class products over the past several years.

What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

An airport lounge membership, hotel perks and a handful of statement credits used to be enough to set a premium travel rewards card apart. These days, that sounds like the starting point.

The faces competition from the (see rates and fees), Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and (see rates and fees). All four offer transferable rewards and airport lounge access, along with benefits designed to offset their high annual fees.

Still, the Platinum makes a compelling case for a place in a frequent traveler's wallet. Its strengths include extensive lounge access, generous earnings on flights booked directly with airlines and hotel benefits that can make a stay considerably more comfortable.

At $895 a year (see rates and fees), it's also the most expensive of these four cards.

Here's where the Platinum stands out — and where another premium card might be a better fit.

Complimentary Priority Pass lounge access is a shared benefit across these cards (enrollment required). What makes the stand out is the additional lounges available through the American Express Global Lounge Collection.

The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes Centurion Lounges, eligible Delta Sky Clubs and other participating partner lounge networks.

The Centurion network has a larger footprint than either Capital One’s or Chase’s own branded lounge network. Citi doesn't operate its own network, although cardholders receive four Admirals Club passes per calendar year.

For me, the Centurion Lounges at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston are particularly useful when connecting to and from Austin. I enjoy the food at the lounges, but after an international flight, the opportunity to shower before my final flight of the day is what I appreciate most.

Delta Sky Club access is another reason to consider the Platinum. Cardmembers receive 10 visits per benefit year when flying on eligible itineraries. (Basic economy tickets don't qualify, and unlimited visits require $75,000 in eligible annual spending.)

There are other limits to consider. Centurion guest access costs extra unless you meet a spending requirement, and the biggest network won't necessarily be the most useful at your home airport.

Check the lounges along your regular routes before choosing a card based on access alone.

Related: My 5 top travel credit cards — and how they elevate my trips

The offers up to $600 in annual lodging statement credits, split into two allowances of up to $300: one from January through June and another from July through December.

Eligible purchases include prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®, plus qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

THC and eligible Airbnb Luxe bookings require stays of at least two nights. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require a two-night stay to qualify for the lodging credit.

I tend to use my credit for THC stays because I often find lower prices than at FHR properties. For January, I've booked two nights at The Standard, Bangkok Mahanakhon for $362. After applying the $300 credit, the stay will cost me $62 out of pocket.

My stay includes daily breakfast for two and a $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges, which I plan to use at an on-site restaurant or for room service. I'll also be eligible for early check-in, late checkout and a room upgrade (subject to availability). Breakfast is an additional benefit at this particular property; it isn't standard across THC.

FHR offers a more consistent package, including daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. That last benefit can be especially useful before an evening flight.

Competing premium cards have their own hotel programs. The Platinum's appeal is the combination of its credit and booking benefits. Just make sure to compare the total price with other available rates before deciding how much you're saving.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers

The earns 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through Amex Travel (on up to $500,000 of airfare purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The ability to book directly is a meaningful advantage. You can earn generously while dealing with the airline directly if you need to change your reservation or something goes wrong.

The earns 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly. It earns a higher 8 points per dollar through Chase Travel℠, while the earns 6 points per dollar spent on flights through Citi Travel.

Here's an example of earnings on a $500 flight:

The Platinum also earns 5 points per dollar spent on eligible prepaid hotels through Amex Travel and prepaid Airbnb bookings through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel app. The Airbnb earning rate applies beyond the Luxe properties eligible for the lodging credit.

Those points offer plenty of redemption options.

Membership Rewards airline partners provide access to Oneworld, SkyTeam and Star Alliance flights through programs such as British Airways Club, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Air Canada Aeroplan. Hotel partners include Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy.

All four cards have useful transfer partners, so consider which programs you actually use. A strong earning rate matters more when it earns points you know how to redeem.

Related: The best premium credit cards: A side-by-side comparison

Eligible applicants can find out their offer and see if they are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on our valuations, the maximum 175,000-point offer is worth up to $3,500 — the highest value among the current publicly advertised offers on these four cards.

The high spending requirement deserves attention. Make sure you can meet it through purchases you already planned to make, and assess the card's ongoing value separately from its first-year bonus.

The 's long list of credits makes more sense when you focus on the ones that fit your existing spending.

Its up to $300 annual digital entertainment credit is one I particularly like. It provides up to $25 monthly toward eligible purchases with participating providers.† I use it for YouTube Premium and Disney+/Hulu; the monthly allowance is shared across eligible subscriptions.

Uber users have two benefits to consider. The card provides up to $200 in annual Uber Cash for eligible U.S. rides and orders (up to $15 monthly, plus an extra $20 in December; you must add the Platinum to your Uber account and use an Amex card to pay). A separate credit provides up to $120 annually toward an eligible auto-renewing Uber One membership.

The up to $400 annual Resy statement credit (available in quarterly allowances of up to $100) can also be straightforward to use if you already dine at qualifying U.S. restaurants.†

There’s also an up to $300 annual Equinox statement credit for eligible Equinox memberships or an Equinox+ digital subscription (subject to auto-renewal).† I use mine for the digital subscription.

These benefits can help cover the annual fee, but only assign them the value they have to you. Signing up for a service you won't use doesn't save money. Monthly expiration dates and U.S. restrictions also make some credits less useful for certain cardmembers.

Related: The gift card trick that helps me maximize my US restaurant credits while I'm abroad

cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold, Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite and Leaders Club Sterling status.† The benefits vary by program, but having status without meeting the usual stay or spending requirements is a useful starting point.

Perks with Avis, Hertz and National† can also improve the experience of renting a car.

The card provides up to $219 in statement credits per calendar year toward a Clear+ membership (subject to auto-renewal),† plus either a $120 Global Entry application fee credit or an up to $85 TSA PreCheck application fee credit (every four years) when you pay with your Platinum.

Clear+ handles identity verification at participating airport checkpoints, while TSA PreCheck provides expedited security screening. Global Entry expedites eligible arrivals into the U.S. and includes TSA PreCheck.

You can also select one qualifying airline to receive up to $200 in statement credits for eligible incidental fees† charged to your Platinum card each calendar year. (Note that it isn't a general airfare credit.)

Outside its limited bonus categories, the earns just 1 point per dollar spent. Dining and everyday purchases are usually better placed on another card.

The Venture X offers a simpler alternative: a $395 annual fee, at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, a $300 annual Capital One Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles. There are fewer credits to track to make the annual fee worthwhile.

The has advantages in travel protections. Its included rental car coverage is primary, while Platinum's included coverage is secondary**.

The Sapphire Reserve also offers baggage delay insurance, reimbursing eligible essentials up to $100 daily for five days after a qualifying delay exceeding six hours. Platinum's baggage insurance*** covers eligible lost, damaged or stolen baggage, but it doesn't offer a comparable standalone baggage delay benefit.

Finally, the may be a better fit if you spend heavily on dining and prefer Citi's transfer partners. It earns 3 ThankYou points per dollar spent at restaurants, increasing to 6 points on Friday and Saturday evenings (between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. Eastern time). It also offers four Admirals Club passes per calendar year, making it particularly appealing if you occasionally fly American Airlines.

**Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. ***Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The is most compelling when its benefits fit how you already travel and spend. Lounge access, a well-priced hotel stay and regularly used credits can make its annual fee easier to justify.

For me, airport showers and elevated hotel stays and credits I already use make the Platinum worth keeping.

If you'd get more use from broad spending bonuses or a simpler set of benefits, one of its competitors could be a better fit.

#6168. Rand Paul chooses ranking member slot at Senate HELP

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”

#6167. Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card

Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:

With the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited currently has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

Admittedly the spending requirement is big (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

When it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

In fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

No Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history

In terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers a minimum of unlimited 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:

All cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like tht.

2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

Meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

This program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

You can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

Personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

It’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

I think the issue is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back, so this is at least a new product for the card issuer. It’s just not a new concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

So who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:

I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

Perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

The upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

Another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

If you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

The card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

In addition to a big welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

Ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

Beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

There are six United credit cards, ranging from a no-annual-fee card to premium personal and business cards with United Club access. Fortunately, figuring out which ones you're eligible for is straightforward.

Holding one United card generally doesn't prevent you from opening another or earning its welcome bonus. Instead, welcome-offer restrictions are largely card-specific: You can’t apply for a card you already hold or earn its welcome bonus if you've received a bonus on that same card in the last 24 months.

Apply here for a limited-time offer on the — Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening (see rates and fees).

All six United cards are currently offering elevated welcome bonuses.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

As of November 2026, TPG valuations place United miles at 1.2 cents each, making these offers worth between $600 and $1,200, excluding the value of any PQPs.

For United cards, applicants need to clear three main hurdles:

Meeting these requirements doesn't guarantee approval, only that you are free to apply and are eligible for the welcome offer if approved.

Chase allows you to apply for multiple United cards, as long as they are separate cards.

For example, if you already hold an , you can also apply for a . However, you can't hold two of the same card, so if you have a Quest card, you can't get a second in order to double up on its benefits.

The Gateway, Explorer, Quest and Club offer different benefits, so holding more than one could make sense depending on your travel habits. Having two or more cards means you also have access to different bonus categories when earning miles and potentially multiple PQP deposits for being a cardholder, depending on which cards you have.

There's one exception: If you are an existing United Club Visa Signature cardmember (no longer available to new applicants), you are not eligible for the current United Club card.

You'll need to close the old card and apply for a new Club card 24 months after you received the initial bonus. Or, you can call the number on the back of your card to product change to the current Club card, which preserves your account history and 5/24 status but won't earn an introductory offer.

The  and United Club Business Card have similar product-specific restrictions.

You won't qualify if you currently hold the business card you're applying for or received its new-cardmember bonus within the past 24 months.

You don't need an LLC or a company with employees to apply. You may qualify with a legitimate sole proprietorship or side hustle, such as freelance work, consulting, pet sitting or reselling.

Chase generally requires business card applicants to be under 5/24. However, once you're approved, a Chase business card typically won't appear on your personal credit report or add another account to your 5/24 total.

Related: United Business Card vs. United Club Business Card: Which should you get?

Yes, you can have multiple United credit cards at one time. Unlike some other airline credit cards, United's cards don't have a broad restriction that prevents you from holding multiple cobranded cards.

You could hold a for its TravelBank Cash and 10,000-mile award discount, the for lounge access and a for business expenses.

There's also an incentive to pair a personal and business United card: Both United business cards offer 5,000 bonus miles each account anniversary if you're also the primary cardmember on a personal United card.

Holding multiple United cards won't make sense for infrequent flyers, since benefits like free checked bags and priority boarding overlap on multiple cards. However, for loyal customers, the collection of slightly different perks and cardholder PQP bonuses could justify the cost of paying multiple annual fees.

Yes, you can get the same United credit card more than once. However, you will only earn another welcome offer if you no longer hold that card and at least 24 months have passed since you received the new-cardmember bonus.

Remember, Chase counts from the date you receive the bonus, not from when you open or close the account.

If you are an authorized user on someone else's United card, Chase does not consider that being a current cardholder for the purposes of that card's bonus restrictions. In other words, you can still apply for your own version of that card and earn its welcome bonus.

However, an authorized-user account may appear on your credit report and increase your 5/24 count.

If you're denied because of an authorized-user account, you may be able to explain the situation to Chase by calling the reconsideration line, although approval isn't guaranteed.

If you're interested in both a personal and business United card, applying for the business card first often makes sense. That's because the business card won't add to your 5/24 limit and tip you over the edge.

However, if you're applying for multiple personal United cards, the order you apply shouldn't matter. Pick whichever card is your highest priority first, considering its benefits and how its current offer compares with past bonuses.

The best choice depends on how often you fly United and which benefits you'll actually use.

The is often a good starting point, since it offers strong benefits like a free checked bag and single-use lounge passes, and it has no annual fee in the first year. The offers TravelBank Cash and an annual award discount for more serious United loyalists, and the is best suited to frequent flyers who value ongoing lounge access.

United's eligibility rules are friendly to new applicants.

For the Gateway, Explorer, Quest, United Business and United Club Business cards, you're in a strong position if you don't currently hold the exact card and haven't received its welcome bonus within the past 24 months, while the United Club card has a minor caveat that won't impact most applicants.

#6164. Buy Avianca Lifemiles With 145% Bonus (1.35 Cents Each): Worth It?

The avianca lifemiles program is currently offering a limited time 145% bonus on purchased miles. With this, lifemiles members can purchase miles for as little as 1.35 cents each. Is this a good deal?

I find lifemiles to be one of the more useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming miles, thanks to the ability to redeem for long haul premium cabin Star Alliance awards. However, let me emphasize that the program doesn’t always have access to the same award space as other Star Alliance programs, so you’ll want to do your own research, based on the travel you’re trying to plan.

I’d only consider buying miles with a very specific use in mind. For what it’s worth, I don’t get any sort of kickback if you buy miles — I just want to make OMAAT readers aware of the deals that are available.

Link: Buy avianca lifemiles with this promotion with a 145% bonus

Between November 18 and November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a bonus on purchased miles. While different members may be targeted for different offers, the standard offer that I see across accounts is for a bonus of up to 145%, structured as follows:

You’ll of course want to check your account to see what offer you’re targeted for, as it could be different. It’s common for lifemiles to promote one amount, and then actually offer a bigger bonus. Note that nowadays lifemiles promotions are generally targeted, so different members may see different offers, and on top of that, some members may not see any offers at all.

Ordinarily you can buy avianca lifemiles for 3.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses. That means that if you purchased 200,000 lifemiles (pre-bonus) with a 145% bonus (assuming you’re eligible for that), you’d receive a total of 490,000 lifemiles for $6,600, which is a cost of 1.35 cents per mile. That’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

If you wanted to buy as few miles as possible at the possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 51,000 miles at a cost of $1,683, and that would get you 122,500 lifemiles.

Unfortunately this isn’t quite the best promotion we’ve seen from the program, as we’ve seen bigger percentage bonuses in the past. However, it’s anyone’s guess when we see a bigger offer again.

The lifemiles program lets members purchase up to 500,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, the limit per transaction is 200,000 miles, so if you really wanted to max out the number of miles you can buy, you’d need to make multiple transactions.

When members purchase lifemiles, they typically post nearly instantly. However, in rare cases it can take up to 72 hours for them to post. Mileage purchases are non-refundable, so once you make the purchase, it’s final.

When the lifemiles program does offer a promotion on purchased miles, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

Mileage purchases are processed directly by avianca lifemiles, which means the purchase of miles does qualify as airfare spending. Therefore you’ll want to consider using one of the below cards for your purchase, since you’d earn bonus points for airfare purchases.

For context, avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of buying lifemiles, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem lifemiles for ideas on how to redeem these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this lifemiles promotion can be a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling in first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me again emphasize that in some cases, lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs. Keep in mind that you can get even more value from the program with a lifemiles+ subscription, and lifemiles’ credit cards offer a discount on that.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider avianca lifemiles to be worth 1.3 cents each. That’s based on the redemption values on Star Alliance partners, as there’s tons of value to be had. I tend to value miles very conservatively, so if you’re maximizing miles you should be able to get way more value than that.

Miles with the lifemiles program don’t expire as long as you accrue some miles at least once every 12 months. Any mileage earning activity, including buying miles, will extend the expiration of your miles. However, redeeming miles as such doesn’t extend the expiration of your miles.

If you’re looking to earn lifemiles, the good news is that there are lots of options beyond outright buying them. Specifically, avianca lifemiles is partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so there are lots of ways to pick up these miles.

For purchases through November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a promotion on purchased miles. Different members may be eligible for different offers, though it appears that the standard offer is for up to a 145% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire miles for 1.35 cents each. This has the potential to represent a solid value, though I’d only recommend buying miles with a specific, short term use in mind.

#6163. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6162. Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

Through October and November, this mediocre flavor and scent are in everything everywhere all the time.

A display of Trader Joe’s pumpkin and fall-themed products at a grocery store in Lafayette, Calif., September 25, 2026.

A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

JetBlue TrueBlue is offering up to a 125% bonus on purchasing points. The offer is structured as follows, with three tiers of bonuses:

Let me emphasize that this appears to be the standard offer, though sometimes different members are targeted for different offers. You’ll want to log into your TrueBlue account to see what you’re eligible for.

JetBlue ordinarily allows TrueBlue members to purchase up to 200,000 points per calendar year. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 300,000 points.

JetBlue ordinarily charges 3.0 cents per purchased point, before the 7.5% federal excise tax. After factoring in the federal excise tax, the standard cost is 3.225 cents per purchased point.

With this JetBlue points sale, you’d pay the following amounts per purchased point, factoring in the bonus:

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to purchase a total of 45,000 points (20,000 points plus 25,000 bonus points) at a cost of $645, which gets you the cost of 1.43 cents per point, including all taxes.

Meanwhile if you wanted to purchase the most possible points, you’d want to purchase a total of 675,000 points (300,000 points plus 375,000 bonus points) at a cost of $9,675, which gets you the same cost per point.

Officially, JetBlue states that it can take up to 72 hours for purchased points to post. However, in practice (based on my test experience of buying points), they’ll typically post almost instantly. There’s no guarantee of that, though.

Note that the purchase of JetBlue points is non-refundable, so only make a purchase if you have a specific use in mind. Furthermore, the purchase of JetBlue points doesn’t count toward Mosaic elite status, in case that’s a consideration.

When JetBlue does offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

JetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

JetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

Just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

As another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

As you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

JetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

For example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

As another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

As I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

At this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

Another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

Through December 31, 2026, JetBlue is selling TrueBlue points with up to a 125% bonus, an opportunity to buy points for as little as 1.43 cents each. I’d only buy JetBlue points with a specific use in mind. There’s value to be had in some situations, such as if you have a particular Qatar Airways or Condor award you want to book, and there’s availability.

Anyone plan on buying JetBlue TrueBlue points with a bonus?

#6160. 14 tricks to getting the most value from your cruise vacations

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

Squeezing the most value out of every dollar on a cruise is a top goal for most travelers. It doesn't matter if you're on a quick escape cruise from a local port or an exotic luxury cruise halfway around the globe, you never want to end it feeling like you should have gotten more for your money.

Cruises are the ultimate all-inclusive vacation, with meals, transportation and entertainment included, and there is even more value-adds on board that you may have never thought to look for. The trick is to hone in on built-in value early, in the cruise shopping and purchasing stage, and then pay attention to every detail that might enhance your experience along the way. Here are 14 tricks to get the most possible value from any cruise you take.

It can feel like you’re bombarded with emails after you book a cruise, but some of them contain hidden treasure.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Princess, MSC and Virgin Voyages are among the cruise lines that use a bidding process to manage unsold cabins as the sailing date gets closer. Carnival Cruise Line offers upgrades without bidding. Pay attention to your email, and you might nab a nicer cabin for less than you’d pay by booking it outright.

Emails also alert you to discounted packages or bundles for Wi-Fi, shore excursions, specialty dining, drinks and even spa treatments. Much of the same information can be found on the cruise planner on the cruise line's website, but unless you log in often, watch those emails for value-oriented offers.

While it's tempting to always look at the newest (and often the biggest) ships, you may find that switching to an older or smaller ship, which may be just slightly less in demand, often helps squeeze more from your cruise budget without limiting your vacation fun.

You can also save hundreds of dollars by opting for inside staterooms, rooms with partially blocked views or those with less-than-perfect locations on the ship. This even works within suite zones or exclusive ship-within-a-ship areas. My dermatologist recently confided that he always chooses an inside suite within the Yacht Club when he cruises with MSC; he gets all the VIP perks, including exclusive dining and entertainment venues, for thousands less than the suites with balconies.

And don't rule out the cruise cabin guarantee option. Regardless of the cabin type, allowing the cruise line to select your stateroom is almost always the better value option than picking a specific room.

While most lines sign you up for loyalty programs automatically after your first sailing, you might need to opt in. Some lines allow you to sign up even before your first cruise, giving you advance offers to entice you to go ahead and book that first cruise.

Status matches between cruise lines are a huge bonus. MSC offers a status match with other cruise lines, hotel brands and tour operators. You can do this before your first booking and get Voyagers Club benefits on your first cruise with the line. These could be as simple as a welcome beverage or as elaborate as a complimentary tasting menu dinner. Ultra-luxury sister brand, Explora Journeys, offers a one-time status match with MSC and comparable luxury lines.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea have an ongoing status match across the three sister brands. That means you can reap rewards on a luxury line by earning status on a mainstream brand.

Similarly, Viking’s loyalty program spans its river, ocean and expedition arms. Once you’ve cruised with the line, you’ll get benefits fleetwide, even if you try out a different kind of ship.

Some lines offer casino status matches with land- and sea-based casinos that might even earn you a free cruise. These often come with exceptions; your casino status on Carnival won't get you a free cruise on sister line Princess, but casino status on Celebrity might. And don't be afraid of free cruise certificates handed out by reputable casinos on land where you have status. They’re the real deal, often based on long-standing partnerships between the casino and cruise lines. The reverse is also true. I’ve never been to WinStar Casino in Oklahoma, but they send me offers of free hotel nights using postcards featuring the Carnival logo, with which I have casino status.

While not every loyalty perk holds a huge value for you, little freebies definitely add up on vacation. For example, Carnival gives you a free 1.5-liter bottle of water on your second cruise. That's one less bottle you might have to buy.

As you move up the loyalty ladder, cruise by cruise, the perks improve. For example, you may be eligible for free laundry, drinks and specialty dining the higher up you go. I once met a couple who were on a five-night Royal Caribbean cruise for the sole purpose of moving up to the top loyalty tier before going on a much longer cruise. The higher tier would give them free Wi-Fi and a handful of other valuable perks for the duration of their longer cruise.

Often the onboard perks are loaded on your cabin keycard, but you might have to ask how to use them. For example, if you are entitled to a free bag of laundry at your loyalty level, nobody will hand you a bag and say, "Fill it up; it's free." It's up to you to know the perks you are entitled to and follow through on getting them.

Amid the barrage of marketing messages for beverage packages of all sorts, it's easy to forget that certain beverages are included in your cruise fare.

Every cruise ship offers standard drip coffee, water, iced tea, hot cocoa, punch or lemonade and a variety of tea bags free of charge. Milk and juice are available at breakfast. Look for self-serve stations at the buffet, or ask your server.

Sodas are included on premium lines like Windstar, Oceania and Viking, as well as on luxury lines like Seabourn, Silversea and Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Disney Cruise Line also offers free soft drinks but only from the beverage dispensers by the pool.

It's surprising how many free (or included) alcoholic drinks you can procure once on board a ship. I've been offered sparkling wine at art auctions, galley tours and captain's events.

Royal Caribbean and Celebrity both have free drinks for the top three tiers of loyalty status.

Celebrity Cruises offers free drinks for anyone gambling in the casino. Carnival and Virgin Voyages are among the lines offering free drinks to select gamblers based on their prior gambling history. You might be eligible for those, even if you only gamble on land.

The cabin you book might come with valuable perks, so know what they are so you don’t miss out.

For example, Celebrity’s AquaClass cabins come with not only thermal suite access and exclusive dining in the line’s health-forward restaurant called Blu, but also a choice of exercise equipment. Yoga mats are supposed to be in the closet when you board, but you'll have to ask for any of the other items listed on the menu provided.

Suites on most lines come with extra perks like included drink packages and specialty dining. On certain ships, even some smaller suite categories come with exclusive dining rooms only for the occupants of those categories. The food in these exclusive eateries is often a step above the main dining room and not to be missed if you are staying in the entitled category.

The same goes for suite lounge access. You generally find snack and beverage stations stocked with specialty treats you won’t find elsewhere on board, making it worthwhile to at least sneak a peek at the lounge offerings if you paid for a category that comes with access.

The cost of going out to the movies these days makes a cruise movie night a big value. Now that most of us watch movies by streaming them at home, actually going to the movies is a treat in and of itself.

Movie nights on a ship are a step above your local movie theater. You might enjoy films on a giant poolside screen while you float in the pool or relax on a lounge chair with bar servers bringing the drinks to you. Disney Cruise Line screens first-run films for free, with costumed characters in attendance. Many lines serve free popcorn wherever movies are being shown.

If staying in for a movie night in your jammies sounds good, take advantage of free or pay-per-view movies on your cabin’s TV. Disney is among the cruise lines with popcorn on the room service menu. On a Silversea cruise, I once told our butler we were staying in for an evening movie. His immediate reply was, "Shall I pop some corn for you?" The answer, of course, was, "Yes, please."

Live music, comedy acts, magic shows and musical theater are luxuries you can pay dearly for on land — but all of those are available on cruise lines at no charge. The larger the ship, the more entertainment options you will have.

Free live music is found daily in lounges, pool areas, atriums and on stage in the main auditorium. Audience participation game shows, sometimes raucous in nature, usually take over lounge space a few nights of the cruise.

The main stage will have a show nightly, either song-and-dance revues featuring an onboard cast or guest magicians, musicians and comedians, some with TV credits to their name. Larger ships might have separate comedy club venues to keep the laughs flowing every night of the cruise, with both family-friendly and adults-only shows. Clubs on dry land where these same performers appear often charge a $30-40 cover. On a recent Carnival cruise, I estimate my visits to the comedy club alone would have cost me several hundred dollars.

Some lines lean heavily into specialty performances. Look for ice skating, aquatic high-diving and dance shows on select Royal Caribbean ships and acrobatic performances on Virgin Voyages and MSC Cruises. Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line both offer Broadway musicals, while Disney produces live musical performances based on its popular animated movies.

With so much free entertainment that would certainly cost a family hundreds in ticket prices on land, you’ll get a ton of value from your cruise if you attend the shows that most appeal to you.

When the night's entertainment winds down, it's time to dance the night away and go clubbing — and cruise ship clubs don’t have a cover. Big ships crank up the party vibe after the last show in the main theater, so you can make the most of every second you’re awake. Hop from dance parties on the pool deck to karaoke in smaller bar venues and even silent discos in the atrium to keep the fun going into the wee hours.

Eating out and trying local restaurants are hallmarks of vacation, but you can blow your budget doing that on land. You can spend a lot on specialty restaurants on board, too, but pay attention to timing to get the most value out of the free dining on board. If you know you would enjoy steak and lobster, do a little research to figure out which night they will be served in the main dining room. You don’t want to find out too late that you booked a specialty restaurant on the same night you could have been eating surf and turf at no additional cost. Themed brunches and afternoon tea are also main dining room events you don’t want to miss.

Looking beyond the buffet and main dining room might turn up surprising food choices you didn't even know were included in your cruise fare. Pool grills serving juicy hamburgers, specialty coffee shops with snacks and even sandwiches and healthy choice salads near the solarium are all yummy examples of freebies tucked away in spots you might not think to look.

As for the specialty restaurants, those are generally still a bargain compared to a similar meal at a land-based restaurant. Carnival's Steakhouse is a good example. The cost is $52 per person. That sounds steep, but if you've priced a filet mignon in a nice restaurant lately, you'll know that $52 barely covers the steak. At Fahrenheit 555, you'll be treated to appetizers, sides and desserts, making the cover charge a vacation value. Book your Steakhouse dinner for the first night of a sailing, and Carnival will usually throw in a complimentary bottle of house wine.

For lounging in your cabin, free or low-cost room service boosts your cruise value. My personal favorite (especially on sea days) is enjoying a "first breakfast" of coffee and croissants from room service before heading out for a more substantial second breakfast.

Private island experiences provide an inexpensive break from paying for excursions in other ports. First things first, the beach is free. Use of the lounge chairs is free (not always the case at some vacation destinations). Swimming in the ocean and in some pools is free.

Depending on the island, you might find hammocks, hiking trails, game and sports areas and interesting snorkeling spots. Rental equipment for snorkeling and other water activities is usually reasonably priced, but you can bring your own gear.

The major private islands all have complimentary barbecue buffets and occasionally other food trucks or fast-casual offerings. As with specialty dining on the ship, even the up-charged food won’t cost as much as at a theme park or on the beach at a vacation destination.

Relying on shore excursions offered by the cruise line is the easy way to plan your days in port. It also keeps you safe from becoming one of those pier-running late-comers at departure time. Those tours are not always the best value, however. Lower-priced reputable port tours may take a bit more research on your part, but can save hundreds of dollars.

I recently enjoyed a 4-hour kayak tour in Ketchikan with pickup near the pier and guaranteed on-time return that I booked directly on the Ketchikan Kayak Company's website, which saved me roughly $60 per person compared to the similar tour offered by the ship.

And don’t forget that skipping organized tours altogether can also net you an amazing day in port. If tours aren't your jam, or you just don’t want the scheduling hassle in every port, consider simply venturing out on your own in search of fun. If the town is walkable, start with that. Or consider renting a car or simply hiring a taxi driver. I've visited Cozumel dozens of times on cruise ships, but had never seen the far side of the island. Last fall, a group of friends and family rented two Jeeps online from a rental agency located walking distance from the pier. We had a marvelous time stopping wherever we wanted, including for an impromptu tequila tasting (for the non-drivers, of course).

Whether you're talking about something as simple as miniature golf, basketball, pickleball or table tennis, or as elaborate as surf simulators and multideck dry slides, cruise lines often load their ships’ upper decks with free fun. As with all things on a cruise, certain activities come with a cost, but you’ll find plenty of fun that does not add to your cruise bill.

On land, you typically need to pay to access waterslides, splash parks, rock climbing walls and adventure and zip lines, but on many cruises, these active onboard attractions come free. Certain activities might require reservations or specific attire (like closed-toe shoes), so check out the details in advance.

Did you know that some cruise lines let you buy VIP packages pre-cruise for a bundle of preferential treatment similar to suite category perks? The real value of these programs lies in not paying for an expensive suite while enjoying extra perks as if you did.

Royal Caribbean's The Key includes early boarding times, a welcome lunch, fast lane access to select onboard activities, premium theater seating, departure day perks and free internet access for each guest who purchases the package.

Celebrity's Premium Access is a similar bundle. The combination of complimentary room service and Premium Wi-Fi for two devices makes this package a cruise value.

Holland America's Club Orange includes a complimentary cabin upgrade when available, priority check-in, priority lines at Guest Services and Shore Excursion desks, bathrobes, an expanded room service menu, a complimentary glass of sparkling wine, exclusive events like behind-the-scenes tours and coffee chats with performers and even separate dining rooms on some ships. With a bit of strategy, the cabin upgrade alone can justify the cost of the Club Orange add-on. This works best in Oceanview and Verandah categories where you can choose an obstructed view cabin at a low cost, banking on the Club Orange upgrade to a full-view room.

Carnival’s Faster to the Fun offers early cabin access, express luggage delivery and priority check-in and embarkation, shuttle boarding, dining reservations, Guest Services line and debarkation. Note that Carnival blocks access to FTTF for some loyalty guests, including some casino loyalty members, to avoid stacking of perks.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Priority Access includes priority security, check-in and boarding processes on embarkation day, plus skip-the-line tendering and debarkation, complimentary standard room service and a $50 spa discount on port days.

Cruises come with so much value bundled into the cost of the fare that it can be easy to overlook all the goodies that aren't costing you anything extra. Adding value to your cruise vacation can be as simple as reading the daily planner or taking a walk around the ship to discover all the included attractions. Whether it’s free entertainment in your favorite lounge, a dance lesson or no-cost prime rib in the main dining room, all those onboard freebies and low-cost add-ons make it possible to get outsize value from your cruise vacation.
