#6159. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6158. Most Airports Cap Concession Prices… But The System Is A Total Joke

Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

Airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

But in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:

If there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread issue? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The issue is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”

For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she said the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

The issue boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:

What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:

VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”

Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

The other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

So to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

Airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The issue is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”

The price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest…

What do you make of this airport pricing situation?

#6156. Emirates Finally Revamping Dubai Lounges: Temporary New First Class Lounge Now Open

Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has announced plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

As is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:

Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:

“Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”

We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:

Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

When it comes to the temporary new first class lounge, here are the details:

As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉

But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

We’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

The new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

What do you make of Emirates’ new lounge concept?

#6153. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6152. FAA Technician Only Unlocked The Door: Inside The Oversight Gap Behind The Nationwide Ground Stop

Last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We quickly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:

So, what’s actually going on here? A new report sheds some more light on this…

CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

According to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”

Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”

With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

While the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

We have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to new levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”

We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

While the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a new system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

What do you make of this FAA contractor oversight situation?

#6150. Atmos Rewards Business Card Changes: Higher(ish) Fee, New Benefits

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

Along those lines, there’s a major update, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, new rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

Let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

With that out of the way, let’s go over the details…

The Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:

What has changed here is the new 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few new benefits that it didn’t previously offer:

The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

Applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

As of now, it sounds like there are no plans to transition people to the new system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

Admittedly it’s hard to do an apples-to-apples comparison between personal and business cards, because at least in theory, they’re supposed to serve different purposes. So here’s my take:

So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has just undergone some major changes, though they don’t impact existing card members. For new applicants, the card now has a $195 annual fee, compared to the old fee of $70 for the company, and $25 per person.

The card is also getting a new set of benefits, including a new rewards structure, additional perks, and new incentives for spending. People will have varying takes as to whether these changes are positive or negative, depending on their consumer patterns.

My biggest takeaway is that the bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending is excellent, and a great incentive to apply for the card.

What do you make of these Atmos Rewards Business Card changes?

#6149. Buy Air Canada Aeroplan Points With 100% Bonus (1.31 Cents Each): Worth It?

The Air Canada Aeroplan program is currently offering a bonus on purchased points. While this is a mystery bonus, where different members may be eligible for different offers, it seems the best version is for up to a 100% bonus.

Is there value with this offer? With a specific use in mind, absolutely, in my opinion. Aeroplan is one of my all-around favorite frequent flyer programs, thanks to the huge variety of airline partners, the ability to have stopovers on one-way awards for 5,000 points, and the generally great online booking experience.

Link: Buy Air Canada Aeroplan points with this promotion with up to a 100% bonus

Between 12AM PT on November 19 and 11:50PM PT on December 10, 2026, the Air Canada Aeroplan program is offering a promotion on purchased points.

Different members may be eligible for different offers, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. However, it appears that the best version of the offer is for up to a 100% bonus, structured as follows:

I should emphasize that other members seem to be eligible for offers of 85%, 90%, or 95%, so it’s no guarantee that everyone will see the 100% offer.

Ordinarily, Air Canada Aeroplan charges $0.0375 CAD (~0.026 USD) per point. Any purchases made with US credit cards and US billing addresses aren’t subject to sales tax either.

If you purchased 500,000 Aeroplan points with a 100% bonus, you’d receive a total of 1,000,000 Aeroplan points at a cost of $18,750 CAD (~$13,101 USD), which is a rate of 1.31 cents (USD) per Aeroplan point.

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 90,000 points at a cost of $3,375 CAD (~$2,358 USD), which would potentially get you 180,000 points, for the same cost per point.

While you can purchase up to one million Aeroplan points per account per calendar year, there’s ordinarily a per-transaction limit of 250,000 points pre-bonus. However, during this promotion that has been doubled, to 500,000 points.

Aeroplan points purchases typically post pretty close to instantly, though in some situations, it could take up to 72 hours for points to post. Note that the purchase of Aeroplan points is non-refundable, and Aeroplan points purchases also don’t count toward elite status.

When Air Canada Aeroplan offer a promotion on purchased points, we most commonly see a bonus in the range of 90-110%, but the exact offers do vary. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 100% bonus vs. a 110% bonus isn’t vastly different.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Aeroplan program, before this one.

Air Canada Aeroplan points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Aeroplan points is billed in CAD, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase. Beyond that, the best options would be cards that offer 2x transferable points, while having no foreign transaction fees.

Aeroplan is one of my favorite frequent flyer programs out there. To cover a few of the basics:

There are lots of phenomenal uses of Aeroplan points, and this is a program that I redeem through regularly. Just keep in mind that Aeroplan now has dynamic award pricing on select partners, including Emirates, Etihad, FlyDubai, and United, among others.

One of my favorite things about Air Canada Aeroplan is that the program has more airline partners than any other frequent flyer program, and you can redeem points on over 45 airlines. In addition to Air Canada belonging to the Star Alliance, Aeroplan also partners with airlines that include Etihad, Azul, Air Serbia, Virgin Australia, Air Dolomiti, Eurowings, Gulf Air, Oman Air, Air Mauritius, and Emirates.

Always look up award availability before buying points, to get a sense of what you can expect.

Many consumers are frustrated by the practice of airlines adding carrier imposed surcharges to award tickets. In the case of Aeroplan, there are no fuel surcharges on award tickets, meaning you shouldn’t expect to pay big fees when redeeming points.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Aeroplan points than that.

Air Canada Aeroplan points only expire after 18 months of inactivity. However, any account activity that leads to earning or redeeming points (including buying them) would reset the expiration.

While buying Aeroplan points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Aeroplan points. Most significantly, Aeroplan is transfer partners with American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, making the currency pretty easy to acquire. From all those currencies, rewards transfer at a 1:1 ratio, and sometimes you’ll even find transfer bonuses.

On top of that, in the United States there’s the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (learn more), which is pretty lucrative.

Air Canada’s Aeroplan program is offering a bonus on purchased points. While people may be targeted for different offers, it appears the best offer is for up to a 100% bonus, which kicks in as long as you purchase at least 90,000 points in one transaction. This is an opportunity to buy points for 1.31 cents (in USD) each.

This could represent a good deal, and there are plenty of situations under which the math will work out for this promotion. Still, in general I’d only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, as there’s always risk to holding onto points for longer periods of time.

Do you plan on buying Aeroplan points with this promotion?

#6148. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

The sweeping results of the midterm elections made the voters’ diagnosis clear. They do not like the current direction of the country. As Democrats prepare to assume control of Congress, they must determine their treatment plan, one that unites the party, achieves results, and can resonate in the next election in 2028. The treatment plan is what industry needs to keep a pulse on.

The diagnosis is the easy part. Don’t like the cost of living? Blame the folks in charge. While that works on the campaign trail, it doesn’t work as a governing agenda. And it won’t hold a coalition together through 2028. The hard question is what Democrats will support to address the concerns of the voters who elected them.

#6145. Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Bonus: 90K Points Welcome Offer

The $195 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card currently has a huge bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. For context, this is the business card of the Atmos Rewards portfolio, the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian. This is a potentially lucrative card that has just undergone a refresh, and you can read my Atmos Rewards Business Card review here.

In this post I’d like to go over the details of the Atmos Rewards Business Card bonus, for anyone who may be considering applying. There are lots of reasons to get this card, particularly the incredible bonus.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card with 90K bonus points

The Atmos Rewards Business Card currently has a welcome offer of 90,000 Atmos Rewards bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, meaning the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Atmos Rewards points, for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, oneworld partners, and non-alliance partners.

Atmos Rewards points have all kinds of uses, ranging from booking short haul one-way economy awards on American for 4,500 points, to booking Starlux business class one-way awards from the US to Asia for 75,000 points. Of course capacity controls apply, so patience and flexibility will be required to get the best deal. Still, I find this to be one of the most useful points currencies out there.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card 90,000-point offer is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that we’ve seen on the card since it launched in August 2025 (which is when the Atmos Rewards program formally launched). How do the previous Atmos Rewards Business Card bonuses compare?

As you can see, the Atmos Rewards Business Card sign-up bonus has varied from 70,000 points to 90,000 points, and the current bonus of 90,000 points is the best publicly available offer we’ve seen. So if there has ever been a time to apply for this card, this is it.

When it comes to getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card, what rules should you be aware of? There are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Bank of America policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

This one-time promotion is limited to company level Business Card clients opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

The good news is that eligibility for the Atmos Rewards Business Card is considered completely independently of any other cards in the portfolio, so you’re eligible if you have either of the personal Atmos Rewards credit cards. Many people even report being eligible for the Atmos Rewards Business Card (including the bonus) if they’ve had it in the past.

Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 rule, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

Beyond the great bonus, there are multiple reasons to consider the $195 annual fee Atmos Rewards Business Card:

If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then having this card should be a no-brainer. The benefits really add up, between the lounge passes, the first checked bag free, preferred boarding, savings on inflight purchases, and more.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has introduced a best-ever welcome offer, whereby you can earn 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending.

This is an exceptional bonus, and this card is absolutely worth picking up for the points, especially given that eligibility isn’t mutually exclusive with other Atmos Rewards cards. In the long run, the card can be worth it for the perks for travel on Alaska and Hawaiian.

Anecdotally I find Bank of America business cards to be quite easy to get approved for, including if you’ve had the card in the past. Applying for this card also shouldn’t count as a further card toward the Chase 5/24 limit, if that’s of concern to you.

Anyone plan to pick up the Atmos Rewards Business Card with this great offer?

#6144. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders with several Capital One business cards, including the following:

Holding one of these cards does not guarantee the free add-on. To check, log in to Capital One Business Travel. If the complimentary rebooking feature is available to you, it will be automatically added to your eligible flight at checkout.

The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

New applicants can potentially get even more value from Capital One Business Travel through the card's current welcome offer, which includes up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds:

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic for Business, Capital One Spark Miles for Business, Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business, Capital One Spark Pro and Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses

This is useful protection, but it comes with restrictions. The original ticket must be booked through Capital One Business Travel, and the disruption must meet the three-hour threshold within 24 hours of departure.

It's also temporary. The complimentary is available for eligible bookings made through the end of January 2027, while supplies last. Capital One hasn't published a final eligible departure date.

Still, this could be valuable for business travelers with time-sensitive trips. It can also eliminate business travel bottlenecks, such as waiting for a manager to approve a costly replacement ticket.

Related: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight

Capital One's new feature will help you with rebooking options, but it won't cover the other costs of getting stranded.

For example, if you're rebooked on a flight the following day, you may need to pay for a hotel, meals or transportation. That's where eligible credit card trip delay coverage could help.

Trip delay insurance covers unexpected costs related to qualifying delays, such as accommodations, meals or transportation while waiting out your delay.

That gap can be especially important during weather or air traffic control disruptions, when airlines generally do not pay for stranded travelers' hotels or meals.

Not every eligible card includes trip delay coverage, though. The Venture X Business covers up to $500 per ticket for meals and lodging when a trip is delayed six hours or more or requires an overnight stay.* Cash-back cards like the Spark Cash don't include it. Check your card's benefits guide before you travel.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

Capital One's complimentary flight disruption rebooking could be a valuable perk for business travelers facing cancellations or lengthy delays, particularly when another airline can get them to their destination sooner.

And it costs you nothing extra when booking on Capital One Business Travel.

The promotion is available to select Capital One customers for a limited time, so check whether the benefit appears at checkout before relying on it for an upcoming trip.

*For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply.

#6142. At the Races: Regional realignment

By Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Niels Lesniewski

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

#6140. Chase Adds Qantas And Cathay Pacific Transfers—More Access To Premium Award Seats

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18. For me, the biggest value is access to business and first class award seats that these airlines don’t make available to members of other frequent flyer programs.

These are Chase’s first new airline transfer partners in more than five years. And they’re an unambiguously positive addition, even if neither becomes the program most cardmembers use most often.

Eligible cards include Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve for Business, Ink Business Preferred and J.P. Morgan Reserve. Both new partners transfer at 1:1. Hyatt transfers are now less generous for Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred: 4 Chase points become 3 Hyatt points, while the Reserve cards retain 1:1. That distinction doesn’t apply to these new airline partners. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) is a strong card for actual spending, with 4 points per dollar on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar on dining. Adding more transfer partners makes the value of those points even greater. Why I Want Qantas Points Chase already had ways to book oneworld flights through programs like British Airways and Iberia. But being able to book an airline doesn’t mean having access to all of its award seats. Airlines increasingly keep more of their premium cabin availability for their own members. As I explained when Rove added Qantas transfers, Qantas offers its members award space that American AAdvantage, Alaska and British Airways members can’t book. I have family in Australia and have had real success finding Qantas business class awards when there’s flexibility over the U.S. gateway and travel date. I’ll set alerts across several flights rather than insist on one. Some flight between Australia and the U.S. will inevitably open up with a couple of business class awards, usually around 60 days out. Qantas can also be useful for Emirates redemptions. I’d generally rather book the same available Emirates business class seat through Copa ConnectMiles, though. Copa charges 80,000 miles one way between the U.S. and Dubai in business class without fuel surcharges. And Qantas is no longer an unrestricted way around Emirates’ first class award limits. Booking Emirates first class with Qantas points requires Qantas Silver status or higher, and passengers must be at least nine years old. Cathay Offers More Award Space And Lower British Airways Surcharges Cathay Pacific is similar. Its own members get access to far more premium cabin award space than members of partner programs. Asia Miles prices can be high, though. I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage. It’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus). American Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added. Chase Is Finally Adding Airline Partners Again Chase’s last new transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it showed Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future.
