#6139. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6137. World Of Hyatt Status Revamps For 2027—Award Stacking And New Benefit Choices, But Cuts Come Also

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027. I’ve wanted that for years. They’re also extending milestone free night certificates from 180 days to a year, and adding rewards after just 10 qualifying nights.

This isn’t an across the board improvement. Suite upgrades will expire sooner. The suite upgrade choice at 50 nights gets cut in half. And My Hyatt Concierge becomes something you select alongside other rewards, rather than something everyone automatically receives at 60 nights. Free parking will no longer be an automatic benefit on award stays for Globalists.

When I covered Hyatt’s last major status benefit refresh in November 2023, I liked it overall. They made awards transferable, added choices, and let members try Globalist benefits before earning Globalist. Guest of Honor became limited, but the Milestone Rewards themselves mostly got better.

This time there are new and better options. I genuinely like a lot of the choices, but there are real tradeoffs. Hyatt is pitching the changes as more choice and flexibility, based on listening to members. That’s actually fair for much of this, though I don’t think members told them what they really wanted was for suite upgrade to expire up to a year earlier.

Hyatt will allow members to combine eligible awards on the same reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and the new Free Parking Awards. This fixes one of the problems I’ve been complaining about for years. A free night certificate is something you often want to use on a special leisure stay. That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable. Combining Guest of Honor with a suite upgrade is useful, too. You can give someone Globalist treatment and confirm their suite ahead of time, rather than leaving the room upgrade to availability when they arrive. Hyatt also promises an enhanced Pay My Way experience, letting members mix awards, points, cash and Points + Cash by night. Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration, Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable.

Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration,

Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights. Qualifying nights / base points   What you receive 10 / 20,000   Choose one: 1 qualifying night credit, $25 FIND experience credit, or $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit. 20 / 35,000   Choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 30 / 50,000   Choose 10,000 bonus points or a Category 1–4 free night. Also choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 40 / 65,000   Receive 1 Guest of Honor Award. Also choose one: 5 qualifying night credits, $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 50 / 80,000   Choose one: $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card. The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade. One Fewer Suite Upgrade, And A Choice About Your Concierge The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time. I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program: [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights.

The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards.

That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card.

The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade.

The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time.

The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive:

You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go.

And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and:

In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time.

I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program:

[B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

As before, lifetime Globalists retain their concierge without having to stay 60 nights.

The new parking award covers a qualifying paid or award stay of up to seven nights, and can be gifted. It appears among the choices at 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights. However it’s no longer simply a benefit for Globalists redeeming points for free nights. I wrote in that Hyatt was surveying turning automatic benefits into awards you could choose and they’ve done that with this one. The benefit is no longer unlimited It comes with a tradeoff – the benefit is instead of something else And you have to plan ahead, one more thing to track and manage, rather than something that’s just ‘taken care of’ in recognition of your loyalty. Hyatt explains the decision to me as, [T]his decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit. If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer! And not using it regularly doesn’t mean the option isn’t valued. It may not have been the most valuable benefit of Globalist for most people, but I wouldn’t personally make the tradeoff (in fairness, I’m someone that did use and get value from it). Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it. A Year To Use Every Award Is Both An Improvement And A Cut Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that currently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. Note that this change applies to Milestone Rewards earned starting in 2027. So any that you earn at the end of 2026, and redeem in 2027, follow the old rules. Hyatt confirms, Only awards earned and selected after January 1, 2027 follow the new 365 expiration from issuance. So, a 2026 award (even if selected in 2027) would carry the current 2026 expiration rules. More Free Night Choices And Delta Status At Higher Milestones Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them.

I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose.

Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into.

Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going.

For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon.

There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards.

The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty.

Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. Hyatt’s concierge service for globalists is generally useless.

So while having to choose concierge service over other benefits is a devaluation of globalist service, it’s, practically speaking, not a huge loss for most members.

The loss of free parking on award-redemption stays is somewhat similar. On paper, it’s a significant devaluation. However, how many guests actually use it? If I’m going a resort, I’m not arriving with a car. Same for if I’m redeeming points to stay at the Park Hyatt in Paris or wherever. So, practically speaking, it may not be a huge loss for many elites.

What I don’t understand is why wouldn’t you come up with better offerings for globalists who do 100, 120 or 150+ nights?

I wish they would have created a benefit to compensate for the growing number of Hyatt Regency and Grand Hyatt properties WITHOUT an open or operational club lounge.

By the way, I would note that eliminating free parking on award stays is great for owners/franchisees. They can’t charge you a resort or destination fee. But now they can charge you $70 or $100 for parking that used to be free. In short, it’s a way to extract a portion of the revenue lost from waived resort or destination fees from a segment of guests who arrive with a car and want to park it at the hotel.

Outstanding article, Gary, with a lot of nuance missed by others. Don’t know if your Hyatt contacts gave you the answer to this, but if you don’t choose a Concierge at 60 nights, will you still have access to the Globalist telephone number? I have used my Concierge once or twice in the last five years, but I have used the Globalist line quite a bit.

Hi Gary. Do you know if not selecting the concierge benefit next year will still give you access to the concierge line? I can live without the MHC, but the concierge line is something I frequently use for everything.

Soooooo what if a Globalist gives another member a Guest of Honor award? Presumably the GofH will no longer be eligible to receive free parking?

@PH – GoH on its own will no longer mean free parking on award redemption, you’d have to gift both a goh + free parking award if you want them to have both but they’ll stack

Interesting. I have used the free parking benefit four times a year in New York. Andaz charges $90/nt for my suv. That’s nearly $200 for two nts The other times have been at other properties for $45-$65/nt for 6 nts@ around $300. I would say that’s a significant devaluation.

@DSK – having a concierge doesn’t preclude you from using the globalist number, but you can also just use the concierge # to speak with a concierge even if your own is not available

I think for the most part, (other than the switch from AA to DL) these are positive improvements overall. When is the last time you could say that about ANY loyalty program? Almost everything I’ve written to Hyatt about for the past two years has finally occurred…particularly the 1 yr expiration on threshold night awards. I agree with @FNT Delta Diamond that they need to enhance the rewards for power users…Perhaps for 2028 they could institute a “rollover” option for elites with 110+ nights: maybe allow excess nights above 100 to rollover to the next year’s qualifying year so that Globalist renewal is automatic or much easier? Or perhaps a single year “boost” if one doesn’t hit 60 in the next year? Just a thought. As this shows, it never hurts to ask!

Rooms for points mostly grossly overpriced. Chase transfer cut last straw. No bueno

I call BS on Hyatt saying Globalists don’t use the free parking. This actively costs them hard cash and they wanted to minimize the cash outlay.

Of course Globalists are using free parking on award stays. They are going after the travel hacking community and not the road warriors who earn Globalist on paid stays, because they weren’t getting free parking on paid stays. Easy for them to blur those lines but we can see through their statement.

https://youtube.com/shorts/WpGW1-wVv7Y?si=uSj-ikgis-9UnX4b

I feel it’s overall a downgrade, but like the fact that FNA will last longer, and the ability to stack awards is great. Also, if the online booking upgrades work the way intended, I don’t know that I will need a concierge. That’s the main thing I call for (combine an award and cash booking, and use on SNA, for example).

I see this as almost entirely a devaluation. Most of the new choices strike me as borderline thoughtless/pointless additions – the award at ten nights is basically useless for me and I’m honestly tempted to ignore it when it hits (probably by mid-January) – and whatever their bloviation may say, when the parking thing matters, it makes a big effing dent, and parking fees are showing up in more and more dubiously-justified places all the time. Losing that would be worth throwing the baby out with the bath water here, and possibly throwing the bath out as well – the “alternatives” it let them introduce aren’t worth the trade.

I realize that perspectives can legitimately vary, but this is a noticeable devaluation with a few minimal bright spots (being better able to bundle three Cat 1-7 awards is nice), but taken as a whole I’d rather tell them to shove the whole package somewhere the sun don’t shine.

To the extent they claim to have been trying to improve the program, they failed miserably and should feel bad about their efforts.

Overall a devaluation, but not a large one. Neither of the key improvements I’ve repeatedly suggested happened (make club awards useable for breakfast at hotels without a club, make cat 1-4 night awards cat 1-5 or 1-6 so they covered most “normal” hotels as they used to).

losing globalist free parking on award stays is a sizable loss. for 2026 qualified globalists, hyatt should add 1-4 free parking awards in 2027 to soften thid unexpected blow. cc spending globalists will feel the brunt. many will rethink and some change 2027 cc spending habits.

I’ve got a reservation using points for NYE + 2 nights. So, am I going to get screwed on the free parking? Of course, this is the first time having to park a car on a points stay in a long time.

They badly need the option to top up cat 1-4 certs with points like Marriott has. The desirable properties keep getting moved to cat 5.

I have a problem with taking away free parking. Do we know if the new rules are taking effect January 1, 2027 for those earning Globalist for 2027? We would not have had the option to get a free parking pass as yet.

Hi Gary, Great review! Any change to the number and type of awards given to lifetime globalist?

Once again, the shorter expiration date on the suite upgrade awards may cause some to delay achieving a milestone so they could have one to use in December, January, or February. Hopefully they still keep the 90 day period to choose.

I like the changes and excellent analysis, Gary-very fair reading!

Now, I want to know when the premium Hyatt card will be launched and what mechanisms it will have to shorten one’s way towards Globalist.

Along those lines, will Hyatt permit holders of this card to top off any and or all certificates? Marriott has permittied this, IHG has permitted this and it is time that Hyatt does as well, seeing that Chase issues cards for all 3 chains.

Moreover, it will be in the spirit of permitting a milestone award seeker a more tailored award.

I may not value many Category 7 properties, but perhaps a Category 5 or 6 speaks more to me — if given a choice between 2 Category 4 awards that can be topped off as opposed to 1 Category 7 award, the choice would be easy.

At this point Cat 1-4 certs are practically useless. With the annual devaluation looming in 5 months they will become even worse. Soon it may just only be an airport hotel at a mid-sized airport in middle America. If they were making changes they should have elevated the Cat 1-4 FNC to at the very least Cat 1-5.

Gary, I have until Jan 21 to make my choice for 50 nights. I used to wait until January to get the longer expiration date (Feb 2029 instead of Feb 2028).

Does this impact choices already earned in other words if I wait until January to choose I will get a shorter expiration date that if I for the suite upgrade awards then if I chose in December?

Anyone know if you earn a milestone in 2026 but select it in 2027 if it will have a Feb 2029 expiration? You have 90 days to choose I can’t imagine two different expiration dates based on when issued but maybe?

My reaction: Cat 1-4 awards remain close to useless. Fix that and we can talk.

Loss of parking sucks. We drive to the Hyatt Regency Huntington Beach resort and parking is $60 a night. Kids grew up at the resort. My concierge has been super helpful. Booking the suite at Grand Hyatt Tokyo you can’t select 4 people to book a standard room but a suite can sleep 4 so I had to call into the concierge to explain the issue since I couldn’t book online and she was able to book us with points apply the SUA and change to 4 person occupancy. Maybe I can do that without a concierge but it sure helps to have someone on the phone doing that for me. Love the upgrade on free night certificates.

@nsx at FlyerTalk — For. Real. Dawg. For. Real.

@principal lewis – LALF stated that Globalist status earned in 2026 included free parking until Feb 2028 so, based on that, they plan to honor it next year. IMHO, a borderline change. Sure I used it a few times if I traveled and rented a car but much of my travel is international w no car. Also, someone complained about it being removed for road warriors who stayed 60 plus nights – well I suspect you are traveling on OPM and can expense the parking so, again, no big loss.

Gary- nice summary. But have you heard anything further on where this story started- with the Hyatt- AA divorce? And the Globalist benefit for CK? For those that don’t know: CK year ends on April 30, 2027. Hyatt year ends on FEB 28 2027.

So like in past years will CK renew Globalists for another year- like ?

In your article from September, you said, “American’s ConciergeKey members who have their accounts linked retain Hyatt Globalist status through February 2028. Confirmed by American (I asked this specifically)”

But many of us are being told by CK team that CK team has no idea. And there is no mention of this in the Hyatt-AA announcement pages.

@Gary – Can you try and work your excellent sources, to get AA or Hyatt to give us something more specific here? Thank you!!!

The loss of parking will directly impact me. I think I’ve probably used that on 6 nights this year, including valet at PH Auckland and Seabird. And while I never email my concierge, I do frequently call the concierge number and greatly value the fast, competent service.

“Only awards earned and selected after January 1, 2027 follow the new 365 expiration from issuance. So, a 2026 award (even if selected in 2027) would carry the current 2026 expiration rules.” This needs some additional clarification from Hyatt, if the 50 night milestone is hit in late 2026 and SUA is selected 1/1/2027… does that SUA count as earned in 2026 and thus wouldn’t expire until Feb 28, 2029? Or would that SUA expire 1/1/2028?

The 365 day expiration for a SUA is horrible. No longer possible to confirm a SUA before registration opens. And if trying to secure a suite a year in advance, you have to time when you earn the reward. This is an incentive to stay elsewhere so you don’t hit the milestone too early and have to select an award before you want it.

Also, can premium suite discount be used on a cash + points booking?

@Retired Gambler: The obvious counter is that if you’re using OPM and you’re using points, either you’re doing something wrong or someone is absolutely flooded with points and using them to pocket cash from work trips.

@Nick – earn a milestone award in late 2026, claim it 1/1/27, and it expires 2/28/29… i asked this (with this example) explicitly

@ZQin – I guess I don’t know what you mean by giving you something more specific? I asked American Airlines explicity what happens to ConciergeKey member Globalist status and was told that they’d get to keep that status through February 2028. What further information would you like me to request?

UnitedEF, that’s exactly where it bites, $60 a night adds up fast on a week by the pier. If you pay cash for some nights, free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from a bunch of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory differ by country. Then weigh that against points plus a parking award. And with the beach path down to Main Street the car can mostly stay put lol

I wish they would address the increasing number of properties that don’t accept suite upgrade awards. The list is pretty long at this point.

Only one possible disagreement on your take-

Regarding the parking: “If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer!”

I suspect that those 5% that used the benefit probably used it a LOT. Outliers (especially travel hackers) can be the 1 percenters of travel, costing them quite a bit. Looks like a surgical strike on the outliers for manh of these and prior changes

#6136. What Pro-Lifers Need to Win Elections

In election after election, pro-lifers are being outspent and outorganized.

Demonstrators participate in the annual March for Life in Washington, D.C., January 23, 2026.

It’s become something of a truism that the pro-life movement lacked a plan for how to pursue its goals after Roe v. Wade was overturned. Indeed, three more states (Nevada, Virginia, and Missouri) saw abortion-related statewide ballot measures go against pro-lifers in 2026. The recriminations have been bitter against the leaders and key advocacy groups on the pro-life side: They are political naifs; they are incompetent at messaging and strategy; they are self-important, wannabe big shots who just want proximity to power; they are too focused on federal politics; their organizations’ CEOs make too much money (hilariously false — ask me how I know) for too little results.

There is plenty of blame to go around, but I think such critiques are missing the key, practical problems the pro-life movement faces. The reality is that the pro-abortion side simply has far more money and organization than the pro-life side, and these gaps have been decisive in election after election. Without the funding for political organization and campaigns, pro-lifers simply cannot win.

Demonstrators participate in the annual March for Life in Washington, D.C., January 23, 2026.

John Gerardi is the executive director of Right to Life of Central California in Fresno. A lawyer and the founding CEO and current development director of the Obria Medical Clinics of Central California, he hosts the radio shows and podcasts The John Gerardi Show and Right to Life Radio.

On “What Pro-Lifers Need to Win Elections”

#6135. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has announced a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage."

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

The good news is that major ride-hailing players Uber, Lyft and Blacklane all have launched Thanksgiving offers, including one that is exclusive to our TPG members.

Here's how to make the most of your holiday ride transport.

Related: Here’s what Thanksgiving foods you can bring in your carry-on and what has to be checked

Through Nov. 30, Uber is running a promotion called "From Bad Seats to Better Rides." If you get squeezed into a middle seat with no armrest or end up in the last row by the lavatory, you could receive up to 30% off your Uber ride home from the airport.

To take part, register your flight and seat details on Uber's Thanksgiving promotion page. Uber provides several examples of undesirable seats but has not published a complete list of what qualifies as undesirable. Individual savings vary, and terms apply, so check the offer added to your Uber account before booking. In our testing, you will not be required to submit a boarding pass or an image of your undesirable seat to receive a discount.

TPG tip: Link your Delta SkyMiles and Uber accounts and select Delta as your earning partner before you travel. You will earn 1 mile per eligible dollar on UberX airport rides, 2 miles per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides and 3 miles per eligible dollar on Uber Reserve rides in the U.S. Note that taxes, fees, mandatory charges and tips do not earn miles.

Related: From Starbucks to Uber: Airline and hotel partnerships that earn points and miles

Uber One Member Days run through Dec. 1, where Uber says members can unlock up to $500 in savings across rides, deliveries, hotels and other offers. Some deals are targeted, so check your email and your Uber app to see if you are eligible, but offers may include:

No purchase is necessary to enter either sweepstakes.

TPG tip: Link your Marriott Bonvoy and Uber accounts and select Marriott as your earning partner. You will earn 3 Marriott Bonvoy points per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides in the U.S., including those booked with Reserve and 2 points per eligible dollar on UberX rides booked with Reserve. Members who have not linked the two accounts can also earn 1,000 bonus points for linking by Nov. 24, plus another 1,000 points after completing an eligible premium or Reserve ride by the same date.

You can link both Delta and Marriott to Uber, but only one can be selected as the earning partner for a ride at a time, so choose which currency is more useful to you.

Related: Marriott announces Uber partnership changes: The good, the bad and the totally worthless

United MileagePlus members can earn 8 United miles per eligible dollar on scheduled airport rides with Lyft through Nov. 30, twice the standard rate of 4 miles per dollar. Link your MileagePlus and Lyft accounts and select United as your active rewards partner before booking.

The offer applies to eligible rides requested, completed and paid for in the U.S. or Puerto Rico.

Make sure you schedule your ride in advance, because unscheduled airport rides only earn 3 miles per eligible dollar, while most standard personal rides earn 1 mile per eligible dollar.

Note that taxes, fees, tolls and tips do not earn miles.

TPG tip: Shift your rewards up a gear by paying with the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees), and you will earn 5 total Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar on qualifying Lyft purchases through Sept. 30, 2027. Both cards earn 1 point per dollar on purchases outside their bonus categories.

Sapphire Reserve cardholders also receive a $10 monthly in-app Lyft credit through Sept. 30, 2027. Unused credit expires at the end of each calendar month.

Related: How to easily earn extra rewards on Lyft rides

If you would rather avoid a crowded airport pickup zone, why not treat yourself to Blacklane? The global luxury chauffeur service operates in more than 500 cities across more than 60 countries, and its fixed prices include standard taxes, tolls, tips and fees.

TPG members can currently receive an exclusive $80 credit toward two chauffeur journeys in the U.S. To claim it, sign in to or create a TPG account through the TPG Member Offers page, then click through to Blacklane from the offer.

TPG tip: Bilt members can redeem Bilt Cash toward Blacklane rides each calendar year: up to $50 for Blue and Silver members, $100 for Gold members and $150 for Platinum members. Blacklane rides booked through Bilt also earn 1 Bilt Point per dollar.

Related: No surge, no scramble: Why I loved using Blacklane for my latest airport transfer

Thanksgiving airport rides can be expensive, but this holiday season you may be able to reduce the cost and/or increase your rewards.

Uber's bad-seat offer is the most straightforward discount if your aircraft seat qualifies and is a fun and lighthearted way to reward those whose seat allocation is unfortunate. Uber One members should also check their accounts for targeted airport and hotel offers, while the Lyft promotion is an easy way to earn double United miles on a ride many travelers will book anyway.

Link your loyalty accounts, select the right earning partner and check your card benefits before traveling to ensure a happy and rewarding holiday.

#6133. Demand For $1,589 In Rental Car Damage Dropped After Pointing Out Illegal Fees

Sixt demanded $1,589 from a customer for splatter and scuffs on a rental car, including nearly $500 in illegal fees. The customer disputed the claim, complained to consumer agencies, and says it went to collections anyway. The bill disappeared once the practice came under scrutiny. Christopher Nienhuis, a Colorado resident, rented a Buick at Milwaukee airport in October while visiting Marquette University. Days after returning it, he received a damage bill for black splatter around the license plate and near the tires, along with white scuffing around the rear windshield. He says he didn’t cause the damage and that the black material could simply be washed off. Sixt dropped the claim a week after being contacted by a news reporter. Four Renters Were Billed Fees Wisconsin Doesn’t Allow Four customers with disputed claims from the same airport location complained of illegal charges. Todd Lofgren: $6,265 for “graffiti.” He described white specks near a tire and along the bumper. The photos and invoice were dated August 18, three days after he returned the car. The bill included $1,161 in prohibited fees. Sixt dropped it September 28 after he challenged it through multiple channels. Brenda Bassett: nearly $600 for a dent already documented. The rear dent was listed in her rental agreement before she took the 2025 Toyota. About $137 consisted of diminished value and appraisal fees. A September 15 letter came from Strala Group, which handles claims for Sixt. The claim was dropped. Autumn Wojciechowski: $872 for a scratch underneath the car. She’d photographed the vehicle before driving away, but not its underside. Nearly $200 of her October 2025 damage invoice consisted of prohibited fees. This claim was dropped, too. All four claims have been withdrawn. Wisconsin law limits damage liability to reasonable repair costs, reflecting discounts available to the rental company, or the vehicle’s value before the damage, whichever is lower. Loss of use, administrative charges and appraisal fees are prohibited. Diminished value charges (loss in resale value) aren’t allowed either. Sixt Already Settled A Damage Billing Lawsuit Sixt’s 2025 damage billing settlement addressed allegations involving estimated repairs, diminished value, loss of use and administrative charges. The $11 million package included about $2.87 million in potential refunds and $6.6 million in abandoned collection claims, along with legal and administrative costs. The incentives are lousy. A customer can pay to make a collection demand go away, turn it over to insurance, or spend hours fighting. If the company withdraws a bad claim only when someone gets enough attention, everyone else still has to decide whether contesting it is worth the trouble. I’ve called rental car fees the scammiest in travel. These damage add-ons are especially difficult to comparison shop because you don’t discover them until after you’ve returned the car. Sixt Isn’t Great, But You Expect Charges To Be Correct I’ve found Sixt offers an inferior experience in the U.S. market. My Miami rental years ago involved a Mercedes they didn’t and a proposed alternative of a $30 a day upgrade for a lesser car. I canceled and went to National. The Milwaukee airport said its lease requires Sixt to follow the law and allows termination for an uncured violation after notice. But the airport said it was waiting for the state consumer protection agency to determine that a violation occurred. It’s not yet clear whether they’ve stopped charging these fees in Wisconsin. This is common practice in Europe. Hertz sent me an invoice and charged my credit card almost a year after a rental in Germany for $460.00 for “damages.” I disputed the charges as I still had my return showing that they signed off with no damage. AMEX refunded my money, so Hertz turned it over to a collection agency in PA. They called me and I told them to go to hell and sue me. The collection dude said, “No one is going to sue you for $460.00,” so I sent them a letter telling them to cease and desist contacting me about the charge and if they wanted to sue, I was willing to counter sue as I had paperwork saying the car was returned undamaged. Last I heard of it and it never turned up on my credit report. Every time I rent in Europe, I get dinged for a toll, or in Italy it was for driving in a “congested area.” You figure they steal $100 to $200 from every renter, that is a good chunk of change a year.

I would never rent from Sixt. Although rental companies overall have become quite sleazy. In June I rented from Thrifty and returned the car full with no complaints or comments from them. A charge of about $160 showed up later with no notice or explanation. Ultimately they claimed it was for “fuel and service”, neither of which had been needed. It was returned full and there was no indication of any amount of fuel or rate per gallon. Basically a random fee. They took a long time to respond to Chase and then responded to claim I never made. Chase would not re-open it because they claimed it was “too old” at that point. An email to the executive office appears to have resolved it and the fee so far is not reinstated. I’ve had the best service with Enterprise off-airport locations and it sounds like AmEx is better about charge backs. But it’s hard to trust any car rental company these days.

Sixt Is the scammiest of all the companies. Decline their insurance at your peril, I’ve had 2 bogus claims from them totaling well over $2000 for “damage”. One in Vancouver where the damage was reported days after returning and then one in the UK where damage reported is an absolute fallacy, a bunch of small scratches and general wear and tear which would never show up in a damage report.

Sixt are horrible! They rented a damaged car to me in Vegas. Wasted time returning it. Made no apologies, or any compensation. A few days after I had returned the car I received a bill for damages to the new car in the trunk area, mainly scratches and damage to the pain. I was only using soft sided bags, so it couldn’t have been me. I had to argue with them over the whole thing. They finally relented. Never ever ging to rent from them again!

Sixt got me for some damage that I know I didn’t cause. I didn’t think I needed to record video of the car after I brought it back. Credit card CDW paid for 90% of it except for a lost depreciation fee of $200. Snakey.

This shady behavior must be part of the rental car playbook. I was charged $200 for small dings to Europcar rental in Portugal 5 years ago that I’m pretty sure were not my fault. The problem was that the car was delivered to me in a dark garage in Porto, and while I inspected the car I was jet lagged and it was dark and I stupidly did not take pics. I’m guessing that for every claim like this that is disputed and charges are dropped, there are 10 where the renter just pays to make it go away.

Im not going to no collections over a damage dispute. Ruining my credit? Pay for it and sue later.

I don’t rent cars very often, but when I do, I video the entire exterior and interior at pickup and again when I return the car along with the guy/girl I hand the keys to. I had one of these BS damage incidents several years ago and I got dinged for something I didn’t do and it was a couple months after I rented. Fortunately I was still in possession of the turn in receipt so I didn’t have to pay. All that being said, they are scam artists of the 10th degree and I don’t trust any of them.. Video and photograph your rentals.

Avis is notorious for ‘cleaning fees’. 9 times out of 10 the claim is dropped. It is important to take pics before AND after.

Maybe I’ve just been lucky, but this is (one of the reasons) why I like National. They don’t seem to want to nickel and dime you over everything. The “allowed” amount of damage is pretty generous. I’ve never had them hassle me over anything. And the refill costs if you bring a car back not full of fuel aren’t totally ridiculous either.

Wisconsin law also requires rental car companies to provide you with independent damage appraisals and a right to inspect before they can just charge you for damages. I once got billed by Avis for repairs for damage that I didn’t cause weeks after my rental. I challenged it to the Avis General Counsel’s office, pointing out that they didn’t follow the law, and they dropped the charges.

It really amazes me Congress doesn’t take on Hertz and now Sixt. This is literally a 99.9% issue. You would get so much publicity and public support.

I had one management job where I had a lot of my team traveli to UK. There was a span where my company was between.major rental contracts in Europe, and in the interim they were pointing us to Sixt, and unlike in the US, we self-insured. SIxt was really good at finding (plastic) wheel cover scuffs and paint scratches, consistently $700 to 800 GBP. Fortunately, they were not selected for the new contract. My company has about 4000 people on travel at any given time.

Ok, on-topic… *serious face* Used to be a fan, but now I hate them the most and will ironically go with Avis or even Hertz instead. The ‘best’ part about Sixt is that once they target you with one of these scams, and you fight back (decline to pay), they then put you on their ‘Do Not Rent’ list, so, even if you mistakenly trust them again, they’ll not let you! Seems like a win-win.

I have rented from Sixt in Manchester, Dublin and Iceland. They are not just “snakes”…they are VIPERS. Iceland was the worst experience. ONE agent for about 30 people in line. Then they try to upsell you on every possible thing in the world. I was finally given the keys to my car. I went to the lot to claim it and…it is blocked in by about 15 other cars! Before I took the car, I took pictures of the car from every angle, every scratch, every mark and dirt speck, gas gauge, car clock and gas gauge with my watch beside it. inside and out! I don’t trust them. I finally got someone to make a hole for me to get out. When I returned the car, 4 hours before my flight, there was one agent and 30 people trying to either get a car or return one. The outside check in person went over the car and noted all sorts of dings and dents. BE SURE to take pictures of the exact same areas when you return, too! When I FINALLY got to the desk clerk, he tried to charge me for the dents and dings. That’s when I pulled out my iPhone and went over every single picture. He capitulated! The meta data on the photos are “gold” as the camera or cell phone camera puts that data on the picture. I’m in the airline business. Seems that other employees got the same treatment. I got Sixt removed from our “authorized” vendor list. WATCH OUT!

Sixt demanded $800 from me a few years ago for a BMW X3 we rented in California. The lady in checkout at SJC airport was chatting on her phone, and SIXT knew we would be turning in the car early in the morning by way of a drop off.

Lesson learned: ALWAYS do a 360⁰ video when picking up the vehicle rather than being slapped a bill for other people’s collective wear and tear. Stay away from SIXT

#6132. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#6131. American Airlines Plans To Nearly Triple Its Phoenix A Gates Lounge Space—And Add 150% More Seats

American Airlines Phoenix lounges are one of the biggest holes in the airline’s effort to offer a better product. They’re been too small, crowded dated, and barely worth visiting even when you have access. Already American expects 18 million lounge visits in 2026 up 80% from 10 million in 2016 while passenger traffic is up just 12.1%. What may have worked in the past no longer does. And American is finally announcing substantial investment in all three Admirals Clubs, adding enough room that getting away from a crowded gate might actually mean getting away from a crowd. Here’s what’s changing: Location   Planned Changes A19–A21   Near term: new food service area, infrastructure for expanded food and drink offerings, and facility updates. B5–B7   New self-service food and beverage area, 20% more seats, refreshed interiors and improved support space. Both A clubs, including A7–A9   Longer term: nearly triple their combined footprint, approximately 150% more seats, and refreshed furnishings and finishes. A club seating would become about 2.5 times current level. American isn’t sharing expected completion dates, actual seat counts or square footage. And there’s no Phoenix Flagship Lounge announcement. What’s perhaps most interesting to me is they’re spending on Terminal 4 even as they committed to invest as the anchor airline for Phoenix’s planned $4.5 billion West Terminal. The airport expects a late 2033 opening (so sometime after that, natch). That’s seven years away. American can’t sell a premium experience today on the promise that its lounges will become better in the mid-2030s. But the American I’ve come to known wouldn’t invest today when they’ll also be investing later. Phoenix unveiled its preferred West Terminal concept at Tuesday’s Industry Day, which American CEO Robert Isom attended. So the timing of this announcement wasn’t a coincidence. American, though, is investing in its lounges in a real turnaround. I suggested last year that I’d believe their commitment to becoming a more premium carrier and focusing on revenue growth rather than just cost control when the capital investments started – clubs and new planes. We’re still waitin on the expected aircraft order, but American is planning to deliver a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month on average over two to three years. Phoenix had been a real omission from the announced pipeline. After years of club closures and renovations I described as “modern hospital,” American developed a much warmer design. Washington National’s E concourse club, followed by Denver, Newark and Philadelphia, showed what they could do with better lighting, wood, and places that are actually comfortable to sit and work. The food has been improving as well. I covered the additional hot dishes and better charcuterie in Admirals Clubs. And Flagship lounge food is getting better. Flagship Dining now offers sit down meals and good wine for long haul business class passengers. The current lounge pipeline includes: Airport   Project Charlotte   More than 40,000 square feet above the atrium, plus a separately announced Flagship Lounge. Dallas–Fort Worth   A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club and Terminal F Provisions. Miami   A new Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club, nearly doubling total lounge space. Chicago O’Hare   A replacement Concourse L club exceeding 10,000 square feet. Washington National   Rebuilding the D club with 50% more seats. Austin   More than 12,000 square feet with an outdoor terrace. Permits are in hand, and I expect a 2027 opening. Nashville   About 17,400 square feet with outdoor terraces. Construction is targeted for 2027. New York JFK   A 3,700 square foot Provisions location with a dedicated barista bar. San Antonio’s new terminal plans also include its first Admirals Club. And Los Angeles Flagship Dining reopened November 5. American announced Citi branding at Admirals Club entrances. It’s part of their new card agreement that is more of a joint venture than supplier relationship. Citi gets an airport lounge presence through American’s network. The Executive card includes membership, while Globe and Strata Elite each provide four passes a year. The clubs help sell three different credit cards. Lounge pricing pushes frequent flyers toward Citi. The Executive card’s annual fee is $695 for new applicants. A full standalone Admirals Club membership is $1,200–$1,400, while even the restricted $750 Single membership costs more than the card and leaves out guests and partner lounges. American is making the card the obvious way to buy access. Better clubs help get customers to apply and give them a reason to renew. Once they’re carrying the card, American and Citi have more opportunities to get their spending. And with Globe and Strata Elite distributing passes alongside Executive memberships, American needs more seats./ Topics on this pageAdmirals ClubAirport loungeAmerican AirlinesCitibankPhoenix Sky Harbor International AirportAustinChicagoDenverMiamiNashvilleNew YorkO'HarePhiladelphiaPhoenixRobert IsomSan AntonioTerminal 4+12 more More From View from the Wing
