What better way to kick off the holiday season than by planning your next vacation?

Whether you’re looking to bask in the sun on a tropical Caribbean getaway or explore glaciers along Alaska’s mesmerizing coastline, Norwegian Cruise Line is offering a noteworthy Black Friday deal you don’t want to miss.

NCL is offering 50% off all sailings* — nearly 350 destinations — regardless of itinerary or ship. This lucrative cruise deal lets families, couples or even solo travelers make their dream vacation plans a reality and map out an itinerary well within their budget.

In addition to this Black Friday promotional discount, guests can enjoy an unlimited open bar, shore excursion credits and much more.

Keep reading to find out how you can save money and get more than $2,000 in value on your next cruise booking with this Black Friday deal.

NCL’s 50% off Black Friday deal* applies to all cruises and is available to book for sailings through 2028. To browse sailings for this promotion, visit NCL.com and filter by destination, port of departure, ship and duration to narrow down your perfect itinerary.

Plus, as an added bonus, this promotion can be combined with NCL’s “Free at Sea” package. Delivering more than $2,000 in value, guests can enjoy benefits such as an unlimited open bar, specialty dining, shore excursion credits and Wi-Fi.

This all-inclusive package is great for guests who want to take advantage of key cruise perks without paying a la carte for additional benefits.

And, as if this Black Friday deal couldn’t get any better, on select sailings, kids sail for free. This is a great perk for families looking to travel at a greater cost-saving value.

Note that fare prices shown are in U.S. dollars on a per-person basis and include taxes, fees and port expenses.

With nearly 350 destinations to choose from, including sailings to the Bahamas, Alaska, Europe and the Caribbean, there is no shortage of adventures and options to choose from.

For instance, you could book a four-day getaway to the Bahamas, departing from Orlando, Florida (Port Canaveral) and stopping at Nassau and NCL’s private island, Great Stirrup Cay.

The Bahamian oasis is now home to a 6-acre private water park that features 19 waterslides, cliff jumps, a lazy river and more. Great Tides Waterpark opened in September 2026 and gives guests flexibility to choose their own adventure.

If a full day of thrills isn’t for you, guests can also opt to relax and enjoy the Great Life Lagoon, a 28,000-square-foot pool. For families or couples looking for a quick vacation, this could be the perfect option.

For those wanting to explore several European countries — without the hassle and additional out-of-pocket cost of booking trains, flights or hotel rooms — guests can embark on a nine-day Eurotrip starting from London and cruising to ports in France, Germany, Belgium and Denmark.

This can be a nice option for couples, those traveling with friends or even families.

As a mom of a two-year-old, it can be challenging (and stressful) to navigate trekking across Europe with a toddler. I like that cruising takes the guesswork off of meal plans, nap times and travel between countries.

Plus, unlike other cruise lines, Norwegian is known for its "freestyle cruising," which means there are no enforced dress codes or assigned dining times. As a toddler mom, I like that NCL gives guests the flexibility to book the vacation they want.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Norwegian Cruise Line ship

If cruising on a megaship is not your style, NCL offers a resort-like ship class known as the Prima Class. These smaller, more upscale ships feature a more modern aesthetic, larger outdoor areas and elevated experiences.

In March, NCL's newest ship, Norwegian Luna, set sail to destinations in the Caribbean, the Bahamas and Bermuda. This ship has signature Prima Class touches, such as Indulge Food Hall and Cagney's Steakhouse, as well as some must-try additions, including the authentic Thai restaurant Sukhothai.

Standout ship attractions include the Aqua Slidecoaster, the world's first hybrid waterslide and roller coaster, waterfront infinity pools, kids' splash pad, adults-only pool area, game room, and so much more.

Basically, the new Norwegian Luna will make it hard for guests to decide to even leave the ship.

If exploring destinations and being one of the first to set sail on a new ship is enticing, NCL is also extending this promotion to its recently unveiled ship, Norwegian Aura. The biggest ship in Norwegian's fleet will set sail in April 2027 and will feature more expansive spaces, waterslides and attractions around every corner. Itineraries for this ship include ports in the Caribbean, Greek isles, Italy and Spain.

With this 50% off Black Friday deal*, now is a great time to book your 2027 or even your 2028 travel plans and experience these brand-new cruise ships.

Whether you're planning to take advantage of this Black Friday deal or book an NCL cruise, be sure to check out the company's Latitudes Rewards program. This loyalty program is free to join and lets cruisers earn rewards and get access to exclusive discounts, onboard experiences and more.

Members can earn 1 point for every cruise night, and 1 additional point per night for reserving select rooms or when booking with a Latitudes Rewards insider offer.

As you reach a certain threshold of points, you can unlock new status tiers, which may include specialty offers, cabin upgrades, dining benefits and more.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line’s Latitudes Rewards loyalty program guide

NCL is an award-winning cruise line that offers itineraries for all types of travelers, giving action-packed thrill-seekers or guests seeking a relaxing, elevated sailing experience the flexibility to book a cruise that matches their vacation aesthetic.

And if you want to save (possibly thousands of dollars) on your 2027 or 2028 travel plans, now is the time to book with NCL and receive 50% off all cruises*.

#6128. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6127. The Return of the War Powers Debate

It’s good news that Congress and Trump will soon be fighting about the war in Iran — and about war in general.

A U.S. Navy sailor signals an F-35C Lightning II assigned to the “Argonauts” of Strike Fighter Squadron VFA-147 as it takes off from the flight deck of the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington (CVN-73), under way in the U.S. Fifth Fleet area of operations, October 7, 2026.

If there’s one subject that unifies the Democratic Party after their midterm election victory this month, it’s ending the war in Iran. Chuck Schumer, who will likely return as Senate Majority Leader when the next Congress is gaveled into session on January 3, declared that terminating the conflict was at the top of his to-do list. The top House Democrat, Hakeem Jeffries, echoed that sentiment: “We need to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. That’s been a commitment that we’ve made.”

At first glance, none of these remarks are particularly surprising. Throughout the midterms, the Democrats pegged the nagging cost of living and higher energy prices stateside to the war that’s occurring thousands of miles away in the Persian Gulf. It turned out to be a winning political strategy. Compelling President Trump into ending hostilities by filing another War Powers Resolution on the Senate floor or by cutting off funds for the war would just be a logical extension of what the party ran on.

Daniel R. DePetris is a fellow at Defense Priorities and a syndicated foreign affairs columnist at the Chicago Tribune.

#6125. Lufthansa Announced Columbus, Ohio Flight—Then City Council Blocked Part Of The Subsidy

Lufthansa announced Columbus’ first scheduled nonstop flight to Europe last month. Now the city council has refused to approve the first $300,000 of the mayor’s promised support for it. The Frankfurt flights are still scheduled to start May 5, 2027. But the fight exposes something that tends to get lost in the celebration of a new international route: local officials helped make the numbers work by offering up taxpayer money to protect the airline if route revenue falls short, and the city’s portion still needed council approval. Lufthansa plans to fly Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays using a Boeing 787-9 with Allegris business class. There’ll be 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 coach seats. The region has 38 German companies, Bayer is building a pharmaceutical plant in New Albany, and Frankfurt offers connections throughout Europe and beyond. With the city using residents’ money to guarantee it, Lufthansa’s downside is protected trying it out. The revenue guarantee draws support from several sources: Contributor Reported Support City of Columbus Up to $1 million over three years. Council blocked the proposed first $300,000 installment. Franklin County Up to $1 million over three years. JobsOhio Participating, with the amount not publicly confirmed. Councilmember Rob Dorans says his briefing identified $1 million. Columbus Partnership and local businesses Financial support promised, with the amount undisclosed. Lufthansa would collect under the guarantee if revenue falls below the agreed target, subject to caps and a three year limit. The airport’s current incentive program also offers Frankfurt service $1 million in marketing support over two years, plus two years of landing fee, terminal rent and international inspection fee waivers. That’s available as long as they operate at least 100 departures annually over at least six months. The city’s $300,000 was included in a proposed $1 million grant to One Columbus, the regional economic development organization. On November 16, council unanimously removed the airline money and subsequently approved the remaining $700,000. Dorans objects both to the spending priority and to how the deal was handled. He says residents needing help should come first, and accuses the administration of negotiating without council involvement. The administration says all nine councilmembers were offered briefings and eight participated, including Dorans. Meanwhile, Council President Shannon Hardin is running for mayor against the incumbent whose administration owns this deal. And the councilmember who introduced the amendment pulling funding actually supports the funding. That was a maneuver that allows him to bring the funding back for another vote. You’d expect Lufthansa to have an agreement spelling out its revenue guarantee before announcing the flight. Oops. It appears not every organization contributing money already made a firm commitment. The city ordinance was seeking authority to enter into a grant agreement with One Columbus. The council wasn’t technically voting to cancel a Lufthansa contract, just on whether to appropriate the funds to the entity that had promised Lufthansa a fixed guarantee. The Columbus Partnership says it still expects the flight to happen. Council could reconsider, or other backers could fill the funding gap. I’ve covered this sort of bidding for service before, including Austin offering incentives for international flights and Pittsburgh subsidizing Qatar Airways cargo service. Usually these subsidies either go to flights that would have made money anyway, or get burned through and the flight goes away. Meanwhile, I’m betting that the money comes back. #6124. So Many People Need Flights To See Dying Loved Ones That A Charity Has Paused New U.S. Requests—Your Miles Can Help

Give A Mile says it’s had to temporarily stop accepting new U.S. flight applications because it doesn’t have the miles and funding to keep up. The people asking for help are trying to reach loved ones in hospice or critical care. Some won’t have another chance to make the trip. If you have United MileagePlus miles you can spare, please help someone get there in time. I’ve supported Give A Mile with my own miles and money, and I serve on their U.S. board. Give A Mile tells me it expects to provide more than 200 flights this year, up from 164 last year. But it’s received more than 1,000 applications. In just the first nine days of November, 80 applications came in, 61 involving the United States. One of the people they’ve helped is Dale, who needed to get from Bismarck to San Francisco after his father went into hospice following surgery. He couldn’t afford the airfare, and driving wasn’t practical. A health care worker suggested Give A Mile. Give A Mile collects donated miles in its own account and uses them to book actual award tickets. Their volunteers review requests, obtain medical confirmation and arrange the flights. The organization also covers the ticket’s taxes and fees. Their holiday campaign aims to provide 50 flights. You don’t need enough miles to fund an entire ticket. Donations are pooled, so 1,000 or 5,000 miles can help complete an award that gets someone on a plane. United’s current minimum donation is just 100 miles. If you’ve got a small MileagePlus balance you haven’t found a use for, or a larger one you can spare some of, I’d appreciate your help. Donate United miles to Give A Mile here. You can also donate Aeroplan points or cash which helps cover very modest expenses like taxes and fees, the organization’s insurance and bookkeeping costs, and occasionally buying tickets when award redemption doesn’t make sense. #6122. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6121. Privatize Air Traffic Control

A plane takes off from Hollywood Burbank Airport in Burbank, Calif., October 7, 2025.

Thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving. Otherwise, Steve Martin and John Candy’s long trek home would have become a near-universal experience.

Over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop. No plane was allowed to take off from a U.S. airport for over four hours. The stoppage was necessary when the FAA’s telecommunications network suddenly failed, apparently caused by a faulty update to its decades-old tangle of copper wiring.

This was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. The previous one happened less than four years ago, in January 2023, and was also caused by technical difficulties. Republican lawmakers blamed the Biden administration last time; now, Democrats are faulting the Trump administration. But the FAA’s antiquated infrastructure isn’t a partisan issue. It’s the institutional consequence of having an unaccountable bureaucracy manage the skies.

Unlike almost every other major country, the U.S. federal government funds and operates air traffic control directly. Congress must appropriate its budget each year, and controllers must work without pay when the government shuts down. Infrastructure investments are subject to political timetables. Meanwhile, the FAA is expected to regulate the very system that it runs.

Usually, it wastes no time in dodging responsibility. Immediately after the grounding, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — who oversees the FAA as part of his department — placed the blame on Congress and past administrations for not adequately funding upgrades to the agency’s aging infrastructure. Yet the FAA received $12.5 billion from last year’s reconciliation law for that purpose. Earlier this month, it requested $30 billion more. Now, Duffy claims that he really needs $50 billion to get the job done. And we thought airlines’ add-on fees were bad.

Improvements don’t have to be so costly. The FAA has spent a quarter century trying to switch its network from copper wires to fiber-optic cables. Its counterpart up north, Nav Canada, completed most of the same transition in just 18 months.

The fundamental difference? Nav Canada was spun off from the national government in 1996 as a nonprofit corporation. The organization is funded entirely by user fees from the airlines and private aircraft that rely on its systems, not general taxes, and it’s structured to be accountable to both private stakeholders and the government. When it needs to finance capital projects, Nav Canada doesn’t have to wait for approval. It can simply issue bonds and recoup the cost over the long run.

The results are impressive. Research finds that privatization lowered costs and boosted productivity for the aviation sector, especially compared with the FAA. Safety has greatly improved, and Nav Canada leads in technological advancement. Dozens of countries have since followed Canada’s lead toward an independent, commercial operator.

Passengers wait at a terminal after the FAA issued a national ground stop following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 2026.

America almost joined that list in 2017. That year, legislation gained traction in Congress that would have transferred air traffic control to an independent entity while retaining the FAA’s oversight role. Regrettably, the plan was shot down by the labor union representing controllers, which feared losing the federal government’s generous protections and benefits. Private aircraft owners also opposed it to avoid paying user fees they are currently exempt from, keeping the revenue burden on commercial flyers.

Aside from placating these entrenched interests, there is no good reason to keep air traffic control in government hands. The public utility model has proven safe and effective elsewhere, and the FAA has shown once again that it can’t measure up. Free the aviation system from political gamesmanship, and watch dependability soar.

#6119. A Top Frequent Flyer Complained About American Airlines Selling Their Free Upgrade For $91—Gets Told To Delete Their Post

An American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits. The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending. But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.” We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending.

But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

@rawdbee We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026

The important takeaway here is that upgrades are mostly dead, that this is generally true across major U.S. carriers, but hiding this isn’t the reason American Airlines asks this customer to delete their tweet.

If this passenger is shocked by $91 upgrade offers, wait till they learn about American Airlines selling upgrades to infrequent customers for $40 (or Delta Delta doing it for $26) rather than honoring the promised complimentary benefit. And wait until they learn that pilots have priority over them too while deadheading.

Of course American Airlines “genuinely appreciate[s]” a customer’s loyalty when they’re being given business by someone based on the promise of an upgrade benefit that they don’t actually need to deliver, selling their excess seats for tens of dollars rather than providing those seats the way they traditionally did as a perk for someone that’s provided tens of thousands of dollars of business. They appreciate the customer sticking around even when they’re no longer delivering the perks.

Lest you think this is uniquely an American Airlines issue, not only have I seen Delta upsell seats for even less than American (on both domestic and long haul international routes), but United Airlines was equally a pioneer of the technique – they used to pitch infrequent flyers not just on the upgrade itself but that a paid upgrade would leapfrog them over a loyal customer.

I imagine – though American failed to explain this – the reason they’d suggest removing the tweet is because the image of the passenger’s reservation includes the reservation number. A bad actor who sees it might use it to social engineer access to the booking and make changes. It’s not advisable to publicly post a “PNR” (passenger name record) on the internet even if probably nobody does anything with it. Airlines generally tell customers their status upgrades are no longer available on the cheapest (basic economy) fares. Frontier Airlines is introducing first class, but saying even their top Diamond members will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades if they spend extra by buying a bundle. Elites are asked to purchase a lottery ticket on top of their regular ticket for the change of an upgrade, in a game that’s rigged because the airline determines whether there’s a prize at all (narrator: there usually isn’t). My issue isn’t the airline’s right to make this decision that they value $40 from a one a year flyer over rewarding the loyalty of a $30,000 a year customer, or someone spending $200,000 or more on an airline’s credit card (though this may be unwise). Instead, it’s the disconnect between the airline’s marketing and what they now actually deliver. Airlines promise upgrades as a benefit of customer loyalty. For many decades they delivered this. Now they not only fail to deliver it the way they did in the past, that failure is intentional, traded for minor ducats from low value flyers. Earlier this year, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom spoke to investors and explained the strategy selling buy ups instead of giving out free upgrades in the same merchandising category as “pre-purchase bags, checked baggage.” Twenty years ago 90% of first class seats went to upgrades and awards. Ten years ago it was about half. Now only around 12% of seats are left for Delta SkyMiles elite members. And that means on many routes and flights there are no upgrades at all. The real effect of this is to make top status unappealing. It removes upgrades as the argument for status, and that used to be the main motivator. It’s mid-tier status that’s now the sweet spot: priority check-in (shorter lines with bags) priority boarding (overhead bin space) free checked bags extra legroom coach seat The value in being at the top of the list of flyers that do not clear for an upgrade is minimal. Still, the extra value in top status is not zero. I value being able to add an extra segment to an American Airlines itinerary as a backup when my flights are delayed, without having to make the decision to switch flights right away. For many flyers that’s pretty niche. For most it’s not worth chasing. Delta works to convince flyers that extra legroom economy seats are an upgrade (“The biggest trick the devil in Atlanta ever played was convincing flyers he doesn’t exist”). They even run an upgrade process to get into those seats. But that just reinforces the notion that status which is sufficient to get into these extra legroom seats is all you need to work to attain. The problem for airlines isn’t just that this reduces the incentive for their best customers to keep flying with them. It’s that elite members are the ones most likely to get and spend on their credit cards. And they’ve been leaning into status as the biggest reason for these customers to focus their spending this way. What I’d like to see is airlines return to offering meaningful benefits even in the face of monetizing unsold first class seats for tens of dollars to once a year customers. They could offer a discount on paid upgrades in lieu of complimentary upgrades. American Airlines will already discount their tickets, including award tickets, all day long – employees and family members can book ‘AA20’ fares for 20% off. Other airlines have similar programs. So offering upgrades at 20% off for elites could make real sense. Similarly, cobrand cardmembers at Delta and United get discounts on award redemption (at Delta this is really just charging non-cardmembers more). That model could be replicated with upgrades. They could bring back middle seat blocking on flights that aren’t full, keeping the seats next to top elite members empty until they’re actually needed at the gate. That’s easier to manage now that much of gate work is being automated. I use a $70 per hour rubric on whether it was worth paying to upgrade, though this is dependent on whether I think I’ll get the upgrade free, anyway (and the cheaper the upgrade, the more likely the airline thinks they won’t sell the seat) and what seat I already have (an exit row aisle makes me less likely to pay than a middle seat in back of regular coach). The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings. I value being able to add an extra segment to an American Airlines itinerary as a backup when my flights are delayed, without having to make the decision to switch flights right away. For many flyers that’s pretty niche. For most it’s not worth chasing.

Delta works to convince flyers that extra legroom economy seats are an upgrade (“The biggest trick the devil in Atlanta ever played was convincing flyers he doesn’t exist”). They even run an upgrade process to get into those seats. But that just reinforces the notion that status which is sufficient to get into these extra legroom seats is all you need to work to attain.

The problem for airlines isn’t just that this reduces the incentive for their best customers to keep flying with them. It’s that elite members are the ones most likely to get and spend on their credit cards. And they’ve been leaning into status as the biggest reason for these customers to focus their spending this way.

What I’d like to see is airlines return to offering meaningful benefits even in the face of monetizing unsold first class seats for tens of dollars to once a year customers.

They could offer a discount on paid upgrades in lieu of complimentary upgrades.

American Airlines will already discount their tickets, including award tickets, all day long – employees and family members can book ‘AA20’ fares for 20% off. Other airlines have similar programs. So offering upgrades at 20% off for elites could make real sense. Similarly, cobrand cardmembers at Delta and United get discounts on award redemption (at Delta this is really just charging non-cardmembers more). That model could be replicated with upgrades.

They could bring back middle seat blocking on flights that aren’t full, keeping the seats next to top elite members empty until they’re actually needed at the gate. That’s easier to manage now that much of gate work is being automated. I use a $70 per hour rubric on whether it was worth paying to upgrade, though this is dependent on whether I think I’ll get the upgrade free, anyway (and the cheaper the upgrade, the more likely the airline thinks they won’t sell the seat) and what seat I already have (an exit row aisle makes me less likely to pay than a middle seat in back of regular coach). The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings. #6117. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6116. Let’s Stop Fighting Gravity in U.S.-Canada Trade

Canada needs the United States. But the U.S. also needs, and greatly benefits from, its relationship with Canada in both trade and security.

A transport truck drives towards Canada at the Canada-U.S. border crossing in Fort Erie Ontario, Canada, April 2, 2025.

U.S.-Canada trade is a little like gravity. You can push against it, but the size and proximity of the U.S. economy and the convenience of a G-7 market like Canada always pull us back together.

Trade negotiations between the two countries had been suspended, but the midterm results may be an opportunity to press forward as Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and Senate shift the political calculus. President Donald Trump seemed to warm to the idea of a deal on the campaign trail. Some analysts are suggesting a deal is imminent, and Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadian and U.S. teams would be working to deliver a deal “in the coming weeks” following a “good conversation” with Trump.

Hendrik Brakel is the former chief economist of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and former chief economic adviser to the leader of Canada’s Official Opposition.

Daniel Dorman is the managing editor and director of operations at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa.

#6115. A Trick To Buy Accor Hotel Stays At 40% Off — And Black Friday May Make It Even Better

Loyalty Lobby flagged Accor’s pre-Black Friday subscription sale. Combined with a weakened Brazilian currency this creates an opportunity.

Accor is much bigger than its presence in the United States would have you think. The French hotel company finished September with 5,857 hotels and 885,219 rooms. They operate in more than 110 countries, with a huge presence in Europe and extensive coverage in Asia and Australia.

Their brands include Fairmont, Raffles, Sofitel and MGallery at the luxury end, along with Swissôtel, Pullman and Mövenpick. Then there are Novotel and Mercure, and the budget ibis brands. U.S. options include Fairmont Austin and Raffles Boston.

I took advantage of the Bilt status match I wrote about this summer, which offered up to Platinum.

Accor points are worth 2 euro cents apiece toward eligible hotel stays. The familiar redemption is 2,000 points for €40. Using November 18 exchange rates, that’s about $43.87, or 2.19 U.S. cents per point.

There’s no hotel award chart. An expensive room requires more points. But you can apply points to paid rates without hunting for a limited supply of standard award rooms, and a lower room rate means fewer points needed also.

Reward points normally expire after 12 months without eligible earning activity. A qualifying points credit extends the whole balance, even if you earn just one point. Partner earning can keep the account alive without another hotel stay. An active ALL Signature subscription also protects Reward points from expiration.

Here’s the calculation using the published monthly prices multiplied by 12, less 20%, and November 18 exchange rates. Dollar amounts are rounded.

Your card’s conversion rate will also differ slightly, and be sure to use a card without foreign transaction fees.

The Explorer plan is the better pure points purchase. You’re buying hotel credit for about 29.8% below its redemption value, compared with 23.8% for Absolute. Absolute buys more points and more status credit, but each redeemable point costs more.

Unfortunately, annual payment doesn’t make all the points available immediately. Absolute deposits 5,000 points a month, plus another 5,000 every fourth month, for 75,000 over 12 months. Explorer delivers 3,000 monthly plus 3,000 every fourth month, totaling 45,000. You can’t sign up and immediately spend the full year’s balance on a hotel booking.

You can stack this with ALL Accor+ Explorer, a separate paid membership offering 15% off eligible rates at participating hotels worldwide, plus benefits concentrated in Asia Pacific. Accor uses “Explorer” for both a Signature subscription tier and a different membership. Apparently someone thought that was a good idea.

Buying discounted points and then spending them against an eligible discounted room rate is where this gets better. Combining a 15% room discount with points purchased 29.8% below face value produces about 40.3% off the underlying room price, before the separate membership cost and the rewards you’d otherwise earn.

Signature’s monthly Status points are separate from its redeemable Reward points. Absolute supplies 1,000 Status points a month, or 12,000 over a full year, versus the 14,000 needed for Platinum. Those points count in the calendar year they’re credited and reset at year end.

There’s also an escape valve if your hotel plans change: Accor points transfer to airlines.

Many other partners offer a worse ratio. British Airways, for instance, takes 4,000 Accor points for just 2,000 Avios. Use Iberia for Avios rather than accepting half as many through British Airways.

At the Explorer subscription price above, you’re acquiring points for about 1.54 cents each. That’s also the acquisition cost of a mile through a 1:1 transfer. But once you have the points, moving them to an airline means giving up about 2.19 cents each in hotel credit.

While I can book these with my American Airlines AAdvantage miles, I don't want to put all my eggs in one loyalty program, since that leaves my rewards vulnerable to future devaluations and other negative program changes.

The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard offers a compelling, easy-to-earn welcome bonus:

On top of that, I'll earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Hawaiian and Alaska purchases and 2 points per dollar spent on dining, gas and groceries.

Without this card, my only way of earning Atmos Rewards points was via Bilt Points transferred from my Bilt account, which isn't a particularly efficient method.

While this card's benefits are understandably focused on Hawaiian Airlines, there are ways to use them on Alaska flights, too. I'll receive two free checked bags whenever I'm flying either Hawaiian or Alaska as long as I book with my card, a nice perk considering mid-tier cards typically only offer your first checked bag free.

Upon account opening, I became eligible for a one-time 50% companion discount for one round-trip main cabin fare between North America and Hawaii. This is redeemable on either Alaska or Hawaiian, but I must use it within 13 months of account opening.

Some possible use cases I have in mind include inviting a friend to join me on a trip to Hawaii or offering it to them as a discount for a positioning flight to Hawaii and back as part of a larger Asia itinerary we take together.

Each account anniversary, this card offers a $100 companion discount for a round-trip main cabin fare, also usable on Alaska or Hawaiian. Both discounts may be subject to additional terms.

While it's unfortunate that these companion discounts are limited to travel between Hawaii and North America, it's not surprising considering this is a Hawaiian Airlines-branded card. It's a good incentive for me to finally start seriously considering some of the trips I've had on my list.

The or its more affordable sibling, the , are likely better first choices for Alaska flyers — and possibly Hawaiian Airlines flyers as well.

Both cards offer a more valuable free checked bag benefit, with the opportunity to check a free bag for yourself as well as up to six people on the same itinerary (when you pay with your card). You'll also get preferred boarding on both airlines, which the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard doesn't offer.

The Summit comes with eight Alaska lounge passes every year, a big upside for those flying Alaska often enough to value lounge access. It also earns well on foreign purchases, earning 3 points per dollar spent.

Unless you never fly Alaska Airlines and fly Hawaiian frequently, I recommend applying for one of these cards first. If you wind up getting declined, as I did, I'd consider the Hawaiian Mastercard as an alternative.

Carefully planning your credit card strategy never loses its importance. As someone with a well-established roster of transferable rewards cards, I'm in a phase where I'm considering how cobranded cards can boost my travels.

The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard isn't the obvious choice on the surface, but the benefits and rewards it offers make a lot of sense for me as an Alaska Airlines flyer. If you're a Hawaiian Airlines fan or travel frequently with Alaska but are ineligible for one of its credit cards, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard may be the right choice for you.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard.

#6113. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6112. FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas. Now the story is becoming about Elon Musk: a claim that DOGE cut FAA employees, oversight was loosened, and this led to the flight stoppage. There’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE. A Router Change Disrupted The National Network The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it shows the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges users and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The new $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions. One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo.

According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.)

Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change.

One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981.

Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date.

There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop.

On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion.

The new $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure.

Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions.

Trump Administration: “$1 for repairs, $4 for Dept of War ( I can barely type that title w/o side ache from laughter ), $1 for repairs, $4 for Dept of War………”

Gary, nice try, but framing this as just “blaming Elon” is a convenient strawman. The real failure is no pre-live isolation, no contingency plan, and weakened FAA change-control oversight—which is why Administrator Bedford owned the responsibility instead of hiding behind L3Harris’s contract.

And let’s not pretend this happened in an ideological vacuum. Hollowing out agency staffing and reducing FAA technicians to door-unlockers fits right into the Project 2025 playbook (pp. 632–634): weaken federal oversight, watch critical functions stumble, and then point to the wreckage to argue for spinning off and privatizing ATC along the exact Nav Canada model you pitch on here almost every month. (Never mind that Nav Canada still relies on strict, independent government safety oversight from Transport Canada—the very guardrail being dismantled here.)

Meanwhile, this should make for a wild comment section as Tim has to defend the administration by deflecting to random details, while inadvertently defending Elon—even though he’s been attacking him recently to defend Delta’s choice to go with Amazon for Wi-Fi. Good luck, bud—I’ll be waiting to remind folks of what Tim wrote right here in January 2023 during the NOTAM outage when he was demanding congressional hearings.

Airline baggage fees can vary greatly, and there’s nothing worse than being hit by surprise fees after booking. To add to the challenge, many U.S. airlines raised fees in 2026, with several increases tied to rising fuel costs amid the war in Iran.

At TPG, we try to help readers spend smarter so they can travel better.

This guide summarizes baggage fees by airline, so you know what fees to expect before booking. It also outlines some smart ways to help you avoid them entirely.

Most major U.S. airlines impose several common bag fees, including for checked bags.

As you'll see in the chart below, the fee for your first checked bag typically starts at $45 to $50 each way, but increases quickly as you add a second or third suitcase.

(For flights ticketed on or after Nov. 3, 2026)

This table assumes you’re purchasing a standard domestic economy fare (not basic economy, which costs more on some airlines, such as American) and checking standard luggage that isn’t overweight or oversized. Note that Frontier Airlines considers a bag overweight if it weighs more than 40 pounds, whereas most other carriers set the limit at 50 pounds.

These prices also assume you have no elite status, do not carry a cobranded airline credit card with a checked-bag benefit and are paying for your checked bag at the airport. Fees on some airlines, such as JetBlue, vary by travel date. Bag fees on international flights can differ significantly, especially on long-haul routes.

Note: Some airlines charge less if you pay for your bags online in advance. American and United take $5 off, and JetBlue’s discount can be as much as $15.

Some airlines also charge for carry-on baggage. This is usually limited to low-cost carriers, but you’ll want to check your allowances before your next flight.

Here are the carry-on bag allowances for domestic flights in economy class with most major U.S. airlines:

You’ll notice that most airlines don’t charge a fee for a carry-on bag, but they limit each passenger to one personal item and one carry-on.

A personal item is considered a backpack, laptop bag, camera bag or other small item you can stow underneath the seat in front of you. A carry-on is typically a larger bag or small suitcase that fits in the overhead bin above your seat. Each airline has different dimension limits, so you’ll want to measure your luggage and check your airline’s policy before heading to the airport.

Related: How to tell if your backpack counts as a personal or carry-on item

No major U.S. airline includes a free checked bag with its standard economy fare. (Southwest's higher-priced Choice Extra fare is somewhat of an exception since it allows two free checked bags.) So, regardless of your carrier, expect to pay to check your bag unless you have elite status or the airline's cobranded credit card. Most major airlines charge similar prices — around $45 to $50 for your first checked bag. However, JetBlue now follows a peak and off-peak model, so if you're flying during a peak time, expect to pay more.

Frontier is the least favorable airline when it comes to baggage fees. Not only are its prices the highest, but they also vary by travel dates and purchase time. And while most airlines allow you to check a bag up to 50 pounds, Frontier caps the weight of a standard checked bag at 40 pounds. After that, you’ll pay a pretty penny for overweight bags. Fortunately, the airline offers a baggage calculator to check the cost in advance.

Also note that most airlines charge additional fees for overweight baggage (generally once your bag exceeds 50 pounds). Suitcases over a certain size (often measured in linear inches, length plus width plus height) usually cost extra. Specialty items, like skis or scuba equipment, may also incur additional fees.

Some airlines don't allow you to check luggage with a basic fare, while others offer bundled fares that include checked baggage. Pay close attention to which fare you purchase to minimize luggage fees.

When it comes to basic economy fares, United is the only major U.S. airline (American, Delta and United) that doesn’t include a free carry-on bag on domestic flights. United also charges an additional gate handling fee (on top of the regular baggage fee) if a basic economy passenger brings a full-size bag to the gate that then must be checked.

Paying for your luggage in advance is usually the least expensive option with most airlines. You'll want to pay special attention as some airlines offer a discount during the booking process, while others require you to simply pay for your luggage when checking in for your flight online.

Many U.S. carriers offer a simpler pathway to free checked bags: opening an airline credit card.

Most cobranded cards from U.S. airlines waive the first checked-bag fee on domestic itineraries. In fact, many of these perks extend to companions — up to eight on the same reservation, in some cases. Some cards have annual fees of less than $100.

In other words, you and your entire family could check a bag for free on your next trip simply by holding the right credit card.

For most carriers discussed in this guide, there’s at least one credit card that waives the fee for your first checked bag. Most also extend the favor to additional companions traveling on the same reservation. If you're a frequent flyer with a particular airline, it's worth investigating whether there is a cobranded credit card that suits your needs.

However, perks vary by card and airline; some are more restrictive than others. For example, to get the free first bag with the (see rates and fees), you generally need to buy your ticket using the card.

With others, such as American's Citi cards, you only need to include your loyalty number on the reservation.

The number of permitted companions also varies: The United Explorer Card covers one additional passenger, whereas the allows up to eight traveling companions to check their bags at no additional cost.

Each carrier uses slightly different rules for these policies, but here's a summary of the cards that offer this perk:

Note: You must purchase your flights with the card for bag perks to apply.
