The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

It's worth pointing out that many of these perks apply automatically based on the loyalty program account associated with the card. However, a few airlines require you to pay for your airfare with the cobranded card to receive the bag fee waiver.

Many travelers aren’t loyal to a given airline, so it may not make sense to hold, say, a United card if you only travel with United once a year. Thankfully, many of the best travel credit cards include credits that can cover checked bag fees when you incur them, and some of them aren’t limited to individual airlines.

Related: The best credit cards with airline fee credits

Additionally, you could consider using a card like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to pay for checked bag fees. The miles you earn on this card can cover travel purchases, and you can use your miles to pay for baggage.

Another option to avoid checked bag fees is to hold elite status with the airline’s frequent flyer program. All airlines mentioned here offer at least one free checked bag to certain elite members.

The vast majority of these tiers — even the lowest ones — allow you to check a bag for free. However, the exact waiver depends on the airline and can vary as you climb the elite status ladder.

For example, all Delta Medallion travelers enjoy at least one free checked bag up to 70 pounds on flights in the U.S. and Canada and 50 pounds on international flights. Within the U.S. and Canada, this jumps to two bags for Gold Medallion members and three for Platinum and Diamond Medallion members.

United also grants Premier travelers a 70-pound weight allowed for checked bags: one bag for Premier Silver, two for Premier Gold, and three for Premier Platinum and Premier 1K.

American follows a similar method for checked bag quantity: one for AAdvantage Gold, two for AAdvantage Platinum and three for AAdvantage Platinum Pro and AAdvantage Executive Platinum. However, unless you're confirmed in business or first class, bags are limited to 50 pounds (except for flights to and from Australia or New Zealand).

Plus, some published policies may offer wiggle room for elite members. For example, elite status holders might be able to get away with a 52-pound bag without tacking on an overweight fee. And, if you have elite status, you may still be able to convince a sympathetic check-in agent to waive the bag fee.

Note that many of these perks extend to partner flights as well. If you hold mid-tier or higher status with an airline in SkyTeam, Star Alliance or Oneworld, you can typically check an extra bag for free on partner airlines.

For more details on the perks of elite status, check out these guides:

When you travel in a premium class of service, you’ll generally enjoy waived checked bag fees — in many cases above and beyond the standard weight allowance as well. These policies typically apply whether you paid cash, points or miles for your ticket, so this can be a great way to use your travel rewards and not have to worry about extra bag fees.

You can check out your operating carrier’s checked baggage page for full details on what’s included for your specific trip.

Here are a few more tricks to avoid checked baggage fees, including overweight or oversize fees.

Most airlines allow you to gate-check carry-on luggage for no additional cost when overhead bin space is tight — and on a fully packed flight, sometimes they'll often require travelers to gate check.

The exceptions are typically low-cost carriers like Frontier, as well as basic economy fares on legacy carriers. Otherwise, most airlines are happy to gate-check just about whatever you’d like — and you may even have luck doing this before boarding starts.

If you gate-check your luggage, ensure the airline checks it through to baggage claim. However, you must claim some items — such as strollers, wheelchairs and even rolling carry-ons on regional planes — at the gate upon arrival.

As punitive as airline baggage policies can be, some helpful exceptions exist. For example, most U.S. carriers let you check skis, snowboards and boots as a single checked bag — even if your skis are in a different bag from your boots. The same often holds for hockey equipment, which typically doesn’t require an additional fee as long as it’s within the standard weight allotment.

Before you go to the airport, take a screenshot of the rules in case you encounter an agent who is unfamiliar with uncommon checked items.

Check-in agents at the curb are often contractors, not airline employees. So, they may have less incentive to strictly enforce the airline’s baggage rules. Additionally, some locations may not have scales to weigh the bags.

In the U.S., carry-on weight restrictions are rarely enforced. So, when packing for your next vacation, put heavy items in your carry-on bag rather than risk paying for overweight checked bags.

For less than $10, you can find a small, lightweight scale to weigh your luggage. These scales are typically quite accurate and will help you stay under your desired weight. You’ll also avoid being that person repacking their bags at the airport and holding up the line.

Beyond the above strategies, many airlines waive checked bag fees for all customers when traveling to specific areas. For example, American Airlines offers free checked baggage on flights to select destinations including Argentina, Brazil, China, India and Japan. This also extends to all transatlantic travels. And, if you’re flying American to either Australia or New Zealand, your free bag can weigh up to 70 pounds.

Basic economy passengers may still pay on some routes, such as transatlantic flights, and there may be seasonal restrictions for certain locales.

Regardless of the airline you’re flying, be sure to research your baggage allowance ahead of time so you know what to expect — and so you don’t encounter an expensive surprise at the airport.

Bag fees are an unfortunate reality of air travel in 2026. In certain situations, your bags could wind up costing hundreds of dollars beyond the original price of the ticket. So, carefully consider baggage policies before jumping on that “great deal.”

If there’s a cobranded credit card or an easy way to earn elite status (one that offers waived baggage fees) for the particular airline you’re flying, it might be worth looking into those options. You might find that the annual fee on your credit card is far less than the checked-bag fees for your family over the course of the year.

#6107. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

#6105. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6104. From Premier Inn to Rick Stein, Britain’s Travel Businesses Are Paying for Higher Labor Costs

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

The UK's 2025 increases in minimum wage, payroll tax and property tax were meant to fall on big employers. Company filings now landing show they hit hospitality and travel businesses of every size, from Premier Inn's owner to a celebrity chef's seaside restaurants and a regional travel agency.

"The 12 months to 28 December 2025 were exceptionally challenging for the UK hospitality sector," the directors of The Seafood Restaurant (Padstow) Ltd wrote in accounts filed this week with Companies House, the UK's company register. Rising labor and property costs, which they called "government forced increases," cost the group "in excess of £600,000 [$800,000] in 2025."

The group, which runs restaurants, hotel rooms, a cookery school and shops, reported a pre-tax loss of £814,000 ($1.1m). That was almost double the year before, on flat revenue of £18.9 million ($25.1 million). Revenue is down 17% since 2022. It closed its central food production unit in October 2025, with 22 job losses. A sister company with the same owners, Stein's Trading, which runs more of the family's restaurants, said the same co

UK company filings show that three policy changes that took effect in April 2025 — a higher minimum wage, a higher employer payroll tax applied to more of each worker's pay, and a cut in the pandemic-era property-tax discount for hospitality — are pushing hospitality and travel businesses into losses. Rick Stein's The Seafood Restaurant (Padstow) Ltd reported a pre-tax loss of £814,000 ($1.1 million) on flat revenue of £18.9 million ($25.1 million), with the directors attributing more than £600,000 ($800,000) of cost to what they called "government forced increases"; sister company Stein's Trading saw its loss nearly triple. The same pattern appears at scale and at the small end: Whitbread said higher UK employment costs and property taxes added £160 million ($213 million), equal to a third of its previous year's pre-tax profit, and it is closing all its branded restaurants and cutting 3,800 jobs; travel agency chain Dawson & Sanderson swung to a £567,000 ($754,000) loss with a payroll tax bill up 30% despite employing 15 fewer people; and the Grand Hotel in Eastbourne swung to a loss as competition pushed room rates down. Hotels face a further squeeze after being left out of two rounds of property-tax relief given to pubs and music venues, with taxable values up an average of 76% in this year's England and Wales revaluation, according to Knight Frank. Demand has softened in places but has not collapsed — the common thread is that costs are rising faster than these businesses can raise prices without losing customers.

Aer Lingus announced a major overhaul of its Airbus A330 fleet, modernizing the interior of the aging jets with a complete nose-to-tail retrofit.

The Irish flag carrier will install its first-ever Premium Economy cabin, along with all-new lie-flat business class suites and updated economy seats. The airline said it will also continue to offer free Starlink Wi-Fi on the refurbished planes.

The retrofit will come to 10 of the airline's A330 jets, Aer Lingus said in an announcement. The airline has a total of 10 A330-300 jets in service, along with two long-range A330-200s, according to Planespotters.net. It was not immediately clear what would happen to the two A330s that are not included in the retrofit.

Review: Flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic in its current A330 configuration

Aer Lingus described the project as one of its "most significant investments in the onboard customer experience in more than a decade."

"Our ambition here is simple," Aer Lingus CEO Lynn Embleton said in a statement. "We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort and connectivity, while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus."

The retrofitted jets will fly transatlantic routes to North America, the airline said, starting on Oct. 1 with flights EI104 and EI105 between Dublin Airport (DUB) and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Let's take a closer look at the retrofit.

Premium economy cabins have become much more widespread among airlines over the past decade, with carriers capitalizing on customers who are willing to pay a premium for more comfort, but are still price-sensitive and won't pay for business class.

Aer Lingus is late to the trend, but clearly ready to commit. The airline will install four rows of premium economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration for a total of 28 seats.

Premium economy will also have its own cabin service, with a three-course meal and drinks throughout the flight, along with amenity kits, bedding, and "noise-reducing" headphones to use during the flight.

The new cabin will be priced squarely in between coach and business class, with fares starting at €700 each way, or about $768.

The business-class cabin will see a major upgrade, bringing a fresh new product to replace one that has become dated.

The cabin will feature 28 business-class suites across seven rows in a 1-2-1 layout, giving every passenger direct aisle access. That's two fewer seats than on the current A330-300, but a big improvement since alternating rows in the existing cabin are configured in a sort of 1-2-2 layout.

Aer Lingus says that it also plans to revamp its onboard dining experience to showcase "seasonal Irish ingredients and contemporary culinary influences," although the airline did not share specifics. There will also be a self-service bar with drinks and snacks in the cabin.

The economy cabin will also see new seats with a handful of features aimed at keeping passengers comfortable on long flights, including a six-way adjustable leather headrest.

Every economy seat in the 2-4-2 cabin will have a 4K seat-back screen with Bluetooth connectivity for headphones, plus USB-C charging. A new in-flight snack station will have bites available after the pain meal service.

The design of economy and the entire plane is recognizably Aer Lingus, with a palette heavy on greens and whites with customized mood lighting to accent the on-board experience.

Aer Lingus has offered a pleasant business-class product with stellar on-board service and decent availability, but there's no denying that its "hard product" has fallen behind the times. The new refresh will bring the airline up to snuff with competitors, and should elevate the overall product to match the service provided by the excellent cabin crew.

The new premium economy cabin, meanwhile, offers travelers a new way to fly to Ireland and beyond with more space for a more comfortable journey, while helping Aer Lingus capture an increasingly important passenger segment.

Overall, we're excited to see the new Aer Lingus hit the skies next fall!

Booking Holdings has carved Priceline out of its new Booking Partner Division because of a potential U.S. Federal Trade Commission complaint against the brand. Omri Morgenshtern, head of the new division and CEO of Agoda, told Skift at Phocuswright in Hollywood, Florida, that the investigation created "operational complexities" and that Priceline "will keep serving their partners." The original plan was to merge Rocket Travel by Agoda, Booking.com partnerships, and the Priceline Partner Network into one B2B unit serving banks, OTAs, airlines, hotels, loyalty programs, and travel agencies. Instead, Booking.com partnerships and Rocket Travel by Agoda will unify, and the Priceline Partner Network will operate on its own. Booking Holdings took a $1 billion charge in the third quarter tied to the FTC matter, after disclosing earlier this year that the FTC intended to file a complaint against Priceline and a B2B affiliate partner over "unfair or deceptive business practices related to disclosures, fees, customer support, and billing practices." Morgenshtern said including Priceline is not the goal "at the moment," and that Booking is likely considering breaking out the financials of its B2B segment, as Expedia Group does. He is relocating to New York to run the division while staying on as Agoda CEO, supported by recently promoted Chief Operating Officer Ittai Chorev.

As luxury Amazon trips grow in popularity, tourism is adding pressure to the very thing it’s sold on: remote, authentic experiences.

G Adventures' VP of product Yves Marceau said lodges outside Manaus that used to be remote are now reachable by car, with light pollution and less wildlife, so operators have to go further out — and that costs. Intrepid Travel's Peru general manager Fernando Rodriguez said higher value, lower volume models can work when managed responsibly, pointing to small group travel, community-owned businesses, and lodges accessed by boat rather than road. Marceau's warning for operators building Amazon product: partner with lodges that are "way out there," because "when you build tours, you have to futureproof."

#6094. Tour Associations Attempt to Take On Package Emissions Reporting

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Oleg Mityukhin from Pixabay

A common framework makes it easier for operators to benchmark against one another and their suppliers, but the burden still falls on operators to collect and crunch the numbers. The best way to get tour operators to calculate their emissions would be releasing a tool to do it for them.

In 2026, hotels tend to report emissions on a per-room basis, trains report per passenger, and a bus company reports its emissions for the whole vehicle. From these fragmented data points, a package tour operator has to fold all of those numbers into one to understand its climate impact.

Two tour operator associations have developed a website they hope can help solve this problem. The idea is to simplify emissions calculations for package tour operators by bringing resources into one place.

The site, called TEMPO, is the work of the European Tourism Association (ETOA) and United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA). It points to free methodologies operators can use to measure emissions and to free calculation tools for each part of a tour, as well as identifying when one doesn’t exist.

“A tour operator has to piece together data from many suppliers, each measuring a different service in a different unit,” ETOA’s director gene

The European Tourism Association (ETOA) and the United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA) have launched a website meant to simplify emissions measurement for package tour operators, who currently have to reconcile hotel data reported per room, rail data per passenger, and bus data per vehicle into a single number. The site breaks a tour into components — flights, hotels, road transport, activities, meals, and sea travel — points to free methodologies and calculation tools for each, and flags where no tool exists. It offers two reporting routes: a quick estimate for operators with little time or budget, and a more rigorous version requiring precise data. Operators including Avanti Destinations, EF Education First, and the Globus Family of Brands helped shape the effort, which is supported by Travalyst, whose members include Booking.com, Expedia, and Google. ETOA's Tim Fairhurst said the idea came from members who wanted an easier way to measure and compare, and he hopes consistent methods will show operators where the most polluting parts of an itinerary sit. Supplier data remains the open question: Intrepid Travel's Susanne Etti told a COP31 session that small suppliers often lack the capital, technology, or expertise to measure or cut emissions alone. Separately, UN Tourism revised its Glasgow Declaration guidelines on Wednesday so signatories can submit emissions reports they already produce elsewhere.

Cruises can be truly affordable vacations — but that doesn’t mean you won’t run up a significant bill booking your sailing or spending during your trip. It’s also easy to overspend on certain travel costs when you don’t know all the best money-saving tricks.

As someone who cruises often, I don’t have a huge budget to spend on onboard purchases for each sailing, so I’ve had to get wise on how to save money on a cruise.

Some of my strategies are obvious and others I’ve learned from trial and error over more than 80 sailings. I’m happy to share the wealth, so to speak, so you can avoid money mistakes and stretch your travel budget as far as it can possibly go. Here are my 35 top tips on how to save on a cruise.

Book early. Most cruise lines increase prices as ships sell out. Book early to get the lowest prices, as well as the widest choice of cabin types and locations, plus dining times.

Book at the last minute. The corollary advice is that cruise lines will sometimes drop prices or offer value-added promotions on cruises that have too many available cabins left a few months before their scheduled departures. You can find cheap deals on last-minute sailings, especially if you’re not picky about which cabin you get. Start looking about 90 days out for most big-ship sailings.

Related: When is the best time to book a cruise?

Book a shoulder-season sailing. Spring and fall tend to be less busy travel times, and cruises during these shoulder-season months are priced accordingly. Pick a cruise at the beginning or end of the Alaska or Mediterranean season when the weather isn’t as optimal, and you’ll save big over the peak midseason voyages. Sailings departing after Thanksgiving but before Christmas are also less popular and, therefore, cheaper.

Book an inside cabin. The cheapest room on the ship is an inside cabin, so choose one of those rooms if you want to spend less on your next sailing. You’ll get access to the same pools, restaurants, shows and activities as the folks in the balcony cabins; all you’re missing out on is a window and some more floor space. Some people actually prefer inside cabins for amazing sleep in the pitch dark or because they spend all their time out and about on the ship and are never in their room.

Be flexible on dates. Many unpredictable factors combine to make one sailing more expensive than the identical itinerary the week before or after. If you can be flexible on which week you cruise, you can save money by choosing whichever sail date is cheaper.

Book an older ship. Newer ships with their one-of-a-kind attractions and up-to-date everything get all the attention — and can command the highest prices. Seek out older ships to get a better cruise deal. Cruise lines maintain their older ships and often give them massive makeovers to add the latest restaurants and top-deck attractions, so you’ll hardly notice you’re on a 20-year-old ship. But your budget will notice the more affordable rates, leaving money in your pocket to spend on splurges like spa treatments and specialty dining.

Look for sales and promotions. Cruise lines run sales so often that you’re wasting money if you book when there isn’t a deal. Some promotions are all about lower fares, while others save you money with included perks, like free Wi-Fi or a complimentary beverage package. Solo travelers should look out for sales that waive the single supplement, saving you up to 50% of the normal single cabin price. Families should watch out for kids-cruise-free sales or other discounted third- and fourth-guest offers.

How do you find out about your favorite cruise line’s latest sales? Sign up for the brand’s email list or a large online travel agent’s deal alert newsletter, and they’ll send info on promos straight to your inbox.

Check for price drops. If you book a cruise and discover that the price has decreased down the road, your cruise line or travel agent will often be able to issue you a price adjustment. Some passengers have even reported receiving more than one adjustment if the prices fall repeatedly. The key is to make sure you spot the lower prices before the final payment deadline passes. After that, the best a cruise line can usually do for your is to offer a cabin upgrade.

Related: The best cruise booking perks — and which ones are actually free

Leverage your casino play. Cruise lines love casino players because they spend money on board. Once you’ve established yourself as a member of a cruise line’s players club, you might find yourself the recipient of cruise discounts and complimentary casino cruise offers. You can definitely save on a cruise when all you have to pay are taxes and fees.

Be loyal to one cruise line. Sail once with a cruise line, and you’re eligible to join its loyalty program. All members are eligible for select past-passenger cruise fare discounts, but the most loyal members can access free upgrades or even free cruises.

Request your shareholder credit. Cruisers who own 100 shares or more of the big three publicly traded cruise corporations — Carnival Corp., Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings and Royal Caribbean Group — can request onboard credit as a perk of being a shareholder. You can request it via an online form on each cruise line's website; the amount you'll receive, if approved, depends on the type of cruise you book. Credit can only be requested on full-fare voyages, and only one shareholder credit is permitted per stateroom.

Choose a drive-to port. Parking a car for a week is almost guaranteed to be cheaper than airport transfers, flights and a precruise hotel for a family of four. Cruise ships depart from ports all along the U.S. and Canada coastlines; consider choosing a cruise that departs from a port within driving distance of your home to save money on your next cruise.

Use a credit card that gives you perks. Even if your cruise fare isn't dirt cheap, you can still get more value from your vacation dollars when you pay for that vacation at sea with the right card. For example, book with The Platinum Card® from American Express, and its Cruise Privileges Program will get you double Membership Rewards points, onboard credit and cruise line-specific perks. Book a Carnival cruise with the Carnival Rewards™ Mastercard®, and you can earn extra Carnival Rewards points that you can redeem for cruise-related purchases and Loyalty Status stars that will fast track your elite status.

Or, perhaps you can use your cruise final payment to make the minimum spending requirement on a new credit card and get a slew of points or miles you can use for a free trip down the road.

Related: Should you get a cruise line credit card? Here’s a closer look

Bid for an upgrade. Several major cruise lines, like Norwegian Cruise Line and MSC Cruises, offer select guests the option to bid for an upgraded cabin. Bid less than the difference between your cabin cost and the price of the nicer room, and if your bid is approved, you’ll get upgraded onboard digs at a discount.

Use a travel agent. Most travel agents won’t charge you to use their cruise-booking services, but they can help you find the best deal on the best sailing for you, and they might even throw in a free bottle of Champagne or some onboard credit. If nothing else, these knowledgeable advisers can save you from making costly mistakes on the wrong cruise purchases, and that is a value in and of itself.

Book your next cruise on board. Most cruise lines run a future cruise sales desk on board ships. If you put a deposit down on a future cruise while sailing on the current one, you can be eligible for discounts and onboard credit (i.e., free spending money for you).

Related: Mistakes to avoid when booking your cruise

Get first-day discounts. Embarkation day can be chaotic. You’re getting familiar with the ship’s layout, signing up for all the things and likely going to the main dining room for dinner to meet your waiters. You might not even realize that the spa and specialty restaurants are open that evening. To lure passengers through their doors, onboard spas might offer first-day discounts and specialty restaurants might throw in a free bottle of wine.

Book activities and packages in advance. Many cruise lines offer discounts for booking drink packages, Wi-Fi plans and shore excursions online before your cruise. It will save you money on your next cruise if you do some precruise planning instead of being spontaneous once on board.

Go to the spa on port days. Most passengers get off the ship when it’s docked in port, so they prefer to book spa treatments on sea days. (The salon is especially busy on formal nights.) Cruise ship spas will often run specials or discounts to entice passengers to book treatments on port days, saving you money on the pricey massages and body treatments.

Enjoy specialty restaurants at lunch. You can rack up quite the cruise bill dining at specialty restaurants each night of your cruise. To save money, look for extra-charge eateries that are open for lunch. The food is usually just as good, but the menu is smaller, and the prices are reduced from the dinnertime fee.

Look for daily or happy hour drink specials. Your ship’s daily activity schedule (found in a printed newsletter or the cruise line's app) is your guide to saving money. Look for daily drink specials or happy hour deals that will save you money on those tropical drinks that are the hallmark of a Caribbean vacation. Or ask at your favorite onboard bar if they ever run drink deals, and plan your visits around those times.

Book a drink or dinner package. If eating and drinking are how you spend your money on a cruise, you could save by bundling your purchases. Look for all-you-can-drink packages that will save you money if you plan to drink a lot each day or specialty dining packages that offer a discounted total price for booking multiple reservations in advance.

Know when to skip the drink package. If you’re a casual drinker who doesn’t order more than a few drinks a day (including coffee and soda), or you don’t think you can drink enough to break even on the beverage package price every day, you will save more by skipping the package and ordering drinks a la carte, especially if you can utilize happy hour specials or loyalty perks to cut costs.

Also note that NCL’s Unlimited Open Bar package that’s part of its Free at Sea booking promotion is not a truly complimentary perk; you’ll need to pay $28.50 to $32 per person, per day. If you typically don’t spend that much on cruise drinks, you’ll save more by going a la carte.

Related: Are cruise line drink packages worth the price? What to know before you buy

Skip the souvenir glass. Step onto a cruise ship pool deck or atrium on the first day of your cruise, and you’re likely to be approached by a waiter offering you a drink in a souvenir glass. You want the cocktail, but do you really need to bring home a cup shaped like Carnival’s funnel? Say yes to the drink and no to the souvenir glass, and you will save a few bucks on the cost of the drink (not to mention the extra bag fees when you realize you can’t carry all those souvenirs home).

Seek out free alcohol. If you pay attention, you can find several opportunities to get drinks for free on a cruise ship. Many of the onboard art auctions pass out Champagne or sparkling wine to attendees, and sometimes the ship’s shops will offer liquor tastings in an attempt to convince you to buy a bottle. If you’re a suite guest or loyalty member, you might be eligible for free drink vouchers, happy hours or events with comped drinks.

Shop the sales for souvenirs. Cruise line boutiques often run BOGO sales or “everything for $10” hours on items like T-shirts, evening purses and sunglasses. If you’re thinking of purchasing some souvenirs, look for promotional events listed in your daily schedule. If you want to splurge on high-end jewelry or other expensive gifts, wait for those onboard shops to announce specials. These purchases won’t be cheap, but you might be able to save a bit or get an extra bauble thrown in for free.

Check out the seminars. Your cruise ship’s spa or boutiques will often host seminars about wellness practices or understanding gemstones. These events are really marketing ploys to get you to sign up for spa treatments or buy shoe insoles or jewelry. However, they often convince people to attend by giving away spa credit or jewelry in a raffle. If you’ve got nothing better to do on a sea day, you might show up in the hopes of winning something. Spa tours and port shopping lectures also run raffles (plus, you might get a free massage for a minute).

Look for midcruise specials. Cruise ships will discount paid attractions on the fly if they need to drum up more revenue in a certain area or if restaurants are not full. If you keep your schedule flexible, you can jump on midcruise specials, advertised in your daily schedule, and save on specialty dining, arcade games, spa treatments and more.

Evaluate laundry costs. Doing laundry on board is a smart way to avoid checked bag fees by packing light. In some cases, sending a bag of laundry to be washed on board (especially if you take advantage of a midcruise laundry special) can be more economical than paying to check a bag. However, you can save even more if you take advantage of a ship’s self-serve launderette or hand wash small items in your cabin’s bathroom sink. Some top suites come with free or discounted laundry, and top-tier frequent cruisers might also get comped laundry as a loyalty perk, so check the options before packing as part of your savings strategy.

Book your own tours. Cruise lines mark up shore excursions because they have to pay the provider and turn a profit. You can often save money by going to the source and booking a tour directly with a provider. Alternatively, a private tour guide for a group might not always save you money, but you will usually get more value out of a small-group tour that you can customize to your preference.

Skip the tour and explore independently. You don’t need to shell out big bucks for an organized tour in every port. To keep costs down, skip the beach break tour and walk or take a bus or taxi to the beach. Do your own walking tour with a guidebook or app. Go on a hike or take yourself to a cathedral or museum. If you tour independently, you won’t have to pay for a guide or cruise line overhead.

Look for less inclusive beach breaks. Sometimes a cruise line will offer several versions of the same resort day pass or beach break excursion — one that just covers your entrance and another that includes lunch and drinks and water toy use. If you don’t plan to eat or drink that much, or at all, you can save by booking the least expensive version of the tour and just paying for the amenities you use a la carte.

Use local transportation. Taxi rides can add up quickly. Consider using less expensive forms of transportation to explore a city during your port stop. Local buses and subways can be more affordable ways to get around, plus offer a glimpse into local life.

Use Wi-Fi in port. Cruise ship internet access is pricey; you might pay more for a week on board than you do for a month at home! If you don’t have to be connected at all hours, skip the cruise ship Wi-Fi plan and seek out free or cheap Wi-Fi in port. Many port terminals have free Wi-Fi, or you can grab a cup of coffee or a drink at an establishment in town with complimentary Wi-Fi for customers.

Negotiate prices. Know when prices aren’t set in stone and negotiate a lower fee to save on your in-port purchases. You can often barter over the price of crafts, food or souvenirs in open-air markets, or negotiate rates for taxi tours or rides. Always be friendly and polite when haggling, and be prepared to walk if the vendor does not accept your offer.

Bring your own beach gear. Most beaches you’ll visit on a cruise, including the cruise lines’ private islands, will rent you snorkel gear, umbrellas and beach floats, or sell you beach toys. Save money by purchasing and bringing your own snorkel gear, beach shade, inflatable beach toys and floats. The upfront cost might be higher than a single rental, but you can use the gear in multiple ports and on multiple cruises. Look for inflatables or collapsible gear that can pack down small or come in convenient carrying cases.

Don’t eat lunch or dinner in port. I always recommend trying the local cuisine in port, both because it’s a fun way to experience a new culture and to support the local economy. But if you’re on a budget and need to cut costs, skip the meals in port and head back to the ship for meals in the many included eateries on board. Don’t forget to fill up on breakfast, so you can spend more time in port before hunger drives you back to the ship.

If nothing else, avoid the overpriced and often inauthentic waterside tourist restaurants and ask around for where locals eat on the cheap — or skip the lunch and treat yourself to a cheaper gelato or pastry instead.

You don’t have to employ every one of these tips to save money on your next sailing, but keep them in mind to make smart decisions as you plan your next vacation and once you’re on board. It’s always OK to splurge a little on vacation, but you want to make sure you’re not spending unnecessarily. What matters is that you’re getting the biggest benefit from your vacation buck.

#6092. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6091. Is There Still Hope for Postliberalism?

The rejections of Viktor Orbán and Donald Trump hold sobering lessons for the nationalist right.

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (left) and President Donald Trump.

NR Illustration; Marton Monus, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

On Election Night this past May in Budapest, I was in the ballroom when a defining political era ended faster than it takes to place a drink order at a party-district ruin bar on a Saturday night. Viktor Orbán, the four-term prime minister who for 16 years was the undisputed sovereign of Hungarian politics, and the monster that haunted the nightmares of globalists from Brussels to Washington, took the stage not long after election results began rolling in — and gracefully accepted defeat. It was as if magician David Copperfield had made the Matterhorn disappear before the audience settled into its chairs on the chalet lawn.

Just like that, Orbán was gone. When I first arrived in Budapest for a fellowship in 2021, a Hungarian conservative friend told me that everybody knows Orbán’s Fidesz Party is riddled with corruption, but people tolerate it because life has been getting better and better for them since the reformist prime minister took power in 2010. “But if the economy ever turns,” he said, “then corruption is going to matter. A lot.”

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (left) and President Donald Trump.

NR Illustration; Marton Monus, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

Rod Dreher is the author of six books, including the New York Times bestsellers The Benedict Option (2017) and Live Not By Lies (2020).

#6089. The Case for Pollution Tourism in India: Sell the Toxic Air

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

India turned its population bomb into a demographic dividend; surely its polluted air deserves the same rebranding.

A few mornings ago, I landed in Delhi and caught the city’s signature scent outside the airport. In the Uber to my hotel, people were out on their morning walks, exercising in thick smog. I barely saw a mask. The tourism ministry should have been filming.

Those of us who grew up in India and moved abroad remember misty winter mornings fondly. Delhi has thoughtfully made the mist available all day. Luxury hotels spend fortunes inventing signature fragrances. Delhi has one that arrives with the airport transfer, free of charge.

Someone should be selling this. I propose…pollution tourism.

In 1968, biologist Paul Ehrlich opened The Population Bomb with a taxi ride through Delhi on “one stinking hot night,” past crowded streets and through a haze of dust and smoke. He forecast mass famine. For decades, India’s population was described as a bomb. Today, with much of the developed world aging,

A satirical Skift column uses the conceit of "pollution tourism" to put a hard number on Delhi's air quality problem and the tourism sector's response to it. In IQAir's 2025 rankings, Loni in Uttar Pradesh was the world's most polluted city and New Delhi the most polluted capital, with India holding three of the world's four most polluted cities. Delhi's official daily AQI averaged 376 on Diwali, November 8 — the worst festival reading in five years — while private tracker AQI.in reported a post-Diwali peak of 2,283 on a different scale. Delhi's worst pollution lands in the middle of India's peak inbound tourism season. Officials have struck an optimistic tone: Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said November brought relief "for the first time in the last 10 years," and Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said the official citywide AQI had not crossed 400 in 2026. Meanwhile, a parliamentary committee found the entire ₹3.5 crore (about $362,000) allocated for overseas promotion in 2026–27 was earmarked for mandatory international tourism-organization contributions, leaving nothing for actual promotion. On the ground, Skift reported Intrepid Travel's Delhi guides now carry N95 masks and shorten outdoor activities on bad days, and a Radisson executive said some guests are postponing trips.

#6088. Turkey Earns More From Fewer Tourists, But Hotels Miss Out

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Istanbul, the capital of Turkey. Getty / Seqoya

Turkey is making more money from fewer visitors, but the gains come from longer stays, not pricier rooms: hotel rates fell in dollar terms. The lowered $65 billion target can be met even if fourth-quarter revenue drops 9%, so clearing it says little about a recovery.

Turkey earned 5% more from tourism in the third quarter from 1% fewer visitors, but hotels aren’t the ones capturing the gain.

Culture and tourism minister Mehmet Ersoy credited the rise in tourism revenue, captured by the Turkish Statistical Institute, to “longer stays and higher overnight spending.”

Average visitor stays stood at 10.7 nights in the third quarter, up from 10.2 a year earlier. Spending per night rose 6.7% to $107, lifting total spending per visitor by about 12% to $1,145.

But hotel rates don’t explain the gain in tourist spending. In dollar terms, average rates fell fractionally to $148 a night in Q3, down from $149 last year, according to Lighthouse.

Package tour expenditures accounted for 32.3% of total tourism income, followed by food and beverage spending at 20.5% and accommodation at 12.5%, the Turkish Statistical Institute data showed.

Turkey's third-quarter tourism revenue rose 5% even as visitor numbers fell 1%, with culture and tourism minister Mehmet Ersoy crediting longer stays and higher overnight spending. Average stays reached 10.7 nights, up from 10.2, and spending per night rose 6.7% to $107, lifting spending per visitor about 12% to $1,145. Hotels aren't capturing that gain: average rates in dollar terms slipped to $148 a night from $149, because the lira's slide against the dollar more than offset a 16% rate increase in local currency, according to Lighthouse. Package tours accounted for 32.3% of tourism income and food and beverage 20.5%, while accommodation made up just 12.5%. The government has cut its 2026 revenue target from $68 billion to "more than $65 billion," roughly level with last year's record $65.2 billion, after the U.S.-Iran war pushed bookings from the eastern to the western Mediterranean. Sellers in the UK and U.S. report demand holding and strong 2027 bookings, though clients are booking closer to departure. COP31 in Antalya has lifted hotel rates 92% above the 2026 average for two weeks, but the gain is confined to one city, two weeks, and mostly five-star properties.

#6087. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6086. Trump Should Press Xi for Joshua Wong’s Release

The democracy activist’s sentence for meeting with American lawmakers ought to be treated as an affront to the U.S.

Pro-democracy activists Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow arrive at the Eastern Court by police van after being arrested on suspicion for organizing illegal protests, in Hong Kong, China, August 30, 2019.

When President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this Thursday, the agenda will be crowded with tariffs, chips, Taiwan, and the war in Iran. One more item should be on it: Joshua Wong, a 30-year-old Hong Kong democracy activist who was sentenced to ten years in prison for the “crime” of talking to Congress.

On September 2, Wong pleaded guilty in Hong Kong’s High Court to “conspiring to collude with foreign forces,” a crime under Beijing’s notorious National Security Law. As prosecutors laid out their case, they cited Wong’s prior meetings with sitting U.S. lawmakers, including then–Senator Marco Rubio, along with testimony he previously gave to the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. On November 5, Wong was sentenced to ten years in prison.

#6085. Travelers Want Less Screen Time and More Time on the Water

Travelers are moving from talking about getting outside to booking experiences that take them there. New research from Boatsetter points to growing participation in outdoor and water-based activities, creating opportunities for hospitality brands to make shared experiences more accessible.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

People have spent years saying they want to spend less time on their screens. Now more of them are acting on it. Boatsetter, a booking platform for boat sharing and on-water experiences, tracks that shift in its new report, Great Outdoor Shift 2.0. The report draws on two online surveys of U.S. adults: 834 in December 2025 and 1,034 in September 2026.

Boatsetter’s 2026 Great Outdoor Shift survey shows people responding to digital overload: 77% of respondents said they had already reduced screen time and social media use, and 63% said they would trade screen time for time on or near the water. The pull is about well-being, too: 84% say the outdoors is important for their mental health.

“People aren’t just tired of their screens. They want something that makes them feel small and present. That’s what awe does, and it’s why time on the water with friends keeps topping the list of what Americans want most,” said Michael Farb, CEO of Boatsetter.

Comparing the two surveys, Boatsetter reports a 64% increase in the number of people who tried fishing or paddlesports, a sign that participation is growing. Research from Tripadvisor supports this: In the first half of 2026, U.S. bookings on Tripadvisor grew 57% for fishing charters and 37% for boat rentals compared with the same period in 2025, according to the company’s 2026 Mid-Year Experiences Trends Report.

For hotels, destinations, and other travel providers, the figures point to demand for experiences that bring people into a destination, not just around it.

Boatsetter’s research also points to a broader shift toward active, social travel. Time on the water with friends remains the experience respondents most want more of. Spending intent is rising, too: 82% plan to spend more on outdoor or water activities in 2027, and 37.5% of this year’s respondents want to spend significantly more, compared with 23.4% in Boatsetter’s 2025 survey. For hospitality brands, the practical opportunity lies in helping guests discover and book experiences, from guided excursions to activities with local operators.

The pull toward the outdoors extends beyond water activities. Hilton’s 2026 Trends Report, based on a survey of 14,009 adults in 13 countries who plan to travel in the next 12 months, found that rest and recharging is the top motivation for leisure travel, cited by 56% of respondents. Spending time in nature was also among their top desires, with 37% citing it as such. Both findings point to demand for experiences that help travelers step away from routine.

Great Outdoor Shift 2.0 explores three questions for travel and hospitality leaders:

Taken together, the findings point to a role for travel companies that goes beyond providing a view of nature. In 2027, hotels, tourism boards, and travel partners can make shared outdoor activities easier to access through local partnerships, clearer booking options, and experiences suited to different interests. The opportunity is to help guests follow through on the time they already say they want outdoors.

“We’ve known the desire to get outside is there. What’s changing is that people are acting on it, and they expect technology to help, not get in the way. Our job is to make the outdoor experiences they want easy to reach,” Farb said.

#6083. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.
